title: Artificial Intelligence (Connecticut Commission for Educational Technology)
full_text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Commission Home
<<
Initiatives
Artificial Intelligence (AI)
1: Introduction
Artificial intelligence (AI)， machine learning， and general algorithmic tools have played a role in teaching and learning for decades， albeit generally an invisible one. From tools that students engage with to deepen and personalize learning to organizational and decision-support systems that teachers and administrators leverage， technology has become ubiquitous in all aspects of learning.
More recently， AI tools have taken on a prominent role in discussions concerning the future of education， for several important reasons:
Access: The public — including students， teachers， and parents — now have easy access to tools that leverage AI， such as ChatGPT from OpenAI， Claude from Anthropic， and other forms of large language models (LLMs). Such applications have enabled anyone to use and understand the power of AI for learning and many other aspects of life.
Integration: In addition to obvious uses of AI， such as standalone tools， software for general and educational use now has AI components that speed and personalize user experiences and inform decision making.
Acceleration: Unprecedented investments in AI and the rapid acceleration of new forms of these tools have spurred a sense of urgency to understand and apply them thoughtfully to teaching and learning.
Now more than ever， innovations in technology remain critical to education as both enablers as well as sources of potential risk. This set of guidance and resources should help to equip educators， leaders， and anyone engaged in the education community to learn more about AI and its role in education， explore and implement approaches to safe and effective integration， and establish consistent frameworks for ongoing innovation and decision-making. This work should continue as new technologies emerge with different potential roles within and risks to teaching and learning. Toward that end， the Commission sees as a common goal that all students would have a baseline understanding of AI in the context of broader digital literacy， a core component of any “portrait of the graduate” in preparation for college and careers.
2: Types and Applications
The term “AI” appears broadly in conversations about emerging technology， often with little context. Use cases can include the generative AI serving as an “assistant” with student writing， all the way to automated robotic systems. As noted above， AI remains a broad and rapidly accelerating area of research and applications. To ground this set of guidance and resources， the following categories of AI may be helpful:
Automated Planning and Scheduling
Computer Vision
Knowledge-Based Systems
Machine Learning
Natural Language Processing
Robotics
For a more detailed schematic of AI definitions and types， see
page 15
of the US Department of Education’s Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning， referencing the work of
Regona et al
. The Center for Integrative Research in Computing and Learning Sciences (CIRCLS) has an excellent and often-updated
Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators
.
In the context of education， especially K - 12 education， AI already has a place in the following arenas (listed alphabetically):
Accessibility and Student Accommodation
Assessment and Reporting
Classroom Instruction
Decision-Support Systems
Facility Management
Finance
Human Resources and Recruitment
Operational Systems
Professional Development
Strategic Planning
Student Services (Special Education)
Teacher Evaluation
Technology Management
3: Instructional and Decision-Making Best Practices
The marketplace of educational tools that leverage AI continues to expand. As individual teachers and leadership teams consider the use of AI-powered apps， the following best practices in software use may provide assistance.
Platform Selection: Use of any software to support student learning or school operations should follow the same， repeatable processes. A set of stakeholders should identify the need (e.g.， increase numeracy skills among fourth-grade students) and consider any shortcomings in the tools and approaches currently in use to address that need. With those specific objectives documented， peer recommendations and research can bring to light potential applications that educators may wish to adopt at the classroom， school， or district level.
Privacy and Data Collection: As part of the selection process and in ongoing use， schools should assess the breadth and type of data that AI-powered tools collect. Public schools must adhere to Connecticut’s data privacy laws， with guidance on doing so available through the
Commission’s Student Data Privacy Web page
. The
Connecticut Educational Software Hub
， powered by LearnPlatform， offers details on thousands of instructional apps to assist with this process.
Training and Support: Teachers will need a baseline understanding of AI technology and how it applies to their particular subject area and grade levels. This professional development applies to the use of AI tools for instruction， planning， and other activities as well as how to model and support effective use by teachers. See the training resources below for ways to begin supporting educators and leaders in the use of AI.
Community Engagement and Input: Many parents and other stakeholders are learning about AI in their personal and professional lives and may have questions about its use in their children’s schools. Leaders may consider forming an advisory around the use of technology generally and AI tools specifically to encourage a culture of learning and transparency， as well as to tap the expertise that community experts may offer. The ILO Group has sound guidance on community engagement in its
Artificial Intelligence Framework for District Leaders
.
Incident Reporting: Considering appropriate and ethical use of AI tools， schools should consider broadening existing incident-reporting protocols to include misuse of technology. For example， AI tools can be used to create so-called “deep fakes，” highly realistic but unauthorized images， audio， or other content.
4: Risks
The above best practices point to a number of potential risks when teachers and school leaders leverage AI-powered tools:
Bias: Machine learning systems improve through the process of interpreting and making predictions off of data sets. For example， a decision-support system may look at inputs such as grades， attendance， and discipline history and predict at-risk students. But the “training” data sets used to hone such tools may have bias incorporated into them. In the above case， human teachers may have been more inclined to discipline students in specific subgroups， leading to increased frequency of detentions， etc. A computer will look at these trends and “predict” that all students in that subgroup are more likely “at risk.” The same goes for the formulas or algorithms that run such systems. They may look at hiring trends， for example， for certain jobs and conclude that specific genders or life experiences make candidates more qualified， even if the existing employee set has been chosen through human bias toward one group or another. Generally， AI does not impose lenses of equity and inclusion on the systems we use.
>>
Steps to Consider: Especially for high-stakes systems that manage large swaths of student or sensitive employee data， and which leaders use to make decisions about instruction， advancement， etc.， districts should engage with providers of such systems to get additional details on training data and algorithms. Educational software developers should already be attuned to these issues and be prepared to address ethical considerations such as bias in the development of their products.
Inaccuracy: The concept of a “human in the middle” is essential in using AI-powered software. Such tools are extremely good at predicting the logical sequence of words， numbers， or code， but at the time of this writing are still not “sentient” and capable of interpreting results through a human-like lens. The content that systems collect and use as the basis for predictions include accurate as well as inaccurate writing， calculations， etc. To use the concept of “quality control，” a certain amount of inaccurate or even harmful and biased content inevitably becomes part of the data on which AI systems function.
>>
Steps to Consider: Always interpret AI-driven results， content， and recommendations with discernment. They can accelerate and inform decision-making and content creation， but they can also include errors.
Intellectual Property and Plagiarism: One of the most common use cases in schools today on the use of AI is students using tools to write papers， complete math homework， or code projects for computer science or data analytics courses. Current AI tools are quite good at this work， and the temptation can be strong to use shortcuts in this regard.
>>
Steps to Consider: Equip teachers with relevant and timely professional development to understand how current AI tools can be used appropriately for designing prompts and interpreting results. Educators should in turn model effective and responsible use of such tools. Engaging in a “dialog” with a large language model， for example， may help students identify errors in their work or hone language for an essay. They will use these tools in their future education and work lives， and schools should model effective use starting now.
Legal: Closely tied to the points above regarding intellectual property and plagiarism， use of AI tools still falls under existing legal frameworks concerning the misappropriation and misuse of content. At the time of this writing， Connecticut had considered but not yet put in place specific laws concerning issues such as the creation of likenesses (see
CT House Bill 24-5421
， “An Act Concerning Unlawful Dissemination of Intimate Images That Are Digitally Altered or Created through the Use of Artificial Intelligence”). During the 2024 legislative session， the General Assembly did put in place provisions for a pilot of “AI tools” in a limited number of schools as well as a call for teacher professional development (see
Public Act 24-151
).
>>
Steps to Consider: Misuse of any type of content still falls under existing statute， so maintaining a solid understanding of existing general school law will help leaders frame current and future considerations regarding the legal ramifications of unlawful creation and dissemination of content.
Social and Emotional: The above example of “deep fake” image creation has already had significantly damaging impacts， especially on female students. The rapid acceleration of AI capabilities points to the likely increase and complexity of issues concerning student access to harmful digital content. Even less damaging scenarios may further isolate young people and negatively impact emotional well-being. The trajectory of digital “companions” is steep， with people of all ages already engaged in chatting with AI-powered bots that simulate behaviors of human companionship. Increased use of such tools may further isolate students， taking the place of authentic relationships.
>>
Steps to Consider: For those leading efforts to support the social and emotional wellbeing of students， become familiar with common AI tools and potential applications. This work can take place through existing professional development in this area， leveraging the resources provided from the
Connecticut State Department of Education’s SEL page
. Honest discussions with and support of students addressing the use of these tools will help identify and address potential risks of new technologies that leverage AI.
Equity of Access: The enormous potential of AI tools to accelerate and personalize learning also comes with a potential to broaden existing digital divides. Students with computers and home broadband connections， as well as strong teacher support to model AI tools， will have an opportunity to learn how to use such apps effectively. In the same vein， learners without access to technology will fall farther behind in understanding and mastering the use of emerging tools.
>>
Steps to Consider: State and school leaders have taken great strides， especially during the COVID-19 pandemic， to ensure equitable access to technology for all students. Laptop programs where students have a computer to take home are nearly ubiquitous at higher grade levels， and leaders should commit to establishing and maintaining such programs. Schools should assess student access to broadband at home as well， a relatively easy exercise by assessing student online activities after hours (e.g.， submission of homework). All major Internet carriers offer low-cost Internet options that schools can promote to disconnected families， and many districts address short- and long-term connectivity issues by offering cellular hotspots for student use or partnering with local Internet service providers to offer volume purchasing. The Commission is actively leading statewide efforts in this area， addressing the needs of residents broadly， through its
Digital Equity Program
.
5: Policy and Guidance
Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies often disrupt education environments and school climates. Each of the above risks provides an opportunity to learn， grow， and address the needs of students and staff.
In this regard， the creation of new school policies that address specific technologies can prove inefficient and burdensome to maintain. District administrators and school board members should consider whether AI truly “breaks'' existing policy (that is， requires separate and new guidance)， or whether existing frameworks can adapt to and address emerging technologies. Ways of addressing plagiarism and cheating， harassment， bullying， and data privacy should remain consistent， even if new technologies may introduce new challenges of understanding and application.
The Commission has encouraged school boards to consider language that encourages responsible use of technology in its policy manuals (see
Policy Guidance to Promote Digital Learning
). Other benchmarks to consider， both within the K - 12 environment and more generally， include the following:
Connecticut Association of Boards of Education (CABE)
Policy Manual
， including its
Generative AI Policy
.
Federal
legislation and guidance
governing educational technology and student privacy (CIPA， COPPA， FERPA， and IDEA).
State statute regarding artificial intelligence:
Public Act 24-151
calls for the Connecticut State Department of Education (CSDE) to create of ”an artificial intelligence education tool pilot program” by the end of the 2024 – 25 school year (see
Section 143
) to include professional development for educators (see
Section 144
). That same law calls on the CSDE in collaboration with the Connecticut Commission for Educational Technology to create a model digital citizenship curriculum for K–12 students (see
Section 145
).
State statute governing student data privacy (
CGS §§ 10-234aa-dd
) and the Commission’s
resource page
on the topic.
Connecticut Office of Policy and Management (OPM)
policies addressing technology
， including a
policy framework on Artificial Intelligence
White House
Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
.

INTRODUCTION
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Office of the State Superintendent of Education (OSSE)， as the District of
Columbia’s state education agency， seeks to support DC local education agencies
(LEAs) as they navigate the opportunities and risks presented by the evolving Artificial
Intelligence (AI) landscape. AI can be a powerful tool when leveraged securely，
ethically， and appropriately. Appropriate AI use augments human expertise; it does
not replace it.
Generative AI can create content and perform tasks based on user prompts. It is
increasingly showing up in the experience of students and teachers in the classroom
in the District of Columbia and across the country. While new technologies have
contributed to innovations in education， they can create additional risks， especially
in the areas of student safety and privacy. Intentional policies and guidance can
help mitigate the risks of AI use. Meanwhile the growing capabilities of AI can offer
meaningful opportunities to enhance administrator， staff， and educator capacity and
student experiences.
OSSE conducted a LEA AI survey in February 2026 to gather insight into usage and
the need for additional support. The findings from 39 unique LEA respondents
indicated that less than half of LEAs have created AI guidance， and the most
useful support OSSE could provide would be a recommended model AI policy for
instructional use.
The enclosed Model AI Policy is intended to support LEAs as they develop locally
informed policies that support the safe， ethical， and appropriate use of AI by staff.
The Model AI Policy is designed to be customizable. LEAs may adopt the sections and
language that best meet their needs and are encouraged to tailor this content to their
school community’s culture， strengths， and goals.
AI capabilities， regulations， and best practices are evolving rapidly. Local AI policies
may need to be reviewed regularly and updated as new information becomes
available. OSSE will review the model policy regularly， and sections may be improved
upon and added to as evidence and technology continues to advance.
The model policy is intended as guidance only and not as legal advice. LEAs should
consult their own counsel for any legal advice when drafting their own AI policy.
3 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
GUIDING PRINCIPLES FOR DEVELOPING AI POLICY
Clear guidance for the responsible use of AI policy does not just outline acceptable use policies for users around AI
but also provides a structured approach for engaging with AI across contexts. The following Guiding Principles serve as
important considerations for developing an organizational Artificial Intelligence (AI) policy. They are intended to support
the creation of clear， responsible， and effective best practices for responsible AI integration across contexts.
• Maintain meaningful human decision-making. AI is fallible and can produce incorrect information or unintended
consequences. Human review of any output produced by AI is essential to its implementation.
• Collaborate with your community， drafting with， not for， them. Diversity of perspectives from community
stakeholders serves a two-fold purpose. First， stakeholder input strengthens the policy， ensuring that what is drafted
reflects the expressed needs and concerns of the community. Second， co-developed policies guarantee stronger
buy-in. Continuing to engage with stakeholders after policies are implemented helps monitor their effectiveness and
supports making revisions as needed， which strengthens overall implementation.
• Prioritize building trust through transparency and proactive communication. Clear communication about when and
how AI is used within educational and administrative settings helps maintain trust across staff， students， and families.
Clearly communicating AI policy to all stakeholders within school communities is essential for building trust through
transparency. Educational institutions have a responsibility to ensure all caregivers and stakeholders understand the
ways in which AI is being used. Educational institutions have a key role in creating clear avenues for caregivers and
stakeholders to share feedback with decision-makers about the use of AI.
• Focus the AI policy on existing institutional values and mission and define additional AI-specific values as needed.
Grounding an AI policy in existing institutional values helps ensure alignment with the school’s mission and purpose.
When evaluating AI tools， keeping institutional values at the forefront of evaluation processes ensures tool use does
not run counter to those values.
• Deploy specific AI tools only to meet specific， identified needs. Evaluating an AI tool and determining its acceptable
use(s) prior to authorizing staff access aligns with evidence-based best practices. Although AI tools can enhance
efficiency， they may not be appropriate for all identified needs.
• Provide training and opportunities to practice for LEA staff. Training staff in the safe， ethical and appropriate use
of AI prior to allowing them to use AI tools in educational contexts is a fundamental component of any AI policy.
Effective training for staff includes methods for using AI effectively and securely， as well as approaches for critically
assessing AI outputs for accuracy and equity.
• AI is not a replacement for research-based best practices. To-date， studies finding discernible positive impact
of AI on K-12 student learning are extremely limited in nature， as demonstrated in the Stanford SCALE Initiative’s
“The Evidence Base on AI in K-12: A 2026 Review.” LEAs interested in using AI may use it to supplement， not
replace， the critical factors that are improving our education system in DC: strategic and supportive leaders， well-
trained teachers， high-quality instructional materials， small-group interventions， and access to high-quality early
childhood experiences and career pathways that bracket the student experience.
• Regularly reassess AI policies. AI capabilities are evolving rapidly. Routinely reviewing approved use cases，
monitoring outcomes， evaluating effectiveness， and updating policies accordingly help ensure policies do not
become obsolete as new technologies and research findings are made available.
4 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
LEGAL CONSIDERATIONS
The enclosed Model AI Policy for Staff Use focuses on LEA implementation of AI and how staff should engage with AI.
The enclosed Model AI Policy for Staff Use does not carry the force and effect of District law or regulation， and no LEA
or school is required to follow or adopt the policies contained within this document. The Model AI Policy for Staff Use
should not be viewed as having any legal effect as it is not intended to be OSSE policy， law or regulation. Please note，
OSSE does not provide incident response or legal advice related to AI use in LEAs or schools. The adoption of any LEA AI
Policy for Staff Use should be implemented after careful consideration and review of the following， but not limited to:
1. Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)ii 5. Protecting Students Digital Privacy Act of 2016vi
2. Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA)iii 6. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability
Act (HIPAA)vii
3. Children’s Internet Protection Act (CIPA)iv
4. Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA)v
This model policy is not intended to have any legal effect or should not be viewed as having any legal effect as it is
not intended to be OSSE policy， law or regulation. OSSE recommends LEAs seek advice from their counsel before
adopting an AI Policy for Staff Use.

The Model AI Policy for Staff Use does not address student AI usage or application. LEAs may consider developing
companion guidance for appropriate student use， procurement， professional learning， and family communication.

Monitoring or Surveilling Staffs’ and Students’ Physical Presence and Behavior
The use of AI for the purpose of monitoring or surveilling staffs’ and students’ physical presence and behavior includes
tracking staffs’ and students’ physical presence within [replace with LEA name]， allowing AI to access CCTV footage
captured by [replace with LEA name] security systems， and use of biometric data for any monitoring purposes. This
includes the use of personal AI-enabled recording tools such as wearables while on [replace with LEA name] premises.
STAFF AI USE NOT PERMITTED
No AI tools may be used for this purpose. Unauthorized AI features of existing enterprise tools are
prohibited.
Rationale: Tools that monitor or surveil staff and students raise significant privacy concerns and AI tools may
cause discriminatory outcomes. There is insufficient evidence about if and how AI tools can be used safely for this
purpose.
Educational Trajectory Decision Making
The use of AI for Educational Trajectory Decision Making includes unilaterally selecting students’ courses， including
determinations for advanced or remedial course enrollment， grade promotion， placement， recommendation for
academic intervention， recommendation for Career and Technical Education Pathways， program eligibility， college
readiness， readiness for an Advanced Placement (AP) or International Baccalaureate (IB) course， or enrollment in
selective programs. In addition， AI should not make final decisions regarding within-class ability-based groups (e.g.，
leveled reading groups). Educational Trajectory does not encompass the use of AI for analysis of placement trends within
[replace with LEA name].
STAFF AI USE NOT PERMITTED
No AI tools may be used for this purpose. Unauthorized AI features of existing enterprise tools are
prohibited.
Rationale: AI should not be used to make final decisions about students’ futures or abilities because AI lacks the
expertise and context humans provide. Additionally， AI tools can cause discriminatory placement decisions.
Student Discipline Decisions
The use of AI for the purpose of administering student disciplinary consequences includes decisions about exclusion
from school or school activities， eligibility for inclusion in Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) or similar
programs， next steps in response to student behavior， or when to contact caregivers. This includes leveraging AI to
determine individual discipline risk or using predictive behavioral analytics that may subject individual students to higher
levels of school scrutiny.
STAFF AI USE NOT PERMITTED
No AI tools may be used for this purpose. Unauthorized AI features of existing enterprise tools are
prohibited.
Rationale: AI should not be used to make discipline decisions in any context because they lack the expertise and
context humans provide. Utilizing AI in this context presents a risk of discriminatory outcomes. LEA staff should
follow existing policies regarding student discipline.
10 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
Evaluating Teacher and Staff Performance
The use of AI for the purpose of determining teacher performance ratings includes conducting formal and informal
evaluations to quantify the effectiveness of instructional staff， including (but not limited to) classroom observations，
evaluation of lesson materials and instructional artifacts， evaluation of subject matter knowledge， and evaluation of
classroom management. Teacher evaluation further includes any decisions related to course assignment， teacher pay or
teacher retention decisions. The prohibitions in this policy refer to AI making evaluative judgments and ratings， not to the
organization of evidence or the use of AI for administrative tasks.
STAFF AI USE NOT PERMITTED
No AI tools may be used for this purpose. Unauthorized AI features of existing enterprise tools are prohibited.
Rationale: Teacher evaluations involve high-stakes observations and decisions that require data and human
judgement. Final evaluations for teachers should not be completed by AI. Evaluations have high stakes for
administrators and teachers; therefore， an activity should be done by trained humans.
Providing Health， Mental Health， and Social Services
The use of AI for the purpose of providing health， mental health， and social services includes diagnosis， treatment， or
clinical decision-making activities. This section includes tools to assess， screen， or diagnose student health conditions
and mental health conditions (including depression， anxiety， and suicide risk)， as well as tools to conduct basic needs
assessment for student or household unmet needs， such as food and housing. In addition， this includes health behavior
tracking and health behavior modification for behavioral health (including substance use)， health risk behaviors， and
healthy habits.
STAFF AI USE NOT PERMITTED
No AI tools may be used for this purpose. Unauthorized AI features of existing enterprise tools are prohibited.
Rationale: Responding to student health needs requires human expertise and decision making， AI tools should
not be used to provide health services. AI may not replace crisis response protocols or mandated reporting
responsibilities.
Individualized Education Program (IEP) and Section 504 Evaluations
This prohibition includes using AI to analyze or recommend diagnostic assessments or make determinations about
educational placement， least restrictive environment， or disability or service eligibility. Staff shall not use AI to evaluate
or determine student eligibility for special education and related services under IDEA or Section 504 of the Rehabilitation
Act of 1973.
STAFF AI USE NOT PERMITTED
No AI tools may be used for this purpose. Unauthorized AI features of existing enterprise tools are prohibited.
Rationale: Determining eligibility for an IEP or Section 504 accommodation are high stakes that requires
human expertise and decision making. Utilizing AI in this context presents a risk of discriminatory or inaccurate
outcomes.
11 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
YELLOW: LIMITED STAFF AI USE PERMITTED:
PROCEED WITH ENHANCED OVERSIGHT
AI can support the following activities; however， additional oversight steps are put into place to ensure that the use of
AI for this purpose remains secure， ethical， and appropriate. For any use case involving PII， only enterprise tools that
comply with all local and federal laws and regulations about student information can be used. Usage for these purposes
is subject to continual evaluation and will be revised regularly.
For each use case below， the “Limited Use Requirements” outline additional regulations in place staff must follow when
using AI for these purposes.
Monitoring or Surveilling Staffs’ and Students’ Digital Presence
The use of AI for the purpose of monitoring or surveilling staffs’ and students’ digital presence includes monitoring or
surveilling online activity of staff and students while on [replace with LEA name] premises or utilizing devices provided
by [replace with LEA name].
LIMITED STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH ENHANCED OVERSIGHT
LIMITED USE REQUIREMENTS:
x [Designated Staff Member] may utilize approved AI tools to assist with monitoring staffs’ and students’ digital
activity while on LEA premises and during operating hours.
x AI surveillance is not a substitute for educator monitoring of student use of classroom devices or staff judgement
about student wellbeing.
x Discipline decisions should never rely on data gathered by AI alone; all detected risks and misuse reports will be
elevated to [Designated Staff Member] who will then follow [replace with LEA names] established discipline，
safety， and mental health policies.
x Staff must keep data on AI surveillance use and continually monitor for equity and efficacy of use.
x Staff， students， and families will be notified about the tools and purposes for AI use in virtual surveillance， including
which tools are being deployed， why they are being utilized， and what data is collected while monitoring a
student’s virtual activity.
Rationale: Schools already monitor student online activity to remain in compliance with CIPA， and acceptable
use policies preclude the expectation of privacy on [replace with LEA name] issued devices. Tools that scan
for signs of cyberbullying and mental health crises can supplement systems already in place to alert staff and
families to risks students face in digital spaces. However， these tools may carry significant privacy risks. All virtual
surveillance uses must comply with existing regulations around staff and student privacy， discipline and legal
requirements for surveillance and data collection.
12 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
Drafting Individualized Education Programs (IEPs)
The use of AI for the purpose of writing IEPs includes generating ideas and/ or objectives for IEP goals or generating
recommendations for accommodations connected to IEP goals. IEP development does not include recommendations
about placement disability category or eligibility.
LIMITED STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH ENHANCED OVERSIGHT
LIMITED USE REQUIREMENTS:
x AI may be used to review or identify trends amongst IEPs in order to improve practices.
x For any use case involving PII， only enterprise tools that comply with all regulations and best practices about
student information can be used.
x AI may support staff member organization and summary of notes collected as part of the IEP process.
x AI may be used to brainstorm ideas for objectives or accommodations connected to a student’s present levels.
x Staff must provide transparency to students and families about where and how AI is used in the IEP drafting
process.
x All AI outputs should be considered advisory only， and staff must utilize professional judgment when evaluating AI
generated accommodations.
x AI use must always ensure plans remain individualized.
x All staff must comply with best practices for IEP development.2
x Use of AI may never violate student protections provided under IDEA.
x AI-supported drafting must never compromise individualized planning or meaningful participation by families and
IEP teams.
Rationale: AI tools can be used to support educators in moving through some parts of the IEP process more
efficiently. However， final determinations must always be made by a human.
2 Special Education Process Handbook
13 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
Reviewing and Grading Student Work
The use of AI for the purpose of reviewing and grading student work includes generating rubrics to evaluate activities
and providing formative feedback on student assignments in which the feedback is generated outside of class time. This
section does not address use of AI for real time student facing feedback. This section does not address the use of AI for
student-facing purposes (i.e.， chat bots or feedback given in real time).
LIMITED STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH ENHANCED OVERSIGHT
LIMITED USE REQUIREMENTS:
x Educators may provide feedback for formative assessments utilizing AI， if utilizing AI allows for feedback to be
given more frequently and rigorously than standard grading methods.
x Educators must be transparent with prompts given to the AI for evaluating student work and about training data
leveraged for AI grading. When returning AI-graded work for students， educators must include the text of prompt
provided to the AI tool for evaluating student work.
x Staff must ensure student identifying data including race and ethnicity are not disclosed to the AI tool， and all
outputs must be evaluated to ensure equity in feedback， rigor， and expectations for all students. Best practices
include setting narrow parameters for AI feedback.
x Educators are responsible for all summative grading decisions.
x Educators must allow students to appeal to any AI grade pursuant to [replace with LEA name] Academic Handbook
and students may ask for a human to provide additional feedback.
x AI may identify trends across student work and generate summaries.
Rationale: AI tools can support educators in grading more efficiently to provide targeted feedback more
frequently. However， getting thoughtful feedback through grading is a significant part of the learning process
and should not rely solely on AI. Further， educators must set careful parameters around feedback provided
by AI to ensure all students receive equitably rigorous feedback and that AI applies consistent standards for
outcomes regardless of student demographic data. Educators must consistently evaluate feedback for equity and
consistency across students.
Providing Supplemental Coaching to Teachers and Staff
The use of AI to provide coaching to teachers includes providing supplemental feedback to educators around
instructional practices outside of existing coaching programs.
LIMITED STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH ENHANCED OVERSIGHT
LIMITED USE REQUIREMENTS:
x AI use for coaching may supplement but not supplant human-centered coaching and instructional relationships.
Staff may use AI tools to provide supplemental coaching to educators.
x All feedback must comply with best practices for teaching and learning， as well as best practices for improving
educator practice.3
x AI use for this purpose must be continually monitored for equity， utility， and rigor.
x For any use case involving PII， only enterprise tools that comply with all regulations and best practices about
student information may be used.
x Staff may opt out of AI use for coaching.
x It is not best practice to use AI to evaluate student management practices.
Rationale: AI tools offer promise to provide teachers with more coaching and feedback than they would
otherwise receive and can be used to supplement existing feedback routines. AI tools can also allow coaches
to more efficiently organize notes and data. However， AI lacks individual context for decision making and may
provide inequitable feedback to educators across contexts.
3 Walkthrough Tools
• OSSE Math Walkthrough Tool
• OSSE Literacy Walkthrough Tool
• Social Studies Walkthrough Tool
14 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
GREEN: STAFF AI USE PERMITTED:
PROCEED WITH AWARENESS
AI is well-positioned to support these activities. Nonetheless， appropriate oversight (a human in the loop) must always be
in place to ensure that AI usage remains secure， ethical， and appropriate. In all cases， staff are responsible for developing
final outcomes， and AI outputs must be used with human oversight and analysis. AI use is subject to continual evaluation
around outcomes and will be revised yearly. For any use case involving PII， only enterprise tools that comply with all
regulations and best practices about student information can be used.
For each use case below， the “Use Considerations” outline additional safeguards users must be cognizant of when they
are leveraging AI for the purposes outlined below.
Use of AI should never replace educator professional judgment， and all staff remain professionally accountable for
student safety and development.
Drafting Lesson Plans
The use of AI to draft lesson plans includes generating central lesson questions， curating source material for use with
students， generating ideas for standards aligned learning experiences， developing scaffolds for existing lesson plans， and
generating student facing prompts and graphic organizers.
STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH AWARENESS
USE CONSIDERATIONS:
x AI may support educators in preparing and customizing lesson plans， provided it does not make recommendations
for individual students and the educator reviews and refines any AI-generated suggestions.
x Educators must evaluate all AI suggestions for accuracy.
x Educators and staff members may not use AI for this purpose until they have completed training that includes
evaluating AI outputs and assessing equity concerns in AI-generated lesson material.
x Educators must carefully evaluate AI-generated lessons for equity and rigor and ensure all lesson materials
comply with best practices for teaching and learning， including the relevant appropriate High-Quality Instructional
Materials guidance and the standards of learning.
x Staff must evaluate output to ensure they are culturally relevant and appropriate.
x All AI-produced lesson plans and ideas must be evaluated for accuracy.
x Lesson plans should always be developed without utilizing prompts that invite an AI tool to consider student
demographic information. Staff must provide transparency to students when AI is used to generate student-facing
instructional resources.
Rationale: Educators can use AI to improve lesson plans without sharing PII or relying on AI for final decision-
making. AI is not a substitute for strong pedagogical content knowledge， or instructional expertise， and school
leaders should ensure staff use of AI to develop lesson plans does not impede the development of professional
knowledge and judgment. Additional support should be provided to educators who demonstrate emerging
professional knowledge.
15 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
Developing Tutoring or Individualized Learning Plans
The use of AI for the purpose of developing tutoring or individualized learning plans includes staff leveraging AI tools to
generate tutoring plans and assignments or evaluate student data. The policy below does not cover student use of AI
technology during tutoring.
STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH AWARENESS
USE CONSIDERATIONS:
x Staff members may utilize AI tools to generate tutoring plans or develop questions and prompts to use with
students.
x Tutoring plans generated by AI must be aligned to approved curriculum and instructional materials.
x Staff members may use AI to generate practice prompts and assignments.
x Staff may not use AI to determine a student’s eligibility for tutoring or placement in a tutoring program.
x Staff members may use AI for real-time coaching and personalized support to deepen content knowledge， support
tutoring skills and improve instruction.
x AI may identify trends across student work and generate summaries.
x AI generated plans and assignments must always be evaluated for equity and rigor.
Rationale: AI tools offer opportunities for staff to individualize student learning. However， these tools can produce
assignments that hold students to inequitable standards for learning and lead to discriminatory outcomes. AI
tools must only be used with careful oversight and monitoring with frequent routines for evaluating their value.
Customizing Student-Facing Lesson Materials
The use of AI for customizing student-facing lesson materials include developing graphic organizers， scaffolded or
modified reading materials， modifying assessments and assignments， and otherwise using differentiated instructional
materials.
STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH AWARENESS
USE CONSIDERATIONS:
x AI may support educators in developing differentiated and customized student-facing materials if it does not make
recommendations for individual students or if it does not utilize PII and the educator reviews and refine the AI-
generated suggestions.
x Educators must carefully evaluate AI-generated materials for equity and rigor and ensure all lesson materials
comply with best practices for teaching and learning.
x Staff must evaluate output to ensure they are culturally relevant and appropriate.
x Materials should always be reviewed for accessibility， alignment with Universal Design for Learning (UDL)
principles4， and readability.
x Lesson plans should always be developed without utilizing prompts that invite an AI tool to consider student
demographic information.
Rationale: AI can assist educators in providing better student-facing lesson materials that are customized to meet
students learning needs， and AI is especially well suited for adjusting text complexity or adjusting formatting for
accessibility in materials.
4 For additional resources about Universal Design for Learning visit the CAST webpage.
16 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year
Analyzing Data Sets
The use of AI for analyzing data sets includes using AI tools to evaluate student outcomes to identify trends and patterns
across classes， schools， and outcomes for students. This section includes leveraging AI monitoring to evaluate trends in
Educational Technology across an LEA’s， classrooms and schools.
STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH AWARENESS
USE CONSIDERATIONS:
x Educators and school staff can use AI tools to conduct analysis of student data sets.
x For any use case involving PII， only enterprise tools that comply with all regulations and best practices about
student information may be used.
x Data analysis can inform programmatic or structural decisions; however， such analysis should not be the sole factor
in decisions regarding individual students.
x AI-generated analysis should be reviewed for unintended bias or disparate impact across student groups.
Rationale: Educators can use AI to analyze and identify trends in student data to tailor their instruction and meet
the needs of all students. LEAs can leverage AI to identify patterns of discriminatory or effective outcomes to
better analyze which practices and procedures increase student engagement， success， and outcomes.
School Communications
The use of AI for school communications includes communicating with parents， creating marketing campaigns， drafting
policy reports， developing board reports， creating meeting summaries， or editing any communications.
STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH AWARENESS
USE CONSIDERATIONS:
x Tools approved by [replace with LEA name] can be used in drafting， brainstorming， and developing school
communications.
Rationale: Utilizing AI tools can help schools communicate more effectively and efficiently with community
members and stakeholders. This use of AI is considered low risk to students and educational staff in this context.
Logistical Planning and Operations
The use of AI for logistical planning and operations include budgeting and budget analysis， creating master schedules，
supporting grant writing， drafting policy， creating meeting summaries， organizing notes and information， supporting
procurement planning， informing strategic planning， or creating menus for school meals.
STAFF AI USE PERMITTED: PROCEED WITH AWARENESS
USE CONSIDERATIONS:
x Tools approved by [replace with LEA name] can be used in drafting， brainstorming， and organizing to logistical
planning and operational tasks， as long as a human remains accountable for any final decisions.
Rationale: School operations take up a considerable amount of time and resources at school. Utilizing AI tools
can free up staff time， allowing them to focus more on instruction and direct support for students. This use of AI is
considered low risk to students and educational staff.
17 | Model LEA AI Policy for Staff Use | 2026-27 School Year

Acknowledgments
The Illinois State Board of Education (ISBE) extends its sincere appreciation to the “Blue Ribbon
Panel” of experts who generously shared their time， leadership， and expertise to assist with the
development of this statewide guidance for Illinois school districts and educators on the use of
artificial intelligence (AI) in elementary and secondary education.
This guidance was developed in response to Public Act 104-0399. In 2025， ISBE was charged
with “develop[ing] statewide guidance for school districts and educators on the use of artificial
intelligence in elementary and secondary education.” Public Act 104-0399 also makes clear
that the guidance should address how artificial intelligence may be used at the district， school，
and classroom levels to inform teaching and learning practices while preserving the human
relationships essential to effective teaching and learning.
That charge matters. The guidance is not organized around artificial intelligence as a technology
to be adopted for its own sake. It is organized around the enduring educational premise that
the teacher-student interaction is the centerpiece of teaching and learning. AI may assist with
planning， access， feedback， communication， operations， and resource development， but it must
remain a means to inform teaching and learning rather than a substitute for educator judgment，
student relationships， or the developmental and civic purposes of public schooling.
Informed use of AI in school settings is complex work. ISBE is grateful for working with and
learning from:
• Mr. Vilas Dhar， president and trustee of the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation， who brings a
public-purpose and civic-infrastructure lens to the use of artificial intelligence in the public
sector
• Dr. Rebecca Winthrop， director of the Center for Universal Education at the Brookings
Institution， whose work is grounded in deep expertise on students， learning， human
development， and education systems in an AI-shaped world
• Ms. Vicki Zubovic， chief external relations officer， and Mr. Jason Hovey， director of
school partnerships， at Khan Academy， whose experiences with educational technology
partnerships; large-scale AI-supported learning; and practical knowledge of district
partnerships， implementation， and school-system readiness provide an international，
national， and state set of perspectives
• Ms. Julia Wynn， senior director of state government affairs for CodeAI， who connects state
policy expertise in computer science， AI literacy， teacher preparation， and equitable student
access
• Mr. James Larimore， co-founder and chairperson of the EdSAFE AI Alliance， whose national
leadership in safe， effective， equitable， and trustworthy AI governance in education
provides insight from which to craft locally responsive policies that prioritize student
learning， well-being， and safety
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 2
• Mr. Bruce Reed， head of AI safety initiatives at Common Sense Media， and who previously
served as President Biden’s deputy White House chief of staff for policy where he led the
administration’s efforts on AI， adds expertise in AI safety， youth protection， family-facing
guidance， and public policy
• Dr. Joseph Fatheree， former Illinois Teacher of the Year and current Innovation Specialist at
Oak Ridge Schools， whose perspective as an educator and innovator attentive to cognition，
learning， classroom practice， and the human dimensions of AI further informs the importance
of “readiness，” writ large， tied to the nuances of AI use in teaching and learning
• Dr. Tina Halliman， 2026 Illinois Association of School Administrators South Cook Region
Superintendent of Distinction and superintendent of schools for SPEED Special Education
Cooperative District 802， whose work centers on student need， access， individualized
support， and the conditions necessary for all students to learn
• Dr. Tony Sanders， State Superintendent of Education， Illinois State Board of Education
• Dr. Jason Helfer， Special Advisor to the State Superintendent of Education， Illinois State
Board of Education
Illinois is very fortunate on account of the time， expertise， and care and tending in support
of guidance that prioritizes the teacher-student interaction while helping districts consider
informed AI use with care， purpose， and local judgment in light of student development as
individuals and citizens. Their contributions helped strengthen guidance that speaks to the
realities of AI use across district， school， and classroom settings while remaining anchored in
human relationships， professional judgment， student assets， developmental appropriateness，
equity， accessibility， privacy， safety， accountability， and civic responsibility. ISBE is grateful for
their willingness to share their experience and expertise in service of Illinois students， educators，
and school communities.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 3
Quick Start FAQ
This guidance was developed to provide an Illinois-specific frame for informed， context-sensitive， and
educationally grounded AI use. The guidance grows out of two Public Acts， including Public Act 104-
0399， which charged ISBE with developing statewide guidance on AI use in elementary and secondary
education. It is meant to help Illinois educators navigate both the uses and the limitations of AI in
prekindergarten through Grade 12 settings.
The Quick Start FAQ is organized around four guiding tenets:

Building upon these tenants， the purpose of the guidance is to serve as a resource for school districts
considering the variety of topics germane to the use of AI to inform teaching and learning.
The structure is intentional. Organizing the FAQ in this way is meant to assist readers in understanding
the scope of the document through considering the tenants framed in question form. Moreover， the
section(s) where a more robust explanation within the document is located is/are shared.
These tenants， threaded throughout the guidance， emphasize the centrality of the student-teacher
interactions as the ground from which all teaching and learning occur. Considerations of how and to
what extent AI adoption can augment this are contemplated through the need to develop common
understandings of purpose and use of the AI by those impacted by it， use cases， legal needs and
requirements， and suggestions for available resources that can be modified by school districts.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 4
Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon
the experiences， interests， and assets each child brings into school.
Question 1: What assumptions about teaching， learning， and the role of artificial intelligence underlie
this guidance?
Audience: Superintendent; principal; teacher; parent/caregiver; advocate/stakeholder group;
community
Answer: The guidance is grounded in the assumption that the centerpiece of teaching and learning
is the interactions between students and their teachers. Artificial intelligence can support aspects of
teaching and learning. Use of AI should be considered in light of how it can inform instructional planning
and delivery and enrich student engagement through its developmentally appropriate application within
acts of teaching and learning. It is not a substitute for professional judgment or a primary means of， or
for， student engagement.
Section(s): Welcome Letter; Start Here: How to Use This Guidance; AI for Teaching and Learning > Using
AI for Instructional Planning - Keeping Students at the Center
Question 2: How does the guidance address the role and importance of prompt development
for teacher use， including its use in the planning and delivery of instruction to enrich student
engagement?
Audience: Teacher; principal; central office administration
Answer: Just as clear language and directions are essential in teaching and learning without AI， strong
and clear prompts are more likely to provide instructionally aligned outputs. Thoughtful prompt design
is an important thread of professional learning for teachers as well as essential in the development of
digital citizenship for students.
Section(s): AI for Teaching and Learning > Developing Prompts Using AI for Instructional Planning
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 5
Question 3: How does the guidance address the role of AI in planning and delivery of instruction?
Audience: Teacher; principal; central office administration
Answer: The idea that AI can support planning and delivery while enhancing the human dimensions
of instruction underpins the document as a whole. The guidance distinguishes between AI as a means
in the planning and delivery of instruction and always in support of teaching and learning and how the
results generated through informed AI use are always in service of instruction.
Section(s): AI for Teaching and Learning > Taxonomy as a Lens for Instructional Planning; AI for Teaching
and Learning > Developing Prompts Using AI for Instructional Planning
Question 4: In what ways does the guidance emphasize how AI may enrich student experience?
Audience: Teacher; principal; student; parent/caregiver
Answer: Throughout the guidance， there is an emphasis on enriching student experience by centering
on forms of engagement (e.g.， between teacher and students， with AI applications， and the like)， and how
these engagements are central in the development of selfhood and as a citizen.
Section(s): AI for Teaching and Learning > Using AI for Instructional Planning - Keeping Students at the
Center; AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use of AI > Development
as an Individual and Citizen – An Ecological Framework
Question 5: What does the guidance suggest to minimize undue reliance on， or overconfidence in， AI?
Audience: Teacher; principal; student; parent/caregiver
Answer: The guidance emphasizes the importance of “trust but verify” when AI is used. Prior to any use
of AI， the purpose and use must be clearly identified by those impacted by the implementation. Doing
so also includes the identification of clear feedback loops to ensure goodness of fit of the AI for the
intended purpose and use.
Section(s): AI for Teaching and Learning > Using AI for Instructional Planning - Keeping Students at the
Center; Appendices > Appendix: Misalignment Scenarios and Prompt Quality Examples
Question 6: How does the guidance address the importance of differentiating student AI use by age
and/or grade level?
Audience: Teacher; principal; central office administration; parent/caregiver
Answer: As uniform approaches that are developmentally agnostic are more likely to lead to unintended
consequences when any educational technology is implemented， informed use of AI as a means to
inform the planning and delivery of instruction and enrich student experience must be predicated upon
developmentally appropriate practice. This guidance addresses this concern through the differentiation
of cases at the P-2， 3-5， 6-9， and 9-12 grade bands as well as frameworks that explicitly contemplate
human development and age-appropriate digital literacy and civic literacy.
Section(s): AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use of AI >
Development as a Student and Citizen - Cases by Grade Band > PreK–Grade 2; AI Literacy and Digital
Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use of AI > Development as a Student and Citizen -
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 6
by Grade Band > Grades 3–5; AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use
of AI > Development as a Student and Citizen - Cases by Grade Band > Grades 6–8; AI Literacy and Digital
Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use of AI > Development as a Student and Citizen - Cases
by Grade Band > Grades 9–12; AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed
Use of AI > Digital Citizenship and AI Literacy Curricula by Grade Band Center; Appendices > Appendix:
Misalignment Scenarios and Prompt Quality Examples
Question 7: How does the guidance keep the healthy development of young people at the center of
teaching and learning?
Audience: Superintendent; principal; teacher; parent/caregiver; advocate/stakeholder group
Answer: The guidance presents student well-being， development of agency (i.e.， a sense of self) and as
a participating member of society with obligations to others as core anchors for policy and classroom
decisions. Informed AI use as a means must be considered in light of how it supports the healthy
development of a child’s identity， competence， confidence， and as a citizen.
Section(s): AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use of AI >
Development as an Individual and Citizen – An Ecological Framework; AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship:
Healthy Development and Informed Use of AI > Development as a Student and Citizen - Cases by Grade
Band
Question 8: How does the guidance consider student social and emotional health and healthy
development in light of artificial intelligence within and outside of schooling?
Audience: Principal; teacher; central office administration; student; parent/caregiver
Answer: Within schooling， the guidance emphasizes that artificial intelligence should support identity
formation emerging from teacher-student interaction. Outside of schooling， it connects healthy
development to awareness of one’s responsibility as a citizen as well as and through acting in ways that
eliminate AI used for manipulation， bullying， and synthetic-media misuse.
Section(s): AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use of AI >
Development as an Individual and Citizen – An Ecological Framework; Appendices > Appendix: Student
Selfhood， Engagement， and Agency in AI-Mediated Schoolwork
Question 9: How does the guidance provide resources on AI literacy and digital citizenship for gifted
and talented students?
Audience: Teacher; principal; central office administration; parent/caregiver; advocate/stakeholder
group
Answer: The guidance addresses considerations of how the use of AI can serve to challenge the
perspectives of gifted and talented students in the creation and evaluation of work products， safeguards，
literacy needs， and instructional implications for students in enrichment programs and accelerated
learning opportunities.
Section(s): Equity， Accessibility， and Student Groups > Gifted and Talented (G/T); AI Resources， Tools，
and Decision Supports > Special Populations
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 7
Question 10: How does the guidance keep the healthy development of young people at the center of
teaching and learning?
Audience: Teacher; principal; central office administration; parent/caregiver; advocate/stakeholder
group
Answer: In addition to the information on AI literacy and digital citizenship for all student populations，
the guidance addresses students identified for special education services through emphasizing
the importance of adult oversight and student awareness of safeguards and the need to ensure that
appropriate differentiation approaches are aligned with the individual student need (e.g.， meeting the
specifics of an IEP/504 plan， integration with other assistive technologies， and the like).
Section(s): Equity， Accessibility， and Student Groups > High-Incidence Learning Disability; Equity，
Accessibility， and Student Groups > Twice exceptional (2e); AI Resources， Tools， and Decision Supports >
Special Populations
Question 11: What guidance is provided for the use of AI resources and， in particular， AI literacy and
digital citizenship for students receiving special education services?
Audience: Teacher; principal; central office administration; parent/caregiver; advocate/stakeholder
group
Answer: In addition to the information on AI literacy and digital citizenship for all student populations，
the guidance addresses students identified for special education services through emphasizing

The Emergence of AI and Illinois Context
Development of Artificial Intelligence
The development of artificial intelligence emerged in mid-20th century. Individuals such as Alan Turing
and John von Neumann each posed questions that considered the role of technologies (e.g.， learning
machines， early computers) in relationship to and different from human engagement in the world. These
questions and the responses to them at a given time both highlight and challenge how one understands
what it might mean to “be” intelligent， as well as issues of identity and autonomy. Initial work with AI in
the later part of the 20th and first quarter of the 21st century extend and complicate these questions.1
The nature and potential of the role(s) of AI use can be considered as interrelated constellations each at a
different level of magnification. International， national， state， and local considerations each contemplate
the various forms of AI， equity， ethics， and data security among others.2 As the considerations become
more local and context dependent， these broad concerns translate into sector-specific questions and of
which P-12 schooling is an example.3
For instance， within P-12 public schools， AI pervades spaces inhabited primarily by administrators，
teachers， students， parents and caregivers， community members， and advocates. The particulars of
decisions around and implementation of AI (e.g.， district policy or/and curated resources identified by
the district) are informed by laws at the federal and state level; regulations; discussions; and guidance
from state， national， and international work as filtered through the needs identified with district and
building leaders， teachers， students， parents and caregivers， community members， and advocates.
This intermingling both provides insight into specific comfort with AI (e.g.， the individual and collective
awareness of and familiarity with) tied to generated questions and the creation of subsequent emergent
lines of inquiry. This underscores the need for reliable， easily digestible， guidance and supporting
resources upon which local policies for AI are determined. Like any educational technology， AI can inform
and enrich teaching and learning. In this guidance， however， AI is treated explicitly as a means and not an
end. Even so， what this looks like within a classroom creates a need to reconsider concepts that serve as
means through which teaching and learning engagements occur.4
For instance， intricate questions of what constitutes creativity and hence， academic honesty or
academic integrity， become differently complex when AI affords the generation of a suite of possibilities
that the student can produce and (should) refine. This is in tension with instructional approaches to
engagement in which learning outcomes are often tied to the use of materials and mediums in the
generation of a creative output.
Relatedly， AI can shape development in ways that extend beyond a child’s role as a student. If， for
instance， students are not cognizant of the limitations of AI for a specific task (e.g.， the production of an
essay， poem， or artwork) or the norms of the discipline (e.g.， scientific writing， creative writing， 2D visual
art)， their sense of membership in practices (e.g.， authoring of written works and creation of visual art)
and ownership of developing expertise essential in the healthy development of a sense of self are likely
diminished.5 This point matters because public schooling serves both developmental and democratic
purposes. Children and young people come to know themselves not only through inward reflection
but also through interaction with other people， shared activity， and participation in social worlds
that shape judgment， belonging， and responsibility. In schools， students therefore learn more than
academic content alone. They also learn how to listen， respond， reflect， collaborate， weigh evidence， and
participate in practices governed by common expectations rather than by individual preference alone.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 31
In that sense， the development of selfhood and the development of democratic citizenship are closely
connected purposes of public education. The informed use of artificial intelligence should be considered
in light of those purposes: whether it supports student agency， competence， confidence， and access
while preserving the human relationships and judgment on which teaching， learning， and responsible
participation depend.
While AI can ease the administrative burden for some tasks， the core of teaching and learning—
responsive， relational work with individual students—is less “automatable.” AI can assist in lesson and unit
planning as well as assessment. Even so， high-quality feedback and instructional tailoring still depend on
knowing a student’s interests， readiness， and learning profile6 and the multiple opportunities for students
to show what they know and in ways that toggle between the student as an individual and as a member of
a larger classroom community. Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon
the experiences， interests， and assets each child brings into school.
Thus， to ensure that the informed use of AI is part of the fabric of professional learning for teachers， and
in ways that create the greatest likelihood that district personnel as well as the larger school community
see themselves as critical partners in decision-making， how districts communicate with those within
and outside the district to provide for the sharing and refining of ideas is critical.
Put differently， emergent technologies developed outside of schools can challenge and often reshape
teaching and learning practices.7 In some ways， adoption of AI parallels the incorporation of the
pencil， five-ring binder， or various audio-visual tools in previous decades. Communities need time and
opportunities to practice with any new technology in order to “get used to” it (e.g.， become aware of
and comfortable with its use in teaching and learning). There are obvious and substantive differences，
of course， between getting used to the incorporation of a pencil or binder in contrast to AI in terms of
student data privacy， cost， and a host of other issues. It is essential for district and building leaders to
deliberately plan for and provide multiple opportunities and means for the ”getting used to” through
feedback loops recognizing the multiple ways in which teachers， students， parents， caregivers， and other
community members bring experiences and expectations for purpose of and use for AI. Put differently，
informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally determined
purpose and use.8

For instance:
• How can teacher preparation and ongoing professional learning incorporate AI in ways that preserve—
and potentially strengthen—the student–teacher relationship that underpins learning?
• How and through what mechanisms can a district determine what AI could lighten the administrative
burden for classroom teachers?
• How can districts introduce expectations for AI in operational tasks (e.g.， attendance) and
instructional work (e.g.， planning and assessing student work) in ways that are clear， supported by
extent resource and sustainable over time， and aligned with teachers’ day-to-day responsibilities?

To add greater specificity， the trajectory of foci between 2015-2025 can be described as: cautious
interest in AI as an instructional innovation; growing recognition and targeted study of AI’s educational
uses; and today’s emphasis on data governance， bias， and the limits of AI in schools—particularly where
AI might supplement， but not supplant， educators’ work.
More particularly， perceptions between 2015-2025 may be described as shifting:
• District leaders: from minimal awareness to a governance focus (e.g.， use policies， staff professional
learning， and related systems)9
• School leaders: from minimal awareness to guidance on integrating AI into school operations，
pedagogy， and professional learning
• Teachers: from minimal awareness to cautious exploration and a need for sustained professional
learning for operational and instructional uses10
• Students: from general awareness and informal exposure (often outside school) to deeper familiarity
and use both in and out of school11
During the same period， parents’ and caregivers’ awareness and comfort with AI in schools may be
described as moving from little awareness of AI’s presence to cautious investigation and selective use to
support their child’s learning concurrent with concern about “AI overreach” inside and outside of school

As is expected whenever new technology is introduced in an educational setting， districts must balance
access outside school with responsible， appropriate classroom use. The tension is more than just if the
technology aids in instruction. It is inclusive of ensuring developmental appropriateness for using the
technology，13 ensuring students are adequately prepared to use the technology， and protecting student
privacy and data. Broadly， a central concern between “AI as opportunity，” “AI overreach，” and “Seduction

erode—students’ agency and the human relationships at the core of teaching and learning.14

Districts in Illinois， like their counterparts nationwide， are integrating AI into administrative and
instructional policies and practices while ensuring teachers and students understand the uses and
limitations of AI and that the larger school community is kept abreast of and can participate in sharing
ideas on the use of AI.
The guidance that follows is the result of two Public Acts. In 2024， the Illinois Department of Innovation
and Technology led a multiagency Generative AI and Natural Language Task Force (Public Act 103-0451).
The charge of this task force was “…to explore the opportunities， risks， and implications of [AI] for
[Illinois] and its residents.”
The report includes considerations of AI use in the delivery of services to residents of Illinois， impact of
AI on labor/workforce and the environment， among others. Of importance for educators in Illinois， the
report also includes information on the awareness of， familiarly with and emergent concern of AI use
in P-12 schools. In particular， survey data specific to P-12 schooling suggests that the ethical uses and
limitations of AI and AI Literacy for educators and students are areas in need of addressing.15
Building upon the recommendations of the Generative AI and Natural Language Task Force， in 2025，
the Illinois State Board of Education was charged with “…develop[ing] statewide guidance for school
districts and educators on the use of artificial intelligence in elementary and secondary education”
(Public Act 104-0399). This Public Act is the genesis for this guidance document.
The myriad of surveys and other data ascertaining use of and comfort with AI resources produced at
the national， state， and local levels， not to mention those targeted to specific topics， require extensive

document is to provide guidance and supporting resources for the Illinois educator， whether district or
building leader or classroom teacher， in navigating the landscape of AI use in and limitations of in their
P-12 school district.

4. Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally determined
purpose and use
These commitments are further operationalized through following assumptions:
• The purpose of any selection and implementation of educational technology is to enrich student
experience and afford them the opportunity to develop and enrich their sense of “Self” through the
use of the specific technology.
• Descriptions of AI concepts relevant to district leaders， teachers， students， families/caregivers， and
community members/advocates are likely very different. Selecting a set of concepts and providing
suggestions of why these matter in light of AI use in P-12 educational settings is an important point
of departure in the development of common understandings and， from these， district policies and
supporting resources.
• Any consideration of the possibility for and benefits of AI use to inform teaching and learning
practices should use a recognizable framework in order to compare current instructional planning
without AI in contrast to when AI is incorporated.
• Regardless of benefits of and limitations for AI in P-12 educational settings， prework internal to a
district and then outside of it to develop common understandings of purpose(s) and use(s) is critical.
The means for and cadence of this work require coalition building to maximize use for instruction and
operations within a district.

Note: The guidance uses “informed use” rather than “responsible use” save if a district or other
organization uses the term “responsible use” in a referenced document. The distinction is an
extension of the degree to which artificial intelligence is used safely or appropriately to include，
indeed focus upon， if its use is educationally warranted， developmentally appropriate， and
grounded in the specific purposes of schooling.
• The tenets make that distinction important. If teaching and learning are shaped by human
relationships and by the experiences， interests， and assets each child brings into school， then AI use
cannot be judged apart from context， learner need， and the professional judgment of educators. If
schools serve academic， developmental， and civic purposes concurrently， then the standard for use
must extend beyond compliance or rule-following to include whether a use supports student learning，
healthy development， and preparation for participation in shared civic life.
• “Informed use” also better reflects the guidance’s view that artificial intelligence is a means to inform
teaching and learning rather than an end in itself. “Responsible use” is valuable， but it can be read too
narrowly， as though the task is simply to avoid harm， follow rules， or use tools with caution. “Informed
use” requires something more deliberate: understanding what the tool is being used for， what it
can and cannot do， what risks or tradeoffs it introduces， what should and must remain human， and
why local educators must oversee implementation in order to determine whether the use fits the
instructional， developmental， and community context. In that sense， informed use names both the
judgment and the conditions the guidance seeks to cultivate.
“Informed use” explicitly must include the principle of “trust but verify.” If AI is used for tasks such as
evaluation of student work or， more minimally， plagiarism detection without notifying those affected
by the AI use， then its use likely will erode trust and increase skepticism (or worse， engender or support
additional cynicism). Moreover， since AI does make mistakes， human oversight and interaction with
the AI outputs is essential to engender trust and ensure that what is provided possesses a “goodness
of fit” with agreed upon purposes and uses determined by those deciding upon and affected by AI
implementation.
Finally， education is rife with acronyms. In order to support the reader， a glossary is provided as an
appendix for all terms that are initially introduced but then referred to by acronym in the remainder of the
document (See Appendix: Acronym Glossary).
