The purpose of this section is to provide some of the central concepts used to develop AI policies—
the terms of art—in support of the use of artificial intelligence as a means of informing and enriching
teaching and learning， while preserving the human relationships， professional judgment， equity， privacy，
safety， transparency， and accountability that are foundational to that end.
Specifically， explanation of the concept， alignment of the concept with the guiding tenants， and
examples of more optimal and less desirable “typical” current uses of the concept in practice are
provided.
Also， an additional way of organizing central concepts in and for AI in P-12 settings different than
previously described and is organized through the lens of “role” is to categorize by Instruction (e.g.，
Teaching and Learning)， Ethics， Governance， and Human-Centeredness. This information is provided in
that it may assist districts in framing their policy work (Appendix: AI Concepts: District Next Steps).
How Concepts Were Selected
The identification of concepts derived from statutory and regulatory requirements， authoritative
national and international frameworks intended for education and schooling， and analysis of risk and
governance frameworks that emphasize transparency， privacy， equity， validity， accountability， and safety
in the design and use of AI systems.
Concepts that function as terms of art within AI (e.g.， machine learning， large language models，
hallucinations)， as well as those that shape how concepts are understood in teaching and learning
contexts (e.g.， intersubjectivity， human nature， theory of mind)， are presented. Rather than attempting
to catalog all concepts currently recognized in AI， generally， this section prioritizes concepts that most
directly influence P-12 district decisions about AI. Finally， all concepts should be read through a lens of
“trust but verify.” Put differently， clarity on purpose and use of the AI and the limits of these based upon
local capacity require that AI is monitored and its outputs modified by those humans who engage with
it. While the potential purposes and use of AI are numerous， maybe close to infinite， in P-12 settings its
potential is in serving as a means of teaching and learning.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 39
AI Concepts
Machine Learning
Explanation
Machine learning (ML) is a method for building artificial intelligence systems that learn patterns from
data rather than being explicitly programmed for every outcome. In school contexts， machine learning
can be embedded in tools that predict student performance， recommend instructional materials，
detect patterns in behavior or attendance， or automate categorization tasks. Machine learning systems
do not “understand” learning the way humans do; they identify correlations and patterns based on
training data.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. ML can identify patterns in data， but it cannot
know a student as a person or interpret those patterns in light of relationships， lived experience，
motivation， language， culture， or circumstance.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life. If ML
is used to sort， flag， or recommend， schools must avoid reducing students to probability scores，
risk categories， or predicted outcomes.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. ML may help surface trends
or possible supports， but it should remain a decision-support tool rather than a substitute for
professional judgment.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts should decide when ML use is educationally justified， what
evidence must accompany it， and what human review is required before action is taken.
Examples of uses
• Early warning indicators that flag students for intervention based on attendance， grades， and
behavior trends
• Adaptive learning programs that adjust content difficulty based on student performance patterns
• Predictive analytics dashboards used by administrators to identify instructional needs or program
impacts
• Recommendation engines that suggest resources， lessons， or interventions to teachers
• Automated categorization of student work into proficiency bands for formative feedback
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 40
Natural Language Processing
Explanation
Natural language processing (NLP) is a branch of artificial intelligence that enables computers to
work with human language—text and speech—by recognizing patterns， extracting meaning， and
generating language-based outputs. In school contexts， NLP can be embedded in tools that translate
languages， summarize documents， support writing and revision， analyze open-ended responses， power
chatbots， or convert speech to text and text to speech. NLP systems do not “understand” language like
humans; they model statistical and computational relationships in language data and can make errors，
especially with idioms， context， sarcasm， dialects， and culturally specific references.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Because language carries identity， culture，
tone， and relationship， NLP tools can support communication but can also flatten meaning or
misread expression if used without human interpretation.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Schools should use NLP in ways that support voice， comprehension， multilingual access， and
participation rather than displacing students’ own communication and sense-making.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. NLP can assist drafting，
translation， summarization， and accessibility， but it should not replace reading closely， writing
authentically， or engaging in dialogue with others.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts should determine what language uses are appropriate， what
data may be entered， and when outputs require verification or human escalation.
Examples of uses
• Speech-to-text transcription for accessibility and note-taking
• Translation support for family communications using approved templates with human review for
high-stakes messages
• Summarization of long policy documents or meeting notes for staff review
• Writing-support tools that provide revision suggestions， organization help， and checklists rather
than final graded work
• Analysis of open-ended survey responses to identify themes
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 41
Computer Vision
Explanation
Computer vision (CV) is a branch of artificial intelligence that enables computers to interpret and
analyze visual information—such as images and video—by detecting patterns， identifying objects，
recognizing text， and classifying or describing what is shown. In school contexts， computer vision can
be embedded in tools that support accessibility， automate document processing， analyze instructional
artifacts， or support specialized learning applications such as robotics， engineering， and career and
technical education. Computer vision systems do not “see” like humans do; they infer features from
pixel data and can make errors depending on lighting， angle， image quality， and training data.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. CV may support access and analysis， but it
cannot interpret students’ lives， intentions， or dignity in the way trusted adults can.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Because visual analysis can affect privacy， trust， and belonging， schools should be cautious about
uses that normalize surveillance or reduce children to observable data points.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. CV may support accessibility or
specialized instruction， but it should serve educational purposes determined by educators rather
than becoming an independent rationale for adoption.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts should distinguish between low-risk instructional uses and
higher-risk monitoring or identification uses， with stricter safeguards for the latter.
Examples of uses
• Optical character recognition (OCR) that converts printed worksheets or scanned PDFs into
editable， readable text
• Document-processing systems that auto-extract fields from forms
• CTE or robotics projects where students train simple vision models to detect objects using
approved datasets
• Assistive technology that describes images or reads signage aloud
• Athletics or performing-arts analysis tools that track motion from video for reflection， feedback，
and revision
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 42
Generative Artificial Intelligence
Explanation
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) refers to AI systems that create new content—such as text，
images， audio， video， or code—based on patterns learned from large datasets. These systems generate
outputs that can appear coherent and human-like， but they do not produce content based on verified
truth; they generate plausible responses based on statistical patterns. In schools， generative AI is
often used for drafting materials， brainstorming ideas， generating practice items， and supporting
writing or communication tasks.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. GenAI can support drafting and access， but it
cannot replace the relational work through which educators know students and build instruction
from their strengths and needs.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Because GenAI can shape how students write， create， and communicate， schools should use it in
ways that support agency， voice， judgment， and responsibility rather than passive dependence.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. GenAI should be treated as a
support for exploration， scaffolding， and drafting， not as evidence of learning in itself.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts should clarify approved uses， disclosure norms， verification
routines， and privacy protections before broad use.
Examples of uses
• Draft lesson materials or parent communications with human review and verification
• Generate differentiated practice prompts， readings， or exemplars
• Brainstorm prompts and question stems to support inquiry-based learning
• Student writing supports such as outlines， revision suggestions， and sentence starters
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 43
Vibe Coding
Explanation
Vibe coding is an AI-assisted approach to software creation in which a user describes what
they want and the AI generates， revises， and debugs the code through a conversational process rather
than through line-by-line programming. In practice， vibe coding often emphasizes rapid prototyping，
iteration， and experimentation; in its loosest form， it can also involve accepting code that the user does
not fully understand. In school contexts， vibe coding may be used by educators， instructional coaches，
technology staff， or students to quickly create small applications， classroom tools， dashboards，
websites， or automations.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Vibe coding may help people build tools
quickly， but speed of creation does not ensure that what is built reflects the developmental，
cultural， linguistic， or relational realities of the students and educators who will use it. Human
knowledge of learners， classrooms， and communities remains essential.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life. If
students or staff use vibe coding to create tools， the educational purpose must extend beyond
novelty or efficiency alone. The work should derive from clear identification of developmental and
coherent instructional goals， additional reflection on how digital tools shape human activity， and
thoughtful participation in shared technological environments.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Vibe coding can help accelerate
design， prototyping， and revision， but it cannot displace educator judgment， sound instructional
design， accessibility review， privacy review， or informed use for the final product. The fact that an AI
can generate code does not make that code educationally appropriate， secure， or reliable if there is
a lack of goodness of fit between the instructional outcome and the AI application.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts and schools should decide when vibe coding is appropriate，
what kinds of tools may be built this way， what testing and approval processes are required， and
when staff or student-created applications may or may not be used with student data. Because vibe
coding can involve producing code the creator does not fully understand， review， documentation，
and governance are essential.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 44
Vibe Coding
Examples of uses
• Creating a simple classroom website or study tool from a plain-language prompt
• Building a prototype parent communication form or event sign-up tool for internal review
• Drafting a small instructional game， quiz interface， or flashcard app for teacher testing before
classroom use
• Generating a first-pass dashboard or script to organize non-sensitive school information
• Helping students in a computer science or design course prototype an app idea while still requiring
human explanation， testing， and revision before use
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 45
Agentic AI
Explanation
Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can pursue a goal with limited supervision by planning multi-step
work， using tools or connected systems， drawing on memory or context， and taking actions on a user’s
behalf. Unlike a system that only responds once to a prompt， an agentic system can sequence tasks，
adapt as new information appears， and in some cases act autonomously within permissions set by the
user or organization. In school contexts， agentic AI could be embedded in systems that coordinate
workflows， gather information across otherwise disparate platforms， draft communications， organize
tasks， or support operational processes.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Agentic systems may coordinate tasks
or surface options， but these systems do not “know” students in the human， relational， and
developmental sense that educators do. The more a system acts within and between systems，
the more important it becomes to ensure that relationships， context， and professional knowledge
remain central in determining informed use and the monitoring of it.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic
life. Because agentic AI can move from suggestion to action， schools should be cautious not
to delegate matters affecting student data broadly and elements tied to identity， opportunity，
belonging， discipline， or access to services to systems that operate primarily through pattern
recognition， optimization， or task completion in particular.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Agentic AI may support
workflow efficiency， planning， and coordination， but it must remain in a support role. It must not
independently make or execute high-stakes educational decisions， nor should its recommendations
be treated as self-justifying simply because they were produced efficiently or at scale. Human
oversight and consideration of outputs for goodness of fit are essential.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Agentic AI requires especially careful governance because it
may “act，” not merely “generate.” Districts should determine those tasks are appropriate for agentic
systems， what approvals are required before action， how activity is logged and monitored， when
humans must intervene， and which uses are off-limits altogether. Controls such as clear framing
of and limits to the spaces in which agentic AI may act， monitoring， and interruptibility (i.e.， when
to “pull the plug”) are particularly important.

Agentic AI

• An internal staff-support agent that gathers information from approved district documents and
drafts a first response to routine policy questions
• A scheduling agent that prepares meeting options， drafts invitations， and organizes materials for
human approval before sending
• A help-desk agent that classifies technology requests， checks approved knowledge bases， and

• A curriculum-support agent that assembles district-approved resources aligned to a teacher’s

• An operations agent that drafts reminders， compiles task lists， and tracks completion across

Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 47
Open Source AI
Explanation
Open Source AI refers to AI models and tools whose code， model components， or other technical
materials are made available in ways that allow outside parties to inspect， adapt， host， or modify them.
In district settings， this can create greater local control over how a tool operates， what data it uses， and
how it is aligned to curriculum， language needs， accessibility supports， and governance expectations.
At the same time， that greater control also brings greater local responsibility for setup， security，
monitoring， maintenance， and oversight.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Informed use of open-source approaches may
better support local adaptation to student needs， community language， and district context， but
those adaptations should strengthen human-centered teaching rather than shift attention toward
technology for its own sake.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Open-source tools may support transparency， shared understanding， and local public accountability
because districts can more clearly explain what a tool is doing and why.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Openness does not itself make a
tool educationally sound， accurate， equitable， or appropriate. The central question remains whether
the tool serves instructional， developmental， and organizational purposes/uses identified by the
district.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. If a district adopts or hosts an open-source system， it also assumes
responsibility for governance， privacy protections， security controls， review processes， and long-
term sustainability.
Examples of uses
• District-hosted writing support tool in a controlled local environment
• Local fine-tuning for bilingual scaffolds or accessibility supports
• Curriculum-aligned chat assistant hosted within district-approved systems
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 48
Closed Source AI
(proprietary/vendor-controlled model ecosystem)
Explanation
Closed Source AI refers to systems in which the core model， technical implementation， or key system
components are controlled by a vendor and are not openly available for local inspection or modification.
Districts typically access these systems through purchased products， licensed platforms， or vendor-
managed services. Such tools may offer convenience， support， and integrated features， but they
also limit local visibility into how the system functions and place greater importance on contracts，
governance， privacy protections， and ongoing monitoring.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Closed systems may be easier to adopt， but
ease of adoption should not displace educator judgment or obscure how a tool affects students，
classrooms， and relationships.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Because vendor-controlled systems can shape opportunity， communication， access， and trust
while limiting local transparency， districts should evaluate them in light of fairness， accountability，
and the broader public purposes of schooling.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. A closed tool may be useful and
well-supported， but neither market presence nor platform integration is enough to justify its use.
The question remains whether it helps inform teaching and learning in ways that are educationally
sound and developmentally appropriate as identified by the district and/or teacher.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts should rely on procurement review， contract terms， privacy
safeguards， role-based permissions， training expectations， and ongoing monitoring to determine
whether vendor-controlled systems align with local goals and requirements.
Examples of uses
• Vendor-provided classroom writing feedback assistant
• Teacher productivity copilots for planning and communications
• Vendor analytics features that flag or predict student needs
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 49
Hallucinations
Explanation
Hallucinations refer to AI-generated outputs that are presented as factual but are inaccurate，
fabricated， or unsupported by evidence. Generative AI systems may hallucinate citations， names，
quotations， policies， or historical facts. Because outputs often sound confident， hallucinations can be
difficult to detect without verification. In school contexts， hallucinations can misinform instruction，
mislead students， or create inaccurate communications if not carefully checked.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Hallucinations make clear why all those who
interact with AI (e.g.， district personnel and students) must stay actively involved in interpreting，
checking， and， as needed， revising AI outputs.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Learning to verify information is not only an academic skill; it is also for civic development and a
demonstration of digital literacy in environments such as (but not limited to) AI where plausible
falsehoods circulate easily.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Hallucinations demonstrate that
AI outputs are drafts or starting points， not authorities.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts should establish norms for verification and communication
to the community， especially when AI is used for facts， sources， policy guidance， and the like.
Examples of uses
• AI-generated lesson plans that cite standards incorrectly or fabricate primary sources
• AI summaries of texts that misstate key events， claims， or character motivations
• AI-generated parent communications that include incorrect dates， policies， or procedures
• Student research responses that include fabricated citations or quotations
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 50
Bias， Fairness， and Equity
Explanation
Bias in AI refers to systematic errors or skewed outputs that disadvantage particular groups or reflect
inequities embedded in training data， design choices， or deployment contexts. In education， biased
AI outputs can affect recommendations， scoring， content generation， or predictions that influence
student opportunities. Fairness and equity considerations require districts to examine who benefits，
who is harmed， and how systems perform across diverse learners.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. A human-centered approach requires
that students be understood in their full individuality， not through biased systems that mistake
difference for deficit.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Schools have obligations to fairness， equal dignity， and participation.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. AI outputs should never be
treated as neutral simply because they are automated.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Districts should review tools for subgroup impacts， differential error
rates， and risk of harm before and during use.
Examples of uses
• Automated writing feedback that penalizes dialect differences or multilingual structures
• Recommendation systems that reduce access to advanced opportunities based on historical data
patterns
• AI-based risk flags that over-identify some groups for behavior concerns
• GenAI outputs that reproduce stereotypes or omit perspectives
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 51
Deepfakes and Synthetic Media
Explanation
Deepfakes and synthetic media refer to AI-generated or AI-manipulated images， audio， or video that
convincingly depict real people doing or saying things they never did. Synthetic media can be used
for legitimate educational purposes， such as simulations or creative projects， but it can also be used
to harass， defame， or misinform. In school settings， deepfakes raise risks for student safety， bullying，
consent violations， and community trust.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Deepfakes will damage trust in AI，
development of an individual as “Self” and citizen， both of which are foundational to learning.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the

Explanation

Informed Use of Artificial Intelligence
Explanation
Informed use of artificial intelligence means using AI with a clear educational purpose， with attention
to context， and with recognition that artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning
rather than an end in itself. Its use should be evaluated in light of what it is meant to support， for whom，
under what conditions， and with what safeguards. In schools， this includes the use of AI to inform
instructional planning and delivery， to enrich student engagement and experience， and to support
district operations in ways that remain educationally grounded， developmentally appropriate， and
responsive to local needs.
Informed use also requires understanding the limits of AI outputs. Artificial intelligence may assist with
drafting， planning， organizing， feedback， translation， explanation， and other tasks， but its outputs are
not synonymous with truth， sound judgment， or educational appropriateness. For that reason， outputs
should be verified and interpreted by the humans responsible for their use. This guidance therefore
distinguishes between assistance， substitution， and professional judgment. Artificial intelligence may
assist educators and students in particular tasks， but it should not substitute for educator judgment，
human relationships， developmental knowledge， or district responsibility for important decisions.
Why this concept is important in light of the guiding tenets
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences， interests，
and assets each child brings into school. Informed use of AI keeps educational relationships
at the center of its use in teaching and learning through ensuring that AI supports， rather than
displaces， the interpersonal relationships that ground such interactions (e.g.， educator professional
knowledge; acknowledging， respecting， and building upon student assets and interests).
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Informed use helps schools evaluate whether AI use strengthens learning while also supporting
student development， agency， responsibility， and participation in shared communities.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Informed AI is a tool for assistance，
not a substitute for teaching， learning， judgment， or institutional responsibility. Its value depends
on how well it serves educational purposes identified by those who use it.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally determined
purpose and use. Informed use requires districts and educators to decide which uses are
appropriate， under what conditions， with what safeguards， and with what degree of transparency，
oversight， and human review， and to communicate this to those affected by its use.

Human-to-Human Relationships & AI Use in Teaching and Learning: What Is， What Will Be，
What Could Be
When asked how AI may inform teaching and learning， clarifying the context in which that information
will be used is essential. Teaching and learning take place in spaces with individuals with unique
motivations， values， and experiences. These mingle together to create assumptions about the purposes
and uses of what is taught， how it is taught， and how what is taught is understood. Another way of
expressing this is that without common understandings about the purposes and use of the teaching and
learning engagements， the means available for what is taught， how it is taught， and how what is taught is
understood can all too easily be misunderstood. Thus， this portion of guidance first considers teaching
and learning apart from any specific tool; it then introduces AI uses through that lens to examine how AI
informs and can enhance student-teacher engagement.
Generally， when teachers engage in instructional planning， they consider the child or children， their
interests， readiness level， and learning profile，27 the curriculum， and the instructional sequence though
which teaching and learning occurs. Teachers， knowing what they know about a student or group of
students， concurrently reflect upon the prior learning of the students in the particular content—the what
was， the ways in which the student engaged with the content—the how was (e.g.， through a performance
of a poem， constructing an essay and other form of representing students’ current understanding of the
topic). From this， the teacher identifies those subsequent experiences—the what will be—and the means
through which emergent understandings are demonstrated.
Missing from the previous broad description of instructional planning are those aspects of teacher
knowledge not easily captured in a planning document/lesson plan/unit plan: knowledge about the student
“as a person”—their interests， preferred ways of showing understanding， and the like. Put differently， the
teacher also reflects upon the hopes， dreams， and fears of the student as gleaned from the previous
interactions with the student “as a person.” Also， professional knowledge of human development (i.e.，
nature) and teacher beliefs28 about how people learn through engagement in the world (i.e.， nurture) and
available resources affect instructional planning.

in instructional planning insofar as the what and the means through which the how what is shown is
important for a teacher to “capture” in order to support student learning.

Developing Prompts Using AI for Instructional Planning
Bloom/A&K is a useful heuristic for instructional planning as it helps focus questions and clarify
what “understanding” can look like. But if it is treated as a strict ladder—ending at “evaluate”—it raises
a practical question: what comes next? And what might this mean for “…preserving the human
relationships essential to effective teaching and learning?”
One image that may provide useful is to extend the notion of a taxonomy as developed by Bloom/A&K to
that of an “AI taxonomy.” This taxonomy is a heuristic—an image that (can) aide in interpretation— that
emphasizes how the subsequent information， which includes AI， also situates its use as a means and
within that which does not require it but could benefit from it (See Figure 2: AI Taxonomy).
Note that the language in the AI taxonomy can assume that the engagements as sequenced lead to the co-
creation of some “output” using AI. While obvious， the stacking and sequencing of the AI taxonomy requires
that one is conversant with how to write a prompt that extends learning in ways that deliberately use AI as
a means as opposed to the teacher or student assuming that “AI will do it for me/us.” This is not an esoteric
distinction. Quite the contrary insofar as development of agency (e.g.， the sense of Self that occurs though
work in the world and resultant sense of confidence and competence) occurs through the refinement of
judgement based upon specific purpose and use within a context—outsourcing of this agency coupled with
the assumption that what is produced is appropriate is a dangerous supposition that must be avoided.
Moreover， the notion of an AI taxonomy should be considered in light of its role in digital citizenship and
informed AI use as an individual and member of various communities. These ideas are further explored in
the subsequent section AI Literacy and Digital Citizenship: Healthy Development and Informed Use.

General Tips for Prompt development
AI supports human work; it does not replace it36
• Treat AI applications as drafting/organizing assistants: humans (teachers and students) set the
purpose， supply the inputs， and make the final decisions.
• Write prompts that make the human thinking task explicit (what you must decide， argue， or
demonstrate)， and use the tool only for support work (e.g.， brainstorming， outlining， formatting，
feedback).
• Do not treat a single AI output as “truth.” Build verification into the prompt and into the workflow
before anything is submitted or used instructionally.37
• Use AI tools in ways that preserve student voice and agency (the student’s reasoning should remain
visible in the final product) and follow local disclosure/attribution expectations when required.
Tips for AI prompts for informing planning and enriching instruction
• Start with the learning purpose and success criteria (what humans must decide/do)， then decide
what parts may be drafted by the AI application (outline， checklist， examples， question stems).38
• Avoid prompts that ask for “the answer” or a fully finished student product; request drafts， scaffolds，
checklists， alternative approaches， or feedback instead.39
• Provide the exact inputs the AI tool should use (excerpt， dataset， sources， notes). If key inputs are
missing， the tool may “fill gaps” with plausible but incorrect details.40
• Reduce ambiguity: specify the audience (teacher vs. student)， grade band or reading level， the
product type (outline， rubric， feedback， quiz)， and how it will be used in class.41
• Name clear boundaries: do not paste student identifiable information or student records into
AI applications unless the district has explicitly approved that specific tool and use case under
applicable privacy safeguards.42
• Add a verification step before classroom use or student submission (e.g.， cross-check against
theprovided text/data; confirm quotations; verify math with a calculator; check claims against a
primary source).43

What follows are a modest set of questions and linked supporting resources to remind the reader that

• How do the district policies keep interpersonal relationships central?
• In what ways can AI enrich teacher-student relationships (without replacing them)?

• What are common “growing pains” with new technology in P–12—and how can they be anticipated，

How do district policies keep interpersonal relationships central?
• Frame AI use as a human-driven process (human inquiry ➞ AI output ➞ human interpretation/
reflection)， which keeps educator and student agency—and therefore relationships—at the center.47
• Explicitly state that AI should support—but not replace—teachers， because teaching depends on
human judgment， interaction， and care.48
• Position AI as a tool to enhance human productivity and creativity， rather than a substitute for human
thinking or relational work.49
• Emphasize that AI can create time for teachers to spend on relationship-building， small-group
instruction， and feedback.50
• Embed social learning expectations (students working with peers and educators)， reinforcing that
responsible AI supports and enhances the relational essence of teaching and learning and resists
solitary automation.51
• Repeatedly return to human evaluation/oversight—especially when decisions affect learning—
because that evaluation is a core educator responsibility.52

In what ways can AI enrich teacher–student relationships (without replacing them)?
• Reducing routine workload (drafting lesson options， communications， resources) so teachers can
invest more time in conferencing， coaching， and relationship-rich instruction.53
• Helping teachers generate multiple pathways and scaffolds for diverse learners—so the teacher can
respond more personally and precisely to student needs.54
• Improving feedback cycles: AI can provide draft feedback ideas， while the teacher supplies context，
priorities， tone， and the relational “why” behind next steps.55
• Strengthening peer-to-peer learning: students can use AI as a “third perspective” and then test ideas
in discussion with peers and educators.56
• Supporting reflective dialogue: teachers can use AI outputs as artifacts for students to critique，
compare， and refine—making classroom talk more evidence-based and collaborative.57
What cautions help districts avoid the “seduction of AI” (abdicating responsibility to “trust but
verify”)?
• Never treat AI output as a final product; humans must evaluate the output and decide what to use，
revise， or reject.58
• Plan for inaccuracies， inconsistencies， and bias in AI responses; verification routines (lateral reading，
fact-checking， source checks) are non-negotiable.59
• Keep educator professional judgment in authority for assessment and decisions affecting students;
AI can assist but must not displace human responsibility.60
• Avoid “automation drift” in instruction: preserve student thinking/time-on-task by requiring students
to show reasoning， revisions， and reflection—beyond the AI’s answer.61
• Protect privacy and avoid oversharing in prompts; districts should provide clear policies about
appropriate data handling and safe tool use (e.g.， the district policy， AUP， and IUP).62
• Be cautious with AI-detection tools; some district guidance advises against relying on them due to
reliability and equity concerns (e.g.， false positives).63
What are common “growing pains” with informed use of new technologies in P–12 settings?
• Policies and norms lag rapidly changing tools; the need for multiple up-to-date guidance documents
emphasize ongoing revision rather than one-time adoption.64
• Early misuse or/and a “weak pilot” can reflect misunderstandings about what AI is (and is not)—
including the mistaken belief that outputs are inherently factual or unbiased.65
• Academic-integrity friction: early reliance on detection or “gotcha” approaches can produce false
positives and erode trust.66
• Equity gaps can widen if access， ongoing training and professional learning， and expectations are
uneven; guidance encourages proactive， equity-centered planning and support.67
• Safety and privacy missteps occur when staff or students share sensitive information in prompts or
use tools outside district safeguards.68

AI for Policy I – Building Readiness， Shared Understanding， and Innovation
Summary
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. The selection of and expectations for
any educational technology will affect the subsequent teaching and learning. AI selection and
expectations should be grounded in how AI supports student efficacy and agency—directly
(instructionally and as individuals and members of larger communities of practice) and indirectly
(administratively)—through clear ties to the collectively identified purpose(s) and use(s) indicative of
the practices and those who engage in them.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Selecting educational technologies is a public decision. A deliberate communications plan—paired
with benchmarking—should memorialize users’ and stakeholders’ perceptions and the changes to
local practice that were modified based upon the individual and collective refinements in judgements
based upon engagement(s).
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Informed AI selection and
expectations should be grounded in how AI supports student efficacy and agency—directly
(instructionally as individuals and members of larger communities of practice) and indirectly
(administratively)—through rich engagement with content.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. AI applications must be vetted for operational and instructional fit
using clear questions tied to purpose， use， and evaluated for bias and alignment upon a regular
cadence which collects ongoing feedback， with options to refine or offboard.
The use of any educational technology for operational or pedagogical uses is rife with consequences.
The goal is to anticipate and reduce unintended effects by collectively clarifying context， purpose， and
intended use with both decision-makers and those impacted.
An initial wonder about AI use for operational and/or pedagogical purposes assumes a set of desired
outcomes. Because unintended consequences cannot be eliminated， districts should make the what
and why explicit—including how outcomes support human flourishing (even when the goal is “operational
efficiency”). This requires shared purpose and use， even without full agreement. For the purposes of this
guidance， building relationships around shared purpose with those directly and indirectly impacted is
necessary—not just nice—especially when decisions shape what students should know and be able to do，
and how learning is supported.
Because AI is rapidly evolving， districts need frameworks that foreground equity and access by
addressing bias， privacy， and how students can meaningfully engage with technologies that are surely a
part of their future work in the world.

Practices That Support Collaboration in AI Adoption (i.e.， getting used to an idea)
Gathering perceptions of those impacted by the implementation of a new idea or change in practice
requires time to “get used to an idea.”70 Surveys， focus groups， interviews， and the like， when used in
tandem， are useful in obtaining feedback as well as providing multiple means for people to get used
to AI through engagement with contextually relevant and recognizable instances (i.e.， the use of AI in
situations by those to whom they are in relation).
To support collective deliberation that clarifies purpose， use， and timeline(s) for implementation of AI，
districts must provide means through which those impacted can share perspectives. Using surveys，
focus groups， and interviews to gather feedback offers multiple ways for people to share ideas and
concerns. Data should be used to refine implementation， strengthen shared understanding， and continue
learning over time. In this section， cases—organized by use/purpose and suggestions for means of
collecting perspectives (e.g.， surveys， interviews， and the like)—are ways of going about forging common
understandings and subsequent policy development.
Benchmarking
While the central example of this section is on the development of survey items， benchmarking should be
understood broadly as a process though which data is collected through a variety of means (e.g.， survey，
focus groups， interviews， listening session， and the like) for the purpose of “taking the pulse” of those
directly and indirectly impacted by decisions over time in order to support the getting used to the ideas
and operationalization of them. Initial benchmarking and regular feedback opportunities also provide
a means for updates of progress and ability to fine tune understandings， expectations， and changes in
perception of AI.
Where AI “sits” shapes what becomes central in the inquiry. For instance， if operational efficiency is the
focus of consideration (i.e.， “to what extent does AI application n increase staff time to engage in x?”)，
that purpose backgrounds other possible areas of foci such as students (i.e.， AI as means and in support
of development of “Self，” evolving content mastery)， teachers (AI and means to inform instruction)，
and content. Naming these tradeoffs matters because what is in the background will still produce
consequences that affect what is foregrounded.
Prior to any gathering of changes in practice， it is often useful to consider the most durable means in
which to share the changes to current practice as well as build a coalition of individuals impacted or/
interested in the change. In light of that， a district needs to map out the “what， why， who， when/how
often.” This is important insofar as it is often more effective for people to respond to a model than
create one—especially likely due to the variety of comfort with and knowledge of the ever-changing AI
landscape. As shared in Table 4， a shared roadmap increases transparency， helps people see themselves

What follows is， in many ways， content agnostic as， AI or not， any new educational technology requires
clarity on purpose and use and multiple opportunities for feedback and refinement. In light of this work，
though， they are essential for districts and educators in “…evaluat[ing] and address[ing] bias， privacy，

As a district develops a process for the selection of AI resources， centering question(s) to ensure
common understanding for purpose and use should first occur internally. This work begins by identifying
“need.” This is an important aspect of the larger work insofar as adoption of AI (or any other educational
technology) should be based on how it can benefit students， whether it is within current and sustainable
resources available to the district， and not on account of a “fad.” Moreover， the identification of need
includes a specific focus on bias， equity， and access broadly and is inclusive of the members of the
cabinet (e.g.， the “internal” what and why)， that may be “baked into” the AI applications and both filtered
through the lens of informing instruction and enriching student experiences. Ensuring that cabinet
members share common understanding on purpose and use and limitations of the AI is essential for the
subsequent considerations of membership of the coalition (e.g.， the “external” what and why and who)
and also developing a plan for how and when to gather feedback.

District and Teacher Selection of AI applications
The previous information focused on work necessary to create common understandings on purpose of
and use for AI to inform the development of district policies to inform and enrich teaching and learning
when AI is used as a means for these. This section extends this through focusing upon the “…evaluat[ion]
and address[ing] [of] bias， privacy， transparency， and risk assessment and management in the usage of
artificial intelligence technologies and applications”80 at the district and， assuming approval/meeting of
compliance/laws， teacher level as well as through “innovation zones” inclusive of those within districts，
between P-12 districts and higher education， and partnerships between for-profit entities or/and
organizations and school districts.
As districts are asked to innovate using AI in support of teaching and learning there is a need to also
protect students and staff， and sustain public trust through clear， explainable decisions about what is
permitted， under what conditions， and why. Balancing the instructional benefits of AI (or any educational
technology or curricular program) must also include operational concerns including protecting student
privacy—bias， privacy， transparency， and risk assessment and management. The protecting of student
privacy requires a series of district policies， authorized uses policies， and informed use policies. These
policies ensure clarity on expectations on authorized use inclusive of repeatable routines， defined roles，
documented evidence expectations， and， maybe of most importance， a monitoring cycle that continues
after adoption to refine， as needed， those policies adopted.
Approaching the evaluation of applications for instructional and operational uses is essential because AI
systems can fail in ways that resemble ordinary instructional mistakes (i.e.， incorrect feedback)， but they
can also fail in ways that create legal， ethical， and equity harms (e.g.， privacy violations， discriminatory
impacts， opaque automated decisions， or normalized surveillance).
Various guidance documents from the federal government and national organizations share principles
and recommendations to support districts in approaching thoughtful selection of AI to inform instruction
and enrich student engagement. For instance:
• Federal education guidance suggests the importance of shared understanding and local policy
development so that districts can realize educational benefits while managing predictable risks.81
• National Institute of Standards and Technology’s AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) and its
Generative AI Profile.82
The goal in sharing what follows is not to outsource decisions that a district or teacher can cut and
paste into a policy and adopt. Rather， it is to ground local decision-making in recognized practices and
communicate decisions in plain language that comports with federal laws， as well as to capture the
unique needs and opportunities for AI to inform instruction and， more generally， the opportunities for
educational engagement offered to students in their school district.

Three-Step Structure to Ascertain “Goodness of Fit”84
Step 1: Identify tool category and risk level
Before debating features， answer four questions:
1. What decisions or outputs does it influence (planning support vs. grading vs. discipline vs.
surveillance)?
2. Whose data does it touch (no student data， aggregated， de-identified， identifiable student data)?
3. Who uses it (staff-only， student-facing， family-facing)?
4. What is the impact if the result is “incorrect” (low stakes vs. high stakes)?
Suggested local risk tiers (raise expectations as tier increases):
• Tier 0: No student data; optional staff productivity
• Tier 1: Instructional support with limited or de-identified data
• Tier 2: Student-facing learning tool using identifiable student data
• Tier 3: High-stakes or safety-sensitive (grading/placement/discipline， student monitoring/
surveillance， automated risk scoring)
Step 2: Minimum evidence checklist (what must be “true” to approve)
For Tier 1–3 tools， require evidence across these domains:
Educational value: Clear use-case(s)， success indicators (i.e.， student outcomes)， training plan， and
explicit constraints (“what it may not be used for”)
Data privacy and contract readiness: Terms aligned to district expectations; terms of service
(ToS)/ data processing agreement (DPA) review completed; clear data flows and retention/deletion
commitments
Safety， security， and incident readiness: Security posture summary; breach notification commitments;
district incident process defined
Transparency and explainability: Plain-language description of what the tool does; what inputs it uses;
what humans must still decide/review
Equity and accessibility: Bias and accessibility evaluation plan; monitoring approach; documented
response pathway

• Adopt (low risk plus strong evidence and contract/privacy readiness)
• Pilot (promising value; limited scope/time; explicit monitoring and stop-use triggers)
• Decline (unclear purpose; weak privacy terms; high-stakes use without protections)

Teacher/Student Instructional Use
This portion of the guidance focuses upon decision-making of a teacher for the possible use of AI as a
means of informing and enriching teaching and learning by providing broad categories of consideration
ascertaining the goodness of fit (or not) for AI in specific instructional instances (Appendix: Misalignment
Scenarios and Why “Goodness of Fit” and Clear Prompts Matter). Assuming there is a goodness of fit that
aligned with district policies， two short cases are shared to further contextualize and practice decision-
making in light of AI as a means of informing and enriching teaching and learning.
Purpose and instructional fit
Write the learning goal as a student outcome (e.g.， “Students will revise claims using evidence”)， not
“Students will use AI.” Name the non-goal clearly (what remains student work). Prefer the simplest tool
that meets the need.
Student role and agency
Treat AI outputs as suggestions. Require students to choose what to keep， explain why， and revise. Build
a short reflection routine so the learning is visible and assessable.
Privacy and data minimization
Map data-in/data-out: what students enter， what the tool stores， who can access it， and how long it is
retained. Minimize inputs. Do not include names， IDs， faces/photos， contact info， or personal stories. If
data handling is unclear， pause use.
Transparency and explainability
You should be able to explain what the tool does， the limits of its outputs， and how students verify
content. Establish a verification routine using trusted sources or course materials.
Bias， equity， and accessibility
Test the tool with diverse names， dialects， reading levels， and multilingual phrasing. Look for
stereotyping or uneven quality. Provide an equally rigorous non-AI pathway. Ensure accessibility
supports match student needs.
Safety and classroom management
Confirm safeguards are appropriate for student exposure. Establish explicit norms (time， purpose，
supervision). Have a response plan for misuse: reteach， restrict， or discontinue.
Academic integrity and attribution
Define allowed vs. not allowed use for each assignment. Require a simple disclosure statement and build
assessment methods that rely on human evidence (drafts， conferencing， in-class writing， oral defense).
Pilot， monitoring， and exit
Pilot first， set a review date， and decide success/stop indicators in advance. Use work samples to
determine whether the tool improves learning outcomes without increasing risk.

Innovation Zones
Innovations zones， for the purposes of this guidance， should be understood as those created and
operated by districts/schools (sometimes with external inputs). Governance， instructional decision-
making， and scaling decisions remain inside the P-12 system even in those instances when the school
district is working with an external vendor or postsecondary institution.
AI innovation zones within P-12 district
The emphasis of “within P-12 district” innovation zones is on creating a “sandbox” for exploration of an
idea to implementation. Importantly， and in addition to the identification of purpose/use， the “within
district” innovation spaces afford the district deliberate opportunities to consider sustainability and
capacity and， potentially， if additional partnerships or relationships are necessary as it engages with AI
for operational and instructional purposes.86

Sandbox for development of “castles” (some of which will be piloted): An environment in which AI
tools are “applied” to instructional and operational uses. Based upon findings， some of the castles will be

Instructional innovation studio: Student-facing applications and/or student creation of AI applications

• Avoid “tool-first” pilots without data boundaries and identification of purpose/use
• Not identifying exit plans for possible acute and chronic instances requiring the immediate cessation

• Valuing meeting timelines over learning about coherence and scaling can result in lack of common

• Run a readiness checklist (see Appendix: Readiness Resources) to identify gaps and then individuals/

• Develop resources and training tied to requirements and expectations in district AI policies， AUPs，

A district may also establish a student-led Artificial Intelligence Council as one form of bounded
innovation space. In this context， the council is not merely an advisory structure or symbolic mechanism
for “student voice.” Rather， it is a structured process through which a district may learn from students’
lived experiences with artificial intelligence within and outside of school and use that learning to clarify
purpose， identify problems of practice， strengthen guidance， and refine implementation over time.89
Framed in this way， the council fits within the broader logic of innovation zones in this guidance: it is
bounded， intentional， linked to identifiable questions， supported by regular feedback loops， and oriented
toward decisions about whether a particular practice should be clarified， expanded， revised， paused， or
stopped.
The composition and operation of the council must be deliberate. Students should be selected in ways
that allow different experiences， concerns， and perspectives to be represented， including students for
whom artificial intelligence may function as support for access， translation， drafting， or confidence，
as well as students who may experience it as pressure， confusion， surveillance， inequity， or diminished
trust. The work of the council should ask students not only to describe preferences， but also to interpret
differing perspectives， recognize competing interests， and consider what uses of artificial intelligence
are fair， meaningful， and educationally sound for the larger school community. In this respect， the council
supports both the healthy development of self and preparation for participation in shared civic life:
students are asked to form judgment， exercise voice responsibly， and engage in shared inquiry about
issues that affect others as well as themselves.
The council should commence by identifying a clearly bounded opportunity space. This space should
be framed through input by district personnel and informed by student experiences with AI and the
questions that emerge from these experiences. Broadly， topics may include those areas with which
the district and students as students in a school and citizens participating in various communities are
grappling.
More specifically:
• What constitutes informed use within a school district?
• How and in what ways can AI applications be vetted for possible use?
• How are problems of practice identified that may benefit from the integration of AI?
• How are students using generative artificial intelligence within and outside of school?
• How is artificial intelligence affecting trust between students and teachers?
• How is academic integrity and creativity understood in light of AI use?
• Where do students perceive benefit， pressure， inequity， or risk with AI?

Once a suite of questions is agreed upon， the district should determine the cadence of meetings， the
expected products or recommendations， and the adults responsible for coordination and follow-up. The
work should be connected to explicit communication routines and sharing of information.
The council’s work should then move through recurring cycles of inquiry， interpretation， and
recommendation. Students may gather input from peers， reflect on current and emergent uses of
artificial intelligence， identify where district guidance is clear or unclear， and surface tensions that
adults may not fully see. Those observations should be documented and translated into district-facing
recommendations tied to concrete areas for action， such as clarifying expectations for disclosure，
strengthening instructional supports， revising family communication， identifying where a pilot may be
warranted， or recommending caution where risks appear insufficiently addressed. Recommendations
emerging from the council should be presented by the council and reviewed by the relevant district team
and， as appropriate， translated into revisions to guidance， communication， professional learning， pilot
design， or district policy.
AI innovation spaces between P-12 and higher education
Partnerships between P-12 school districts and colleges/universities and/or schools within them
can provide a useful opportunity to jointly explore how artificial intelligence may inform teaching，
learning， professional learning， and district operations while also building local capacity and coherence
over time. These relationships are strongest when they are rooted in a clearly identified problem of
practice， shared purpose/use， and agreed-upon roles and responsibilities rather than a vague interest in
“doing something with AI.” A productive partnership should help the district answer a practical question，
generate a usable artifact， and strengthen local understanding of what implementation would require if
the work continues.
Common models
Research-Practice Partnership (RPP): A school district and institution of higher education co-design
an approach to investigate a problem of practice identified by the P-12 district. Most often， the school
district serves as “laboratory space” for implementation and the institution of higher education collects，
and potentially， publishes findings from the implementation.
University-hosted lab/pre-college program: Students and/or teachers participate in structured AI
learning experiences within specific content areas (e.g.， student-generated “problems of practice” in
areas such as mathematics or fine arts) supported through mentorship and public sharing of work at/
through an institution of higher education (See Appendix: Student AI Challenges).
Curriculum + Professional Learning (PL) model: Programming for professional learning needs of a
school district is developed and offered through an institution of higher education.
Co-development of tools in authentic classrooms: Researchers build and test AI-enabled supports with
teachers as co-designers.

AI innovation spaces between P-12 districts and for-profit companies or other organizations
While the relationship between a P-12 district and for-profit company or organization can accelerate
access to tools， training， and real-world problem contexts， they also create the highest risk of missteps
when data rights， use of student or district work for marketing purposes， and decision authority are
unclear. Successful relationships are explicit about data security and ownership (e.g.， what data is
collected， who owns the data， and the scope and use of products); student and school protections; cost;
cadence of and timelines for evaluation and needed refinements; stop and scaling criteria; and the like.
Common model and application pathways
Vendor pilot within district: Deployment of a platform developed by a company or organization for broad
instructional or operational purposes within a P-12 district. It is necessary to ensure scope of and length
for pilot (inclusive of all necessary guardrails—data share， contract(s)， district permission form， points of
contact， communications for parents/caregivers).
Two more common deliverable pathways are:
• Credential pathway: In this pathway， a module or credential structure is utilized to deliver specific
professional learning (PL). PL could lead to a credential recognized for meeting requirements for
professional license renewal or/and a subsequent endorsement tied to assignability.92 In addition to
any ”AI component” of this pathway， aspects such as mentoring and research， among others， may be
part of the initial implementation or emerge on account of it. If these are identified as necessary，
then the scope of the work that requires both parties must be explicitly described within relevant
contracts and other documents that are required.
• Studio/lab pathway: Related， at least partially， to the “sandbox” approach identified previously，
this pathway utilizes AI as a centerpiece to both test AI but through the specific application of
“challenge problems” (i.e.， problems of practice) emerging from the AI. This is in subtle distinction，
albeit artificial， to the “within district” sandbox approach insofar as the direction of and scope for
AI occurs initially from outside the P-12 district (i.e.， the company or organization may approach a
district) and support (capacity) is provided from the company or organization. Issues of capacity and
sustainability， while important in both approaches， are differently approached in light of who provides
what and when (e.g.， company supports equipment， mentors， or/and identification of challenge
problems). Regardless， it is essential that the district retains instructional authority and ability to
stop the work when issues of student safety or data privacy are identified during implementation.
For either model， it is common for a company to want to “field test” an application for purchase by
a P-12 district and， prior to doing so， conduct a beta test. However， there are instances in which a
research organization funded in whole or part by federal and philanthropic grants and/or funding may
wish to test an application and require a P-12 school， classroom， content area， or grade band to meet
approved deliverables of the grant. While caution and clarity are necessary in both instances， in the
case of the latter， the scope of deliverables are often， but not always， part of a grant application prior
to the identification of P-12 district. Thus， a district ought to be especially cautious in these instances
(See Appendix: School District Vendor Relationship Examples for specific examples of well-curated

AI for Policy II – District Policy， Governance， and Accountability
Summary
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. Familiarity of relevant AI concepts as used in
P-20 settings is important in contextualizing the history of federal and state laws tied to data privacy
generally and those data privacy issues unique to educational settings. This is especially important
with AI due to the speed in which development is and will likely continue.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
District AI policies and guidance emerge within a constellation that includes federal and state
regulation focused upon privacy， confidentiality， and public records. Most of these laws were written
before modern cloud services， social media， or AI. However， the core ideas—protecting student
information， limiting disclosure， maintaining accurate records， and ensuring transparency—carry
over into today’s AI decisions.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Due to the rapid development of
AI outside of educational settings， and to best ensure that its potential is implemented in ways that
inform instructional planning and delivery and enrich student experience， issues of data security and
student safety are paramount.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. Due to the rapid development of AI outside of educational settings，
and to best ensure that its potential is implemented in responsible ways within educational settings，
the development of three related policies， at minimum and in consultation with district legal counsel，
are needed: an AI district-wide policy， an Authorized Use Policy， and Informed Policy.
Note: The guidance uses “informed use” rather than “responsible use” save if a district or other
organization uses the term “responsible use” in a referenced document. The distinction is an
extension of the degree to which artificial intelligence is used safely or appropriately to include
if its use is educationally warranted， developmentally appropriate， and grounded in the specific
purposes of schooling.
• The tenets make that distinction important. If teaching and learning are shaped by human
relationships and by the experiences， interests， and assets each child brings into school， then AI use
cannot be judged apart from context， learner need， and the professional judgment of educators. If
schools serve academic， developmental， and civic purposes concurrently， then the standard for use
must extend beyond compliance or rule-following to include whether a use supports student learning，
healthy development， and preparation for participation in shared civic life.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 167
• “Informed use” also better reflects the guidance’s view that artificial intelligence is a means to inform
teaching and learning rather than an end in itself. “Responsible use” is valuable， but it can be read too
narrowly， as though the task is simply to avoid harm， follow rules， or use tools with caution. “Informed
use” requires something more deliberate: understanding what the tool is being used for， what it
can and cannot do， what risks or tradeoffs it introduces， what should remain human， and why local
educators must oversee implementation in order to determine whether the use fits the instructional，
developmental， and community context. In that sense， informed use names both the judgment and
the conditions the guidance seeks to cultivate.
District AI policies and guidance sit on decades of regulation focused upon privacy， confidentiality，
and public records. Most of these laws were written before modern cloud services， social media， or AI.
However， the core ideas—protecting student information， limiting disclosure， maintaining accurate
records， and ensuring transparency—carry over into today’s AI decisions. This section will share relevant
federal and state privacy laws; highlight the differences between a district-wide AI policy， an Authorized
Use Policy， and an Informed use Policy， and why each is necessary; and provide links to exemplars that
can support the development of local polices needed in Illinois districts.
Within Illinois and beginning in the late 1950s， Illinois’ State Records Act (1957， 5 ILCS 160) and Local
Records Act (1961， 50 ILCS 205) established baseline expectations for how public entities create， keep，
and dispose of records. For school districts， as work moved from paper to email to cloud platforms—
and now to AI-assisted drafting and chat logs—these statutes remain the backdrop for retention
schedules， appropriate disposal， and defensible recordkeeping.
Early federal privacy statutes introduced principles that still guide district practice. The Fair Credit
Reporting Act (FCRA， 1970) emphasized data accuracy and an individual’s right to correct information
used in decisions affecting them. The Privacy Act of 1974 established fair information practice
expectations for government-held data. In education， the Family Educational Rights and Privacy
Act (FERPA， 1974) anchored student education record protections—access， amendment， and limits
on disclosure. These early laws matter for AI as AI systems create new derived information and can
be mistakenly treated as “verdicts” rather than supports for decision-making. So too， as AI uses
the information available for its outputs， accuracy of data is essential to avoid inaccuracies and
hallucinations.
The Illinois School Student Records Act (ISSRA， 1975， 105 ILCS 10) complements FERPA by defining
student records responsibilities in Illinois contexts. Together， FERPA and ISSRA set expectations that
student records are handled with care， disclosures are limited and purposeful， and families have rights
to access and request corrections. When AI tools touch student information—directly or indirectly—
districts should treat those tools as operating inside this student-records environment.
Some information categories heightened protections. Illinois’ Mental Health and Developmental
Disabilities Confidentiality Act (MHDDCA， 1979， 740 ILCS 110) underscores strict handling of mental health
information. Health Insurance Portability and Protection Act (HIPAA) privacy and security rules (1996–
2003) shaped modern expectations for protecting health data where applicable. For districts， these
frameworks reinforce a practical rule: avoid using AI tools in ways that collect， infer， or store sensitive
health or mental health information unless the district possesses clear legal authority， safeguards， and
sustained capacity to manage risks.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 168
Illinois’ Freedom of Information Act (FOIA， 1984， 5 ILCS 140) reflects the public’s right to understand
how government entities operate. As districts increasingly use digital systems (and now AI) to create
documents， messages， and decisions， FOIA and records laws raise practical questions: what is retained，
for how long， where it is stored， how quickly it can be retrieved， and what exemptions may apply. AI use
does not remove public accountability， yet it can increase the volume and complexity of records. That
this is the case means that districts must manage its records with even greater care.
As the internet became part of daily life， laws such as the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act
(COPPA， 1998) and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA， 1999) elevated expectations for protecting
children’s online information and strengthening security controls in vendor-managed environments.
Illinois’ Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA， 2005-2020， 815 ILCS 530) and Identity Protection
Act (IPA， 2010， 5 ILCS 179) further emphasized safeguarding personal information and who “owns” this
information. This matters for AI because many AI tools are cloud-based， rely on vendor infrastructure，
and can expand the number of systems where personal information is stored or processed.
Illinois’ Internet Safety Instruction requirement (105 ILCS 5/27-410， formerly 27-13.3) reflects an evolution
from “keep students away from risky tools” to “teach students how to use technology safely” (See
Appendix: Federal and Illinois Privacy and Data Security Laws). In today’s environment， that instruction
increasingly intersects with social media dynamics and AI-enabled content creation. District guidance
can treat AI as part of broader digital citizenship: safety， privacy， integrity， and responsible participation.
Illinois’ Student Online Personal Protection Act (SOPPA， 105 ILCS 85) responded to widespread edtech
and cloud adoption by setting concrete expectations for vendor relationships and student data
protections. In practical terms， SOPPA reinforces that district should not rely on informal or “free” tools
without clear agreements， safeguards， and district oversight (i.e.， who “owns” outputs produced by AI，
and the like). For AI tools， this is often the most immediate day-to-day driver of approvals， contracts，
and required security/privacy terms.
Taken together， these laws form a layered foundation:
• Protect student records and limit disclosure
• Treat sensitive information with heightened confidentiality
• Maintain transparency and proper records management
• Ensure vendor-managed services meet security and privacy expectations
District AI policy work operationalizes these foundations through three coordinated instruments: the
district-wide AI policy (governance and guardrails)， an authorized use policy (approval conditions and
limits)， and an informed use policy (day-to-day practice and expectations).

Laws.
