The information provided in previous sections serves as a foundation to support the creation of common
understandings of purpose. By extension， this foundation and clarity of purpose should inform the “first
pass” assessment of whether an AI application， regardless of perceived potential， is a “good fit” for
instructional and/or operational uses.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 169
This part of “AI for Policy II” extends this through the development of AI policies inclusive of authorized
use and informed use policies. These are related notions but also serve at subtly different “levels of
magnification.”
As districts are asked to innovate using AI in support of teaching and learning， there is a need to also
protect students and staff and sustain public trust through clear， explainable decisions about what is
permitted， under what conditions， and why.
To reiterate， balancing the instructional benefits of AI (or any educational technology or curricular
program) must also include operational concerns including protecting student privacy—bias，
transparency， and risk assessment and management. The protecting of student privacy requires a series
of district policies， authorized uses policies， and informed use policies. These policies ensure clarity on
expectations on authorized use inclusive of repeatable routines， defined roles， documented evidence
expectations， and， maybe of most importance， a monitoring cycle that continues after adoption to
refine， as needed， those policies adopted.
Various guidance documents from the federal government and national organizations share principles
and recommendations to support districts in AI policy development so what is available for use is on
account of the thoughtful selection of AI to inform instruction and enrich student engagement. Federal
education guidance suggests the importance of shared understanding and local policy development so
that districts can realize educational benefits while managing predictable risks.94 So too， the National
Institute of Standards and Technology’s AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)95 and its Generative
AI Profile96 provide framework and terminology that is likely important as a district engages in policy
development.
Generally， AI policy is for system-level governance and safeguards， the AUP for permissions and
minimum conditions of access， and the IUP for shared norms and accountability and instruction for the
competencies needed to comply.97
The goal in sharing what follows is not to outsource decisions that a district can “cut and paste into a
policy and adopt.” Rather， it is to ground local decision-making in recognized practices， communicate
decisions in plain language that comports with federal laws， as well as capture the unique needs of a
district while also considering capacity and sustainability (See: Appendix: AI Concepts: District Next
Steps [AI Policy， AUP， IUP] for suggested connections between central concepts in AI and AI Policy， AUP，
and IUP).
District Policies for AI
What follows is a description of each policy， rationale for its necessity， and questions surrounding the
need for concurrent consideration of capacity and sustainability. Then， suggested categories and
minimum components are presented (Table 8: Categories and Components).
The suggestions are not legal advice. As in the development of any policy within a P-12 public school
district， a district should consult with its legal counsel.

District AI Policy (District governance: oversight， procurement， risk， accountability)98
The district AI policy is the district’s governance instrument: it establishes decision rights， approval
gates， risk-tiering， lifecycle oversight， and vendor/procurement expectations for AI used for instruction
and operations. It should align to statewide AI guidance requirements (where applicable)， student
data privacy/records law， public records/retention obligations， and nondiscrimination/accessibility
obligations.
• District AI policy minimums (governance and safeguards): define AI scope/definitions; establish
approval/procurement requirements and vendor controls for edtech/AI systems; set privacy/
security requirements for data sharing， retention， and breach response; require human review for
consequential decisions; and require monitoring， evaluation， and incident reporting
• District AI policy transparency and accountability: specify recordkeeping expectations for approvals，
evaluations， and contracts (including public transparency obligations and retention schedules as
applicable)
• Civil rights and disability access: require evaluation for discriminatory impact and accessibility
barriers; ensure accommodations and equal access for students with disabilities and protected
classes when AI tools are used in instruction or services. Artificial intelligence systems should
not independently determine special education eligibility， student discipline outcomes， teacher
evaluations， hiring decisions， or other high-stakes determinations without documented human
review and district accountability processes
Rationale for necessity (why the district AI policy must exist as its own instrument):
• Governance is required to make AI use auditable and consistent district-wide (who can approve，
what evidence is required， and what monitoring must occur)， rather than relying on ad hoc building-
by-building decisions.
• Procurement and vendor controls must be centralized to ensure student-data protections and
enforceable operator obligations (including data-use limits， retention/deletion， and breach response
expectations).
• Public-sector transparency and records obligations attach to AI-related approvals and
documentation (contracts， evaluations， and decision records)， which requires an explicit governance
framework for retention and lawful disclosure/exemptions.
• Civil rights and accessibility obligations require proactive evaluation and mitigation when AI
influences services or decisions， particularly where disparate impact or accessibility barriers may
arise.
• Statewide expectations for AI guidance make it necessary to codify district practice in a formal
policy framework rather than leaving AI use to informal norms.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 171
Capacity and sustainability
• What district outcomes are we willing to fund and staff for two to three years (not just one semester)?
What outcomes are not resourced and therefore should not be promised?
• What decisions must remain human-led regardless of tool performance (e.g.， grading， placement，
discipline， special education determinations， staff evaluation)?
• What is the governance operating model (who approves， who monitors， who can pause use， and how
quickly)?
• What is our minimum support model to avoid fragile dependency on single champions (coverage for
PD， onboarding， troubleshooting， incident response)?
• What is our change-management rule when tools/models change mid-year (re-approval triggers， re-
training triggers， communication triggers)?
• What is the district’s sustainability threshold for scaling (minimum staffing， minimum budget line，
minimum infrastructure readiness)?
Acceptable Use Policy
The AUP is the district’s permission structure: what users may access， under what conditions， and what
must be true before a tool can be used (approved accounts， age/grade restrictions， supervision， and
data-handling rules).
• AUP minimums for AI: use district-approved tools when student data/work is involved; do not enter
identifiable student information into public tools; treat AI output as a draft/hypothesis requiring
verification
• AUP enforcement: prohibited uses (cheating， harassment， impersonation/deepfakes to harm，
bypassing controls)， reporting routes， and graduated consequences
Rationale for necessity (why the AUP must exist as its own instrument):
• The AUP is the enforceable access/permission layer that translates legal and operational

Informed Use Policy
The IUP is the district’s norms-and-conduct document: how users are expected to exercise judgment
(not just comply with technical rules)， including honesty/disclosure， safety， respect， and accountability
for outcomes when AI is used.
• IUP minimums for AI: disclose meaningful AI assistance when required; do not use AI to impersonate，
humiliate， or deceive; cite sources and verify factual claims; follow teacher/district boundaries for
assessment and collaboration
• “Trust-but-verify” norm: humans remain accountable; students must be able to explain and
defend work with non-AI evidence; staff must corroborate AI-supported decisions with appropriate
professional judgment and district-approved evidence
Rationale for necessity (why the IUP must exist as its own instrument):
• Rules alone do not create safe practice; behavior norms are required to prevent predictable misuse
(deception， impersonation， harassment， and harmful deepfakes) that can occur even when access is
technically permitted.
• The IUP explicitly protects students’ civil rights and inclusion in daily use by establishing
expectations that reduce discriminatory conduct and ensure respectful participation—particularly
critical where AI can amplify bias or harassment.
• It supports instructional integrity by setting expectations for disclosure， verification， and source
integrity—especially important where AI can fabricate content or citations and blur authorship.
• It operationalizes internet safety education and well-being expectations by making clear what
responsible online/AI behavior looks like and how to report concerns.

Summary
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school.
Student well-being in the context of social media and AI emerges within nested systems of
development that include relationships， routines， institutional policies， community conditions，
cultural norms， and change over time.
Providing multiple means through which students can grapple with concerns， questions， and
recommendations through facilitated conversations， as well as through reflection on their “real-time”
use， is especially important.
Curation of AI applications must privilege student development and be grounded in a teacher’s local
knowledge of the class and of individual students， including their interests， learning profile， and
readiness level.
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life.
Questions about social media， AI， and student well-being are not only matters of academic
performance or technical use. They also involve the development of Self， confidence， competence，
judgment， and participation in shared life with others.
Curation of AI applications should not be limited to content-specific learning alone but should also
support the broader developmental purposes of schooling.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning.

development and as a participant in larger society and through content-specific learning.
• AI should not be treated as a stand-alone solution or as a neutral presence but as a tool whose

healthy and holistic development.

determined purpose and use.

environments， community conditions， cultural norms， and change over time. Because of this，
facilitated conversations， reflection on “real-time’” use， and the teacher’s deliberate decisions based
on local knowledge of students are essential.

Development as an Individual and Citizen – An Ecological Framework
The central purpose of this document is to provide guidance on how a district may capitalize on the
potentials of AI while mitigating its potential negative effects and erosion of the student-teacher
relationship that is central to teaching and learning. Apart from what a student likely needs to know，
understand， and be able to do with technology， it is even more important that the child as a student is
aware of the appropriate use of the technology and an understanding of ‘Self.’ Thus， this section benefits
from a grounding in a recognized theory of development. For this， Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems
Theory of development is used. Teachers understand that all learning is social and emotional. In this
section， Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory of development will ground the consideration of
student learning and growth and consider ways that the use of AI can align with teachers’ efforts to foster
social and emotional learning
Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory explains human development as the product of dynamic，
reciprocal deliberate interactions (i.e.， “proximal processes”)101 between a developing person and a set
of nested environmental systems that range from immediate， face-to-face settings (e.g.， family， peers，
classrooms) to the broader interconnections among those settings， to indirect contexts that shape
daily life (e.g.， workplace policies， community institutions)， and finally to the cultural， economic， and
political patterns that organize society; development is also shaped by change over time (life transitions
and historical context).102 This framework shifts attention away from “the child as independent agent”
toward the conditions and relationships (i.e.， child as citizen) that make healthy development more or
less likely， emphasizing that outcomes depend on how systems align (or conflict) and on the quality and
consistency of everyday interactions and supports.103
There are five interdependent systems (See Figure 4: Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory).
The brief descriptions that follow are contextualized through the broad lens of digital literacy and digital
citizenship.
1. Microsystem – The child’s development over time is most directly shaped by their immediate settings
and interactions with caregivers， teachers， peers， and immediate environments (e.g.， classrooms，
team rooms). Note， that in the current world， group chats and other means of interactions via social
media and available applications constitute “interactions.” This suggests that students are supported
in clarity on the use of AI/edtech as a support (not substitute for) human guidance， feedback， and
emotional regulation coaching.
2. Mesosystem – The student’s development is influenced by how settings， individuals， and particulars
of experiences within each are interconnected (e.g.， home and family caregivers， school and school
personnel). The likelihood of healthy development over time is increased when use of AI in these
settings is framed with consistency of and clarity about ethical use and appropriate expectations
for using common language， shared reporting pathways， coherent norms for AI use expectations
consistent across settings and that a student is able express and to reflect on how they are thinking
and feeling about their ‘Self’ in light of these.
3. Exosystem – these systems affect， albeit indirectly， the development of the child. The child is
affected by decisions made in settings they do not control (e.g.， local customs， district and school
policies). It is essential that the adults with whom the child interacts prioritize the safety of the child
‘as a student’ and in concert with opportunities for engagement with AI that accentuate learning
about content and reflect upon how experiences support or hinder development of ‘Self.’
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 181
4. Macrosystem – the larger culture， norms， law， and values that ‘surround; a child ‘as a’ citizen， student，
and the like. Ensuring the child is aware of cultural norms and policy choices broadly and with the use
of AI in particular frame what is considered acceptable， safe， and equitable is paramount. Moreover，
opportunities for a child to reflect on they interpret their identity， belonging， and status through their
different roles and the tools that are used within each is essential.
5. Chronosystem – Development unfolds across time; the availability of and access to resources
changes over time as do the interests， readiness level， and learning profile of the child (and eventually
adult) ‘as a’ citizen， student， caregiver， and the like. While it is likely impossible to predict the precise
changes to what resources are developed and how these are used， it is essential that a child ‘as a’
student is provided regular opportunities to engage upon how their view of ‘Self’ is affected by the
unavoidable interactions with it through their work in the world. Use of and reflection upon AI is a
powerful means of doing this.104

Selection of AI Applications
The previous cases use AI for teacher- and student-facilitated reflection on feelings toward AI and
questions about particular interactions with AI in respect to “Self” and as a citizen. This iterative set
of engagements is， as suggested through the lens of Bronfenbrenner， essential due to unavoidable
time-laden reality in which development occurs. Moreover， students do possess opinions on the
appropriateness and comfort with AI use for instructional purposes (see Appendix: Students Sense of
Self， Engagement， and Agency in AI – mediated schoolwork).
There is， then， utility in suggesting questions a teacher could use when contemplating the
appropriateness for using AI in a lesson or unit.105
Teacher Questions Before Selecting AI to Enrich Content Engagement
The subsequent questions can aid a teacher in determining if there is a likely goodness of fit between
their intuition that AI may enrich student experiences—balancing content and supporting student well-
being—and if， where and when AI is used， it is positioned as a support for student thinking and not a
replacement for reasoning， explanation， or identity/agency.
Purpose and learning value
• What specific content goal will AI strengthen (conceptual understanding， representations， feedback
cycles)—and what evidence will show learning occurred?
• What is the learning problem I’m solving—and is AI the right tool for that problem (versus non-AI
routines)?
• If AI were unavailable tomorrow， what would I do instead—and is that actually better for the learning
goal?
Agency and identity (selfhood and ownership)
• What part of the task is the student’s thinking work that must remain student-owned
(strategy choice， representation， justification)?
• Where is the required decision checkpoint that preserves agency (accept/reject/revise/verify)?
• Could this use signal “the tool is the smart one， not me”? If yes， what language and routines will
protect competenceand identity?

Developmental fit and SEL
• Is this use developmentally appropriate for my students (impulse control， privacy understanding，
frustration tolerance)?
• Which SEL skill will be practiced through the lesson (perseverance， help-seeking， collaboration，
repair)—and where is it explicitly taught and rehearsed?
• What emotional risks might this tool trigger (shame， dependence， anxiety， comparison)， and what is
my plan to notice and respond?
Instructional design: deepen learning rather than replace it
• Am I asking AI to generate thinking for students—or to support thinking (hints， questions， alternative
representations)?
• Where will students explain reasoning in their own words (partner talk， written justification， exit
ticket)?
Accuracy， verification， and integrity
• What is the trust-but-verify routine for AI outputs (model/estimate/corroborate/partner/teacher)?
• How will I prevent AI from becoming an answer key that undermines meaningful practice?
Equity and accessibility
• Will AI use widen gaps (tech familiarity， language privilege， access outside school)? How will I
mitigate?
• Does this support learners while preserving dignity (no public ranking， no deficit labels， no
surveillance-like uses)?
Privacy， safety， and well-being
• What data will students enter? Is it minimal， necessary， and appropriate for children?
• What is my plan if the tool produces biased， unsafe， or emotionally harmful content (stop， support，
report， alternative activity)?
Practical capacity and sustainability
• What are the routines to preview， monitor， and debrief tool use—and can I sustain it without crowding
out “relationship work?”
• If I find that this application is appropriate and enriches student experiences， what supports
are required to sustain it (training， supervision， fallback plans)?

Digital Citizenship and AI Literacy Curricula by Grade Band
The inclusion of digital citizenship with AI literacy is on account that they operate together in nearly
every modern learning context: students must be able to participate safely and responsibly in digital
environments (privacy， security， identity， respectful communication， and credibility of information) and
also understand what that means insofar as AI systems generate， filter， and influence information and
decisions (limitations， hallucinations， bias， transparency， and appropriate human oversight). Digital
citizenship informs AI literacy—the most practical， protective AI behaviors are extensions of core digital
citizenship habits—verifying claims with credible sources， recognizing persuasion and manipulation，
protecting personal data， attributing sources and disclosing assistance， and pausing before sharing or
acting. In other words， AI literacy adds AI-specific concepts and safeguards， but it rests on the broader
foundation of digital citizenship that helps students evaluate information quality， manage risk， and act
ethically across all digital tools and platforms.

The Integration of Development of Self and Citizen and AI Competencies
Recall， this guidance is grounded upon the following four tenets:
1. Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and by the experiences， interests， and
assets each child brings into school;
2. Schools serve academic， developmental， and civic purposes concurrently;
3. Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning rather than an end in itself;
4. Informed use requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally determined purpose and use.
Throughout this document， the notion of concurrent development of a child as “Self” and child as citizen
are interrogated and in light of the work that occurs in schooling. So too， grade band examples of what
digital literacy and AI literacy may “look like” are shared. What follows is a suggestion of an “integration” of
the aforementioned. This is important in order to more fully contemplate how and in what ways teaching
and learning are informed by the use of AI.
Children and adolescents engage in recurring tasks over time， but the ways those tasks are lived depend
upon relationships， routines， opportunities， expectations， and the experiences， interests， and assets
students bring into school. For instance， the expectations for a writing assignment or art project are
likely very different for a child in Grade 1 and a child in Grade 12. While both are tasked with the creation
of a written or artistic artifact， the presentation of the task， expectations for what is produced， and
evaluation criteria will differentiate based upon assumptions about the nature of the learner and specific
aspects of development (e.g.， cognitive development， social and emotional development， and the like). In
sum， instructional design should not separate cognitive demand from context.
This same framing supports a broader understanding of schooling. Academic learning， development
of self， and civic formation are interdependent dimensions. Students learn not only how to show what
they know but also how to participate， deliberate， contribute， and exercise judgment in shared settings.
Instruction， relationships， and participation structures should therefore cultivate intellectual growth
and responsible membership in community. As suggested in the guidance， the particulars of this are
collectively determined and contemplated in the creation and curation of common understandings of
purpose and use and their resultant “work products.”
None of this requires the use of AI. If， however， AI can inform teaching and learning， how might the
informed use of it support development? Most simply， digital citizenship， digital literacy， and AI literacy
are best treated as means in support of these larger aims.
Thus， in light of the four tenants that ground this guidance， it is reasonable to assume:
• Digital citizenship emphasizes participation， responsibility， privacy， relationships， and conduct in
digital spaces.
• Digital literacy emphasizes interpretation， verification， and evaluation of information.
• AI literacy extends both by helping students understand how automated systems classify， predict，
recommend， and generate， where error and bias may enter， and why human judgment remains
necessary.
• Informed use requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally determined decisions.

The matrix that follows provides a concise set of general artificial intelligence competencies and grade
band-specific suggestions for practice. These competencies are meant to support educational judgment
in light of the four tenets that ground this guidance:
1. The centrality of human relationships and student assets;
2. The concurrent academic， developmental， and civic purposes of schooling;
3. The use of artificial intelligence as a means to inform teaching and learning rather than as an end in
itself; and
4. The need for deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally determined purpose and use.
In that sense， the suggested competencies are “targets” that are part of instructional planning and
student experience and meant as part of ordinary work occurring in schools. They are drafted in ways
that allow for the local context to drive what any specific demonstration could look like and to help
practitioners consider what students and educators should understand， do， and reflect upon when AI is
introduced into teaching to support students as individuals and citizens.
So too， they are drafted as points of departure for districts in building common understandings across
audiences by clarifying what informed use may require at different grade bands and in different contexts.
Competency here includes more than familiarity with tools. It includes judgment about fit， responsibility
for use， attention to verification， and awareness of how AI may affect student learning， development， and
participation in shared civic life.
The competencies that follow are grounded in the guidance’s four tenets and should be read in light of
the larger purposes of public schooling in Illinois. The point of departure is not artificial intelligence as
an innovation in search of application but the use of AI in support of teaching and learning as relational，
developmental， and civic work. For that reason， the competencies are organized around the educational
purposes AI use is meant to serve: strengthening student learning， supporting the development of
agency and judgment， and preparing young people to participate responsibly in shared civic life.
Throughout the guidance， “common understandings” and “purpose and use” are the frames through which
any competency， tool， or practice should be interpreted. In this frame， competencies matter insofar as
they help educators， students， and school communities decide when AI use is warranted， what human
responsibilities must remain primary， and how AI may inform teaching and learning without displacing
professional judgment， student voice， or the relational conditions through which learning becomes
meaningful.106

The suggested competencies are meant to help districts and educators think more clearly about what
students should come to understand， practice， and demonstrate in a world in which learning about
computer science， generally， and artificial intelligence， in particular， is increasingly present in school and
civic life. In other words， an ecological model of development suggests that growth is a set of interacting
and reciprocating layers in which:
• The individual as a “Self” and citizen (i.e.， Microsystem)
• Engages with AI in schools and outside of them (i.e.， Mesosystem)
• These interactions are informed by:
• Immediate communities (i.e.， Exosystem)
• Societal norms， values， beyond immediate surroundings (i.e.， Macrosystem)
• All through time (i.e.， Chronosystem)
Of course， it is desirable that this occurs in ways that allow for healthy development. Thus，
considerations of AI use must move beyond how and in what contexts it is used (i.e.， limited to AI
as a ”tool”). AI use must also contemplate “outcomes”—those tied to what occurs in schools as well
as those inclusive of development of “Self” and as a citizen. Introduction to the range of ethical and
practical issues surrounding the informed use of artificial intelligence should prefigure any actual use.
Put differently， and like considerations of developing common understandings provided in an earlier
section of this guidance， taking the time to engage with students in regard to current perceptions of
the ethical and practical issues outside of “real time” applications provides teachers insight that informs
instructional planning and delivery. Moreover， these types of conversations， regardless of topic， are an
essential experience for young (and older) individuals to undergo as they learn to engage in and learn
from engagements that affect their lives and the lives of others. Movement from the inner portions of
Bronfenbrenner’s model to its outer realms are part and parcel of healthy and robust development as a
citizen. Schools are an important catalyst for this.
In sum:
• AI is important as a tool for instruction or learning and as a foundational technology for empowering
students to show their understanding of content. That empowerment requires AI literacy， the ability
for students to understand the technology and how to interrogate it (i.e.， its “fitness for the occasion”
and/or “goodness of fit”).
• All Illinois students should receive education about AI， including what it is (and is not)， how it works，
its impact on society (perceived and “real”)， and how to shape it， before and while using AI tools in the
classroom.
• AI literacy requires both fluency of the data and algorithms that power AI， how they produce certain
outputs， and the opportunity to show that one is aware of these aspects through the application of AI
for specific learning engagements.
• AI education provides an opportunity for students to gain civic and technological agency in the world
as informed and fluent in contrast to “user passive consumer.”
• Broadly， AI literacy is part of a comprehensive computer science education (e.g.， AI is “built upon”
computer science， so the topic is a critical foundation for comprehensive AI fluency).

What follows provides suggested research and policy resources on student outcomes associated with
AI use. Consideration of the impact of AI tied to student outcomes is a necessary and natural next step
emerging from the use of AI as a tool in “product development.”
Read in light of the four tenets of this guidance， the significance of these materials is broader than
whether artificial intelligence appears to “improve performance” in a narrow sense. If teaching and
learning are shaped by human relationships and by the experiences， interests， and assets each child
brings into school， then outcome claims should be examined in relation to context， development， and the
lived realities of students rather than in isolation from them. If schools serve academic， developmental，
and civic purposes concurrently， then questions about AI use must include not only achievement but also
student well-being， agency， participation， and responsibility. If artificial intelligence is a means to inform
teaching and learning， then faster production， greater convenience， or stronger task completion are
necessary but not sufficient. Moreover， if informed use requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use， then the evidence that follows should include how the implementation
improves student outcomes (or not)， in addition to descriptions of use and product development.
Accordingly， the resources gathered below are meant to help districts ask better questions about the
relationship between AI use and student outcomes. They provide a basis for considering not only what
AI may help students do but also what kinds of development， participation， and educational experience
schools intend to preserve and strengthen through its use. In that sense， this section supports the policy
work of determining whether particular uses of AI are aligned with the purposes of schooling and with
the conditions under which informed use can be justified.

Equity， Accessibility， and Student Groups
Summary
• Teaching and learning are shaped by human relationships and build upon the experiences，
interests， and assets each child brings into school. All children are “bundles of assets.” For
classroom teachers， particular attention to the interests， readiness level， and learning profile of all
students should also be applied to those identified as part of a “special population” (e.g.， multilingual
learners， gifted and talented learners， and those with IEPs/504 plans).
• Schools serve multiple purposes—they are places for academic learning and support the
development of the selfhood and prepare young people for participation in shared civic life. In
order to best support the emergence of and development for a child as an individual and member of
larger communities， it is critical for a district to pay attention to those in special populations.
• Artificial intelligence is a means to inform teaching and learning. Districts and teachers must pay
specific attention to and carefully monitor different forms of bias and in light of the goodness of fit
and fitness for the occasion of AI as a means of informing and enriching teaching and learning.
• Informed use of artificial intelligence requires deliberate， context-sensitive， and locally
determined purpose and use. District policies should， in addition to student data privacy and other
protections， specifically identify how the needs of students who are identified within a special
population are protected.
This section may also be understood through the lens of Universal Design for Learning. Similar to the
use of other frameworks in this guidance， Universal Design for Learning provides a useful point of
departure for considering AI and special populations because it begins from the premise that learner
variability is expected， an asset， and that design for teaching and learning should be responsive to
and build upon students’ interests， learning profiles， and readiness (i.e.， variability). In this sense， the
use of AI should not be understood only as a compensatory support or accommodation layered onto
instruction after barriers emerge. Rather， it should be considered in light of whether it helps reduce
barriers in advance and in ways that support the healthy development of a young person through
engagements that enhance agency.
Applied here， this means considering the extent by which AI supports multiple ways for students
to engage with content and learning experiences， access and make meaning of information， and
communicate and show understanding. This framing is important because multilingual learners，
gifted and talented learners， and students with IEPs/504 plans do not simply need “more technology”
or “different tools.” They require careful attention to the goodness of fit and fitness for the occasion
of AI as a means of informing and enriching teaching and learning. In this way， Universal Design for
Learning helps clarify why accessibility， bias control， human review， and the monitoring of student
outcomes remain cross-cutting non-negotiables throughout this section.
This section is an extension of the previous section through its focus on special populations. To be
sure， student use of AI is not one-size-fits-all.”107 In practice， multilingual learners， gifted/talented
learners， and students served under IEPs/504 plans can benefit from AI-enabled tools and AI-mediated
classroom routines. Even so， educators must be mindful that AI (or any educational technology) can also
limit or eliminate possible benefits if not carefully tailored to the needs of student groups and， more so，
individual students.108
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 230
Potential benefits include when AI is used as a scaffold for access (e.g.， translation support， multimodal
explanation， text-to-speech/speech-to-text， chunking， and extension prompts) because it can reduce
and/or expand access to both the technology and the productive use of it by a student. Without
guardrails and careful oversight of instructional purpose with actual implementation， the AI can， through
avenues of engagement and the subsequent outputs， appear to suggest developing familiarity and
mastery of content. However， what might occur， especially without careful oversight and monitoring， is
the opposite where student agency and developing content mastery is muted.
Specifically， a district that treats AI literacy and digital citizenship as generic or without specific
guardrails109 can unintentionally deny supports to students who need them， create inequitable discipline
and integrity practices， and select and scale tools that introduce disparate impacts across language，
disability， and neurodiversity patterns.110 When this occurs， there are likely undesirable consequences for
the child and their healthy development that can manifest inside and outside of school.
District AI literacy should be designed around three cross-cutting non-negotiables:
• Design for and engagement with content is predicated upon the needs of students as a learner (e.g.，
differentiated instruction/Universal Design) and what that means in light of healthy development over
time.
• AI outputs are decision support， not decisions (human review of how students can show what they
know even if/when supported by AI).
• Deliberate and regular monitoring of “bias control” through representative pre-testing and ongoing
monitoring， including prompts and student-generated work samples that reflect multilingual
language patterns， disability-related writing/communication differences， and “space” for students to
explore and show what they know in multiple ways.
• Awareness of policies and practices for identifying and eliminating limitations of AI when used for
purposes of grading and placement.
• Ensuring that if or when a district early warning is used， that data collected for it is not biased toward
specific stereotypes tied to any specific student group (e.g.， discipline data， grades， attendance
patterns).
For the purposes of this guidance:
• Multilingual learners (MLLs): Students developing English proficiency (emergent bilingual students/
English learners). Language demands are treated as individual assets， not learner deficits in planning
instruction.111
• Gifted and Talented (G/T): Students who require increased pace， depth， and complexity; in AI
contexts， common risks are over-acceleration112 without reflection and under-challenge through “fast
output.”113
• High-incidence IEP/504 needs: Common supports (e.g.， specific learning disability， ADHD/Other
Health Impairments (OHI)，114 speech-language， anxiety-related 504s). Use accessibility-first selection
and civil rights-aware implementation.115
• Twice-exceptional learner (2e) needs: Careful review for and identification of areas of strength
and those requiring additional supports. Special monitoring of social and emotional needs and
scaffolding due to the negotiation between strengths and areas of supports.116

1. Principles upon which a district or teacher can reduce bias in the selection of AI with particular

2. “Cross-cutting non-negotiables” for how AI should be considered with regards to special populations

The reader will note that these strategies are appropriate for all students and those who are charged
with their care. Further， the presentation of the subsequent information does not assume that those who
work in Illinois’ public schools are not already engaging in these practices. Rather， and what is a thread

Tips to reduce bias in selecting/using AI and related technologies
• Start with function， not labels: identify how the instructional goal(s) in light of AI as a means to
inform and enrich teaching and learning may be minimized if/when AI is used and what can be done
to anticipate and avoid (e.g.， language access， organization， reading load， anxiety coping) before
selecting a tool.
• Pre-test with representative inputs: run prompts/samples reflecting your students (names， dialect
features， multilingual phrasing， disability-related writing patterns) and document failure modes.117
• Do not treat AI outputs as verdicts: maintain human review for grading， placement， discipline， or well-
being decisions.118
• Separate accessibility tools from answer generators: explicitly permit assistive tech; define what
crosses into outsourcing thinking; teach a simple disclosure routine.119
• Use a least-harm default for well-being: if a tool mimics counseling or increases compulsive reliance，
route students to human support pathways.120
• Transparency norm: “If AI helped， say how; if AI made a mistake， we correct it.”
• Civil rights check before scaling: confirm the practice does not create disparate impacts and that a
review/appeal process exists.121
Cross-cutting non-negotiables
AI outputs are means-based and require the insight， experiences， and knowledge about those who are
the ends (i.e.， students) in determining the “goodness of fit” for AI (and in light of informing instruction
and enriching student experiences).
Design for variability from the start (i.e.， differentiation): multiple ways to access information， express
understanding， and sustain engagement.122
Bias-control through pre-testing and monitoring: representative prompts， documented failure modes，
and clear “do-not-use” boundaries when harms appear.123

Multilingual Learners
Universal Design
AI may be beneficial for multilingual learners when it expands multiple means of representation and
engagement—for example， by supporting translation， alternative explanations， vocabulary clarification，
oral language supports， or culturally responsive companion resources. In this way， AI may be appropriate
when it helps preserve language as an asset， broadens access to content， and supports participation
across home language and English， while still requiring educator review for accuracy， bias， and
consequential decisions.
High-value AI uses:
• Language access supports (clarifying directions， vocabulary supports， sentence frames) aligned to
language goals—without outsourcing thinking
Common risks to anticipate:
• Translation drift (meaning/tone changes)
• Culturally confusing idioms
• AI overcorrection that flattens bilingual voice
Norms:
• Do: Require a “meaning check” (student paraphrases in own words; oral is allowed)
• Do: Use WIDA-informed prompting (grade cluster， proficiency level， language function) to avoid
generic outputs
• Do not: Treat “sounds different” as suspicion; integrity concerns must be conversation-first and
evidence-based
Classroom protocol — two languages， one idea
• Student drafts an idea in the strongest language (words/sketch/bullets)
• AI supports one target only (vocabulary OR sentence frame OR clarity check)
• Student discloses: “Here’s my idea， and here’s how AI helped.”
Example: A student drafts in Spanish， then uses AI to generate two sentence-frame options
in English. The student chooses one and explains the meaning orally; the teacher affirms
authorship and bilingual identity.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 233
Gifted and Talented
Universal Design
AI may be beneficial for gifted and talented learners when it increases opportunities for challenge，
depth， complexity， autonomy， and varied forms of action and expression. In this context， AI should
be understood less as a shortcut to faster answers and more as a means to support inquiry， critique，
simulation， design， and advanced production. In this way， AI may be appropriate when it extends rigor
and metacognitive challenge while preserving originality and student voice.
High-value uses:
• Complexity and depth (counterarguments， critique practice， debate simulation) when the student
must justify choices and reasoning
Common risks to anticipate:
• Over-acceleration without reflection
• Perfectionism/identity drift (“Was it me or the AI?”)
• Confident-but-wrong outputs presented as authoritative
• Misuse in instances of enrichment (e.g.， the AI application limits the engagements that are beneficial
for all students)
Norms:
• Do: Require metacognition as part of the deliverable (“Why accept/reject that suggestion?”)
• Do: Use AI primarily for critique/audit/providing alternative perspectives (sources， logic，
counterarguments) rather than drafting final products
• Do not: Reward speed as a proxy for learning; score process evidence and intellectual honesty
Classroom protocol — AI as sparring partner
• Student writes a claim
• AI generates a strong counterclaim
• Student responds using evidence and identifies one weakness in AI reasoning
Example: A student submits a highly polished draft. The teacher shifts the task to a critique
memo: where the AI overgeneralizes， where sourcing is weak/missing， and rationale and
support for the student’s “authentic stance.”
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 234
High-Incidence Learning Disability124
Universal Design
AI may be beneficial for students with high-incidence learning disabilities when it increases access
through multiple means of representation and action and expression， such as text-to-speech， speech-
to-text， visual supports， simplified explanations， executive-function supports， or alternative formats
for showing understanding. AI may be appropriate when it reduces barriers to participation and
communication， but it should not be treated as a substitute for educator judgment or as independent
evidence about student ability， behavior， or level of need in consequential decisions.
High-value uses:
• Accessibility and executive-function supports (text-to-speech， speech-to-text， planning/checklists，
chunking)
Common risks to anticipate:
• Conflating accommodations with cheating
• Using AI features that replace skill-building rather than scaffold it
• Inequitable integrity enforcement based on heuristics or automated flags
Norms:
• Do: Explicitly distinguish assistive/access tools and limits of GenAI outputs
• Do: Use gradual release: AI supports outlining/checking; student owns claims and justification
• Do not: Use AI detection or automated flags as determinative evidence; require human review and
student conference
Classroom protocol — barrier ➞ support ➞ proof of learning
• Identify the barrier (reading load/organization/transcription)
• Select the matching support feature (text-to-speech， dictation， outline， checklist)
• Require proof of learning (oral explanation， annotated draft， mini-conference)
Example: A student with dysgraphia dictates a response (access)， then uses AI to clarify
sentences. The student highlights three revised sentences and explains intended meaning
and why the final wording fits.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 235
Twice Exceptional125
Universal Design
AI may be beneficial for twice-exceptional learners when it augments student strengths while also
providing scaffolding where needed. Because Universal Design for Learning begins from the premise
that learner variability is expected rather than exceptional， it is especially useful in considering students
whose profiles combine advanced capability with other needs. In this way， AI may be appropriate
when it supports both challenge and access—for example， by enabling advanced exploration， creative
production， or problem solving while also supporting organization， communication， or executive
functioning.
High-value uses:
• Simultaneous enrichment (ceiling) and support (access/executive function) explicitly designed so
gifts and needs are both addressed
Common risks to anticipate:
• Adults see only strengths or only challenges
• AI can mask disability needs (over-smoothing) or dilute challenge (over-simplified personalization)
Norms:
• Do: Plan with a dual lens: “raise the ceiling and lower the barriers”
• Do: Co-design AI boundaries with the student: what is scaffold versus what must remain student
authored
• Do not: Assume high verbal ability implies high executive function; make planning supports explicit
Classroom protocol — Ceiling and scaffold plan document
• Column A of document: Make it more challenging (depth/novelty)
• Column B of document: Make it doable (access/structure)
• AI is permitted only for pre-approved items in Column B
Example: AI generates a lab report outline/checklist (scaffold)， while the student must add
original hypotheses and critique limitations (ceiling). Conference prompt: “What part is yours
versus scaffold?”

Avoiding personal bias and identifying bias within AI tools under consideration
Personal bias checks (teacher self-audit)
• “What am I assuming about ability， motivation， honesty， or home support—and what evidence do I
actually have?”
• “Would I respond the same way if this student’s name/voice/home language/disability status were
different?”
• “What language might I inadvertently use that is ‘deficit based’? What can I replace to focus on the
student as a ‘bundle of assets’?” (e.g.， replace trait claims [“lazy，” “doesn’t care”] with barrier claims
[reading load， processing time， language demand， sensory load].)
AI bias checks (tool audit before classroom use)
• Run 6–10 prompts that reflect your students (names， dialect features， multilingual phrasing，
disability-related writing patterns)
• Look for stereotypes， lower expectations， harsher tone， unsafe well-being advice， and confident-but-
wrong claims
• If the tool influences high-stakes outcomes (grading， placement， discipline， safety)， require human
review plus clear override and appeal processes
Implementation safeguards (during use)
• Remember: “AI may assist; humans are accountable.” Share with students how AI is used and the
expectation that they disclose how they used AI.
• Even though students may engage with the same content， make clear that different supports are
used so each student may show what they know in ways based upon their individual assets (e.g.，
interests， readiness level， and learning profile).
• Make clear with students the ongoing monitoring that is used to avoid bias and the various means
through which they can share their examples of where the tool fails/harm is experienced， for whom，
and under what conditions.
• Artificial intelligence systems should not independently determine special education eligibility，
student discipline outcomes， teacher evaluations， hiring decisions， or other high-stakes
determinations without documented human review and district accountability processes.

• Speech-to-text
• Predictive writing
• Executive functioning supports
• Visual supports
• Multilingual scaffolds

AI for Operations and Instruction
Districts must verify， document， and continuously monitor compliance with applicable federal and Illinois
requirements before approving any AI tool or feature for operational or instructional use. This includes
(as applicable) SOPPA (105 ILCS 85)， the Illinois School Student Records Act (105 ILCS 10)， FERPA， COPPA，
PPRA， and relevant board policies and procurement rules. Nothing in this document constitutes legal
advice. Districts should consult legal counsel and their data privacy officer before approving tools，
enabling AI features， or changing data-sharing practices. The subsequent list reflects tools that are
commonly considered for district use and may be eligible for approval when procured and configured
under district terms.

Final Considerations and Next Steps
The purpose of the guidance is to provide cases， frameworks， and suggestions for how to approach the
work of informed integration of AI in school district practices. This integration， and reflection upon it，
deliberately emerges from the belief that AI is a means to improve teaching and learning and not an end in
and of itself. As supported throughout the guidance:

Stated differently:
• The purpose of any selection and implementation of an educational technology is to enrich student
experience and afford them the opportunity to develop and enrich their sense of self as an individual
as well as a participant in multiple communities.
• Familiarity of AI concepts relevant to district leaders， teachers， students， families/caregivers， and
community members/advocates is likely very different. Selecting a set of concepts and providing
suggestions of why these matter in light of AI use in P-12 educational settings is an important point of
departure in developing common understandings and subsequent identification of purpose/use.
• Any consideration of the possibility for and benefits of AI use to inform teaching and
learning practices should use a recognizable framework in order to compare current
instructional planning without AI in contrast to when AI is incorporated.
• Regardless of benefits of and limitations for AI in P-12 educational settings， “prework” internal to a
district and then outside of it to develop common understandings of purpose(s) and use(s) is critical.
The means for and cadence of this work is deliberate and requires coalition building to maximize use
for instructions and operations within a district.
• Once purpose(s) and use(s) are clear with different audiences， considerations of specific
applications should focus on informing instruction and enriching student experience， and creating
efficiencies in and for district and school operations by ensuring compliance with federal and state
laws and regulations through district policy development.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 253
• Whereas district policies are necessary to frame the landscape of engagement for districts
and schools， these engagements take place in classrooms. Providing students and teachers
opportunities to consider the “ethical uses” of AI， inclusive of special populations and in
developmentally appropriate ways， is important.
The Illinois AI Guidance treats AI as a means to strengthen student learning， well-being， equity， and
operational reliability—never as an end in itself. From the outset， districts must balance decisions about
AI and AI-enabled decisions upon purpose， use， and outcomes， with an explicit expectation that districts
surface tradeoffs， anticipate unintended consequences， and articulate how AI-enabled decisions
support human flourishing even when or if the initial motivation is efficiency.
To reiterate another theme from this guidance， the teacher possesses the professional knowledge
to appropriately make decisions about what particular students require to learn content and， more
importantly， develop a sense of “Self” through engagements that build upon the numerous assets that
they bring into the classroom. The “Self” is a bundle of assets that each child brings to their engagements
inside and out of school. Those closest to the child， their interests and preferred ways of engaging
in them， are critical in supporting the engagements and subsequent reflections upon them that are
essential in healthy development as an individual and participant in multiple communities within and
outside of schools. To be sure， the school is a common place in which a child can “try on” different
identities through engagement with others and academic content. These engagements， while they may
include AI in some instances， cannot replace and should not replace the interpersonal engagements that
are part of the school day.
AI is neither a replacement for student-teacher engagement nor a shortcut to instructional delivery
of the ways in which a student may show understanding. AI can， however， extend access to feedback，
translation， drafting supports， and planning efficiencies—while honoring the centrality of and importance
for teacher expertise and student agency demonstrated in the everyday interactions in which teaching
and learning occur. It is through these “real” engagements with “real” people that a sense of “Self”
emerges. AI is likely an unavoidable part of these engagements; thus， vigilance of its use in support of the
healthy development of a child is necessary.

Appendix: Implementation Checklist
1. Purpose and instructional fit
Write the learning goal as a student outcome (e.g.， “Students will revise claims using evidence”)， not
“Students will use AI.” Name the non-goal clearly (what remains student work). Prefer the simplest tool
that meets the need.
• I can state the learning objective in one sentence (what students will learn/do).
• I can state the non-goal in one sentence (what AI must NOT replace).
• The tool improves learning or access versus a non-AI option (not just novelty).
• I identified the “human decision points” (where teacher and/or student judgment is required).
2. Student role and agency
Treat AI outputs as suggestions. Require students to choose what to keep， explain why， and revise. Build
a short reflection routine so the learning is visible and assessable.
• Students must make decisions (choose， justify， revise)， not simply accept outputs.
• A short reflection is built in (“What changed and why?”).
• The task requires evidence of student thinking (notes， drafts， oral explanation， annotations).
3. Privacy and data minimization
Map data-in/data-out: what students enter， what the tool stores， who can access it， and how long it is
retained. Minimize inputs. Do not include names， IDs， faces/photos， contact info， or personal stories. If
data handling is unclear， pause use.
• Students will not enter names， IDs， faces/photos， contact info， addresses， or personal stories.
• I know what data is entered/uploaded， what is stored， who can access it， and retention/deletion rules.
• Student accounts are district-vetted if needed; otherwise， use teacher-mediated access.
• Classroom norm is explicit: “No personal data in prompts.”
4. Transparency and explainability
You should be able to explain what the tool does， the limits of its outputs， and how students verify
content. Establish a verification routine using trusted sources or course materials.
• I can explain what the tool does (and cannot do) in plain language.
• Students understand AI can be wrong， incomplete， or biased.
• Students have a verification routine (check with trusted sources/class materials).
5. Bias， equity， and accessibility
Test the tool with diverse names， dialects， reading levels， and multilingual phrasing. Look for
stereotyping or uneven quality. Provide an equally rigorous non-AI pathway. Ensure accessibility
supports match student needs.
• I tested with diverse names/dialects/reading levels/multilingual phrasing.
• I looked for stereotyping， uneven tone， or uneven quality of support.
• A non-AI pathway exists that is equally rigorous and accessible.
• Accessibility needs are supported (readability， read-aloud， translation supports， and the like).
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 289
6. Safety and classroom management
Confirm safeguards are appropriate for student exposure. Establish explicit norms (time， purpose，
supervision). Have a response plan for misuse: reteach， restrict， or discontinue.
• Safeguards are adequate for student exposure (filters， reporting， teacher controls).
• I have clear norms for when/how long/how the tool is used.
• I have a plan for misuse (reteach ➞ restrict ➞ discontinue).
7. Academic integrity and attribution
Define allowed vs. not allowed use for each assignment. Require a simple disclosure statement and build
assessment methods that rely on human evidence (drafts， conferencing， in-class writing， oral defense).
• Allowed vs. not allowed use is stated for this assignment.
• Students disclose how AI was used (one or two sentences).
• The assessment includes “human evidence” (in-class work， drafts， conferencing， etc.).
8. Pilot， monitoring， evaluation， and exit
While these four aspects are more frequently tied to district-level selection of products， they are
important to map out prior to the selection of an AI product at the classroom level.
General Tips
Pilot first， set a review date， and decide success/stop indicators in advance. Use work samples to
determine whether the tool improves learning outcomes without increasing risk.
• I will pilot first and set a review date.
• I have success indicators (learning， engagement， access).
• I have stop indicators (privacy concern， inequitable outcomes， repeated misuse).
Hard “Stop” Flags (do not proceed until/unless resolved)
• Requires student personal accounts without district approval.
• Unclear retention/reuse of student inputs.
• Produces final work with minimal student thinking.
• Encourages surveillance-like monitoring or high-stakes decisions.

Grade- Band Specific Example Extensions
Grade-Band Add-On Checklist — Pre-K through Grade 2
• Default is teacher-operated (no student accounts; no direct student chat).
• Student-facing use (if any) is highly constrained (short， scripted， supervised).
• The tool supports language， play， curiosity， and teacher-guided talk (does not replace human
interaction).
• Families receive a plain-language note about purpose， supervision， and data minimization.
Grade-Band Add-On Checklist — Grades 3–5
• Tool use is bounded to brainstorm/outline/feedback/revision work (not full answers).
• Students use structured prompts (sentence starters， rubric-aligned questions).
• Students use a verification routine: True? Fair/kind? Mine?
• Students provide a short disclosure: “I used AI to ___; I changed ___.”
Grade-Band Add-On Checklist — Grades 6–8
• Tool use explicitly strengthens AI literacy: verification， bias detection， revision， source evaluation.
• Students must produce process evidence (annotations， revision log， reasoning steps).
• Guardrails address peer dynamics (misuse， harassment， rumor spreading， deepfake-like behavior).
• Teacher checks that the tool does not substitute for core skill development.
Grade-Band Add-On Checklist — Grades 9–12
• Integrity design is explicit: authorship， citation， and process evidence are required.
• Students defend work through oral explanation， drafts， and evidence trails.
• Tool terms (ownership/reuse) are acceptable for school use; students avoid uploading copyrighted or
sensitive materials.
• Use mirrors responsible real-world practice: versioning， citation， verification， and data ethics.

Appendix: Misalignment Scenarios and Prompt Quality Examples
This appendix provides scenarios to illustrate what can occur when the prompt does not align with the AI
tool category (text vs. image vs. audio; generation vs. editing; evidence vs. illustration).
PreK-Grade 2 – Asking an image generator for an editable poem (Text task -> Image tool)
• Misaligned ask: “Write a 4-line rhyming poem about sharing that I can copy into my journal.”
• Tool category misfit: Image generation (2D)
• A cute poster image with text embedded in pixels
• Misspellings， broken words， incorrect rhyme， odd line breaks
• Not copy/paste-friendly; difficult to revise with young learners
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: If the goal is editable text， use a text-generation tool. Image tools can display
text but are not optimized for rhyme， meter， or editable output.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): Use a text tool: “Write a 4-line poem for Grade 1， AABB rhyme， simple
vocabulary， include a title， provide as plain text.”
PreK-Grade 2 – Asking a text chatbot to “make a picture” (Image task -> Text-only tool)
• Misaligned ask: “Create a simple 2D drawing of a squirrel holding an acorn for my phonics slide.”
• Tool category misfit: Text-only chatbot (no image output)
• A description of a squirrel or step-by-step drawing instructions
• No usable image asset for the slide
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: If the deliverable is a visual asset， select a tool that can generate or edit
images (or use a design tool with embedded image generation).
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): Use an image tool: “Flat 2D cartoon squirrel holding an acorn; clean
shapes; classroom-friendly; no text; white background; 16:9.”
Grades 3-5 – Requesting an accurately labeled diagram from a style-forward image tool (Precision ->
Aesthetic)
• Misaligned ask: “Generate a labeled diagram of the water cycle with accurate labels and arrows.”
• Tool category misfit: Image generation focused on aesthetics rather than editable labeling
• A visually appealing diagram with incorrect arrows， invented terms， or misspellings
• Labels rendered as garbled or inconsistent text
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: Image generators often struggle with accurate， editable labels. For
instruction， separate illustration from labeling.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): “Create a water cycle illustration with no labels.” Add labels manually in
Slides/Docs to ensure accuracy and readability.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 299
Grades 3-5 – Asking a general text generator for real citations (Citation task -> Non-verifying tool)
• Misaligned ask: “Make a bibliography for my animal report with real sources.”
• Tool category misfit: General text generation without a source-verification workflow
• Plausible-looking citations that are incomplete， mismatched， or not real
• Students assume citations are valid because they look academic.
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: Citation building is a verification task. Use a workflow that requires traceable
sources.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): “Use these 3 approved links (paste URLs). Create a bibliography in the
required format. Do not invent sources.”
Grades 6-8 – Asking a stem-separation tool to compose original music (Creation -> Editing tool)
• Misaligned ask: “Make an original beat and melody for my podcast intro.”
• Tool category misfit: Stem separation (designed to split existing audio into parts)
• The tool asks for an upload and returns separated parts of an existing track.
• Students conclude “AI can’t compose” when the real issue is the wrong tool type.
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: Generating new music and editing existing music are different tool families.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): Use a music-generation tool: “Create a 20-second instrumental intro，
90-110 bpm， upbeat， no vocals， simple structure (intro -> hook).”
Grades 6-8 -–Using a writing/polish tool for multi-step math reasoning (Reasoning -> Prose tool)
• Misaligned ask: “Solve this ratio problem and show each step clearly.”
• Tool category misfit: Text tool optimized for style/rewrites rather than mathematical verification
• Smooth explanations with incorrect calculations
• Steps that sound logical but do not check out
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: For math， good fit includes a verification routine (recompute， alternate
method， sanity check)， not only fluent prose.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): “Solve and show steps. Then verify using a second method. If answers
differ， explain why.”
Grades 9-12 – Using an image generator to create evidence for a history claim (Evidence -> Synthetic
media)
• Misaligned ask: “Make an image of a 1968 protest that proves my argument; I’ll cite it as evidence.”
• Tool category misfit: Image generation (synthetic output) used as documentation
• A plausible image with anachronisms， invented signage， or false details
• Students treat synthetic media as a primary source.
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: AI images can be illustrations， not evidence. History claims require authentic
sources.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): “Create an illustrative image inspired by the era. Add a visible label: ‘AI-
generated illustration (not a historical photograph).’”
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 300
Grades 9-12 – Asking for peer-reviewed scientific citations from a general text tool (High-accuracy ->
Ungrounded draft)
• Misaligned ask: “Explain CRISPR and include peer-reviewed citations.”
• Tool category misfit: General text tool without guaranteed grounding
• A coherent explanation with shaky attribution
• Citation-like references that do not match claims or cannot be located
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: Science writing requires source traceability. AI can draft， but the workflow
must enforce verification.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): “Summarize CRISPR using only these verified sources (paste links). For
each claim， include the source link next to it.”
Grades 9-12 – Asking a music generator to precisely edit a copyrighted track (Editing -> Generation
tool; rights mismatch)
• Misaligned ask: “Remove vocals， master the mix， and export a performance-ready instrumental of this
popular song.”
• Tool category misfit: Text-to-music generation (creates new audio， not precise edits of provided
tracks)
• The tool generates a new track that does not match the original.
• Students confuse style imitation with editing.
• Potential rights issues depending on intended use/distribution
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: Precise audio edits require editing/restoration tools. Fit also includes legal/
ethical fit.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): “From an original student-created recording， remove background noise
and balance levels. Do not use copyrighted tracks.”
Grades 9-12 – Asking for detailed audio feedback without audio input (Audio analysis -> Text-only tool)
• Misaligned ask: “Listen to this choir recording and give detailed feedback on blend， intonation， and
diction.”
• Tool category misfit: Text-only model without the ability to ingest audio
• Generic feedback not tied to the actual performance
• Specific-sounding language that is not evidence-based
• Goodness-of-fit lesson: If the tool cannot access the input modality， it cannot provide authentic
analysis—only general coaching.
• Better-fit prompt (clear ask): Use an audio-capable tool if policy-approved， or provide time-stamped
notes (e.g.， “0:12 sharp sopranos”). Ask for targeted warm-ups and rehearsal strategies.
Artificial Intelligence Guidance | 301
Why Goodness of Fit Matters
• Match the modality to the deliverable: editable text is not pixels; waveform edits are not new
composition
• Match the task type: generation vs. editing vs. layout/publishing require different tools
• Name constraints in the prompt: grade-level vocabulary， length， format， reading level， and “do not
include” items
• Separate illustration from evidence: AI-generated media can support explanation， not serve as proof
• Build verification into the ask: recompute， cross-check sources， cite only provided links， label
generated artifacts
• Include P-12 guardrails in prompts: avoid student PII; ensure age/terms compliance; require teacher
review for high-stakes use
Prompt Clarity Mini Checklist
A clear prompt specifies:
• Deliverable (what will be produced)
• Audience/grade band (who it is for)
• Constraints (length， style， reading level， format)
• Inputs allowed (approved sources/links; no student PII)
• Non-goals (what not to do)
• Verification step (how to check correctness)

Sec. 27-410. Internet safety education curriculum.
a. The purpose of this Section is to inform and protect students from inappropriate or illegal
communications and solicitation and to encourage school districts to provide education about
Internet threats and risks， including without limitation child predators， fraud， and other dangers.
b. The General Assembly finds and declares the following:
1. it is the policy of this State to protect consumers and Illinois residents from deceptive and unsafe
communications that result in harassment， exploitation， or physical harm;
2. children have easy access to the Internet at home， school， and public places;
3. the Internet is used by sexual predators and other criminals to make initial contact with children
and other vulnerable residents in Illinois; and
4. education is an effective method for preventing children from falling prey to online predators，
identity theft， and other dangers.
c. Each school may adopt an age-appropriate curriculum for Internet safety instruction of students in
grades kindergarten through 12. However， beginning with the 2009-2010 school year， a school district
must incorporate into the school curriculum a component on Internet safety to be taught at least
once each school year to students in grades 3 through 12. The school board shall determine the scope
and duration of this unit of instruction.
The age-appropriate unit of instruction may be incorporated into the current courses of study regularly
taught in the district’s schools， as determined by the school board， and it is recommended that the unit
of instruction include the following topics:
1. Safe and responsible use of social networking websites， chat rooms， electronic mail， bulletin boards，
instant messaging， and other means of communication on the Internet.
2. Recognizing， avoiding， and reporting online solicitations of students， their classmates， and their
friends by sexual predators.
3. Risks of transmitting personal information on the Internet.
4. Recognizing and avoiding unsolicited or deceptive communications received online.
5. Recognizing and reporting online harassment and cyber-bullying， including the creation and
distribution of false representations of individuals created by artificial intelligence， including， but
not limited to， sexually explicit images and videos.
6. Reporting illegal activities and communications on the Internet.
7. Copyright laws on written materials， photographs， music， and video.
d. Curricula devised in accordance with subsection (c) of this Section may be submitted for review to
the Office of the Illinois Attorney General.
