Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools 2025 – 2026
Purpose
This policy supplements State of Maryland Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy and Implementation
Guidance as published by the Department of Information Technology (DoIT)， and Maryland
Executive Order 01.01.2024.02. In particular， the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE)
adheres to the guiding principles provided for AI use.
This policy outlines the MSDE’s approach to the secure， legal， fair， and accountable procurement
and use of AI systems. Our goal is to leverage AI to enhance our work while protecting students，
staff， and the public from unnecessary risks. This policy applies to all MSDE employees，
contractors， and partners who use AI systems with MSDE data or on MSDE systems.
Maryland State Department of Education | 4
Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools 2025 – 2026
Use of AI Systems within MSDE
All use of AI systems in MSDE or adoption of AI features in existing tools must be reviewed and
approved by both MSDE and DoIT. MSDE will periodically review and affirm the security， privacy， and
accessibility of these systems in accordance with applicable state and agency IT policies..
DoIT approval does not constitute MSDE authorization. MSDE IT must evaluate specific use cases and
data handling requirements separately. Significant changes to approved use cases require additional
review.
Approved tools must be documented and provided annually to DoIT as required by the State for the AI
inventory. MSDE’s submitted inventory must include all tools which use AI to perform MSDE business
or process data， regardless of the cost of the tool or its inclusion within another tool.
The MSDE CIO serves as the AI Lead as per DoIT AI Implementation Guidance and delegates IT staff to
assure all parts of this role are fulfilled by MSDE. MSDE divisional and programmatic staff employing AI
must inform MSDE IT promptly of their intention to use such a system and provide regular status
updates.
This document will not and cannot be wholly inclusive. Artificial Intelligence is a changing field， and
every possible circumstance cannot be examined. MSDE employees， contractors， and affiliates are
expected to follow both the spirit and letter of this guidance. Please reach out to the MSDE IT Branch
with any questions or as soon as you begin to consider using any AI-based tool for MSDE business.
Use of Generative AI Systems
Generative AI systems are increasingly used in government operations.. Examples include commercial
services such as ChatGPT， CoPilot， Claude， Gemini Applications such as Canva and Beautiful.ai
incorporate AI capabilities for content generation. Generative AI systems are not limited to text， but can
produce art， formatted documents and presentations， and other digital artifacts， as well as
summarizing meetings and transcripts.
Staff may only use AI systems approved through MSDE and DoIT processes for agency operations;
this prohibition includes tools that may be free， open source， or provided by a partner. Not all work can
be performed with the assistance of an AI tool.
Please note: creating an account on an online tool with your Maryland.gov account and/or purchasing
a tool on a credit card without going through the approval process does not make that tool an
approved tool， a tool provided by MSDE or Maryland， or a permitted platform. These tools are
unapproved and prohibited regardless of whether AI is in use.
Generative AI systems require human oversight. Technology enables our work; we are accountable for
that work and for employing good judgement. The person using a tool is responsible for its use and the
results， both intended and unintended and the implications using such technology has for the MSDE
and Maryland residents.
Maryland State Department of Education | 5
Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools 2025 – 2026
MSDE Approval Process for New AI Systems
Start with your IT Partner who can help you smoothly work your way through this process.
1. Define Need: Identify the business need for a new AI tool.
2. Check Approved List: Verify if a suitable tool is already on the MSDE or state-approved (DoIT) list.
3. MSDE IT Review: If no approved tool exists， ask for an MSDE review
4. DoIT Review: If the internal review is successful， submit the tool for State review through Maryland
DoIT's AI intake process.
5. Develop internal procedures for your unit
6. Approval， Implementation， Adoption: Upon successful completion of all reviews， the tool will be
approved for use.
CUSTOMIZED TOOLS
Most AI systems will be software products or services or exist within another piece of software. There
are cases where MSDE may want to build or include an MSDE-specific AI tool in a solution. Some
Generative AI systems are available for private， more limited use where MSDE could define the data it
learns from in order to make a tool specific to our services and compliant with policy.
Any unit considering developing or procuring an AI chat bot， a tool for specific business process
support， or similar to be trained on your department’s data， must consult with MSDE IT. Place a
consultation request as soon as you are considering a tool of this type and do not wait until you are
deep into the project.
Consultation with IT will ensure that your project proceeds with proper support and considerations for
an effective outcome that also protects MSDE and resident data. IT will be able to discuss and provide
advice regarding available options， and the applicability of tools you may be considering.
Please be aware that for the AI to produce desired results， the data it will learn from may need anything
from basic refinement to a whole new structure and network security architecture. To address this， you
will likely need to work with qualified professionals. The data work， as well as building and defining the
AI tool， may take more time than you expect and will affect your overall project cost and timeline.
MSDE’s Responsibilities in Using AI
AI NOTETAKING AND SUMMARIZATION
Having an AI “take notes” or summarize a meeting for you can be a timesaver， but this is not without it’s
concerns:
• AI notetakers have notorious accuracy issues
• These tools cannot always accurately separate the salient points of a meeting from the routine
conversation and may not highlight the important content
Maryland State Department of Education | 6
Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools 2025 – 2026
• Some meeting content is confidential， and it is not appropriate to use a summarization tool
• While transcription and automated notetaking are not considered “recording” by Maryland law，
others may be uncomfortable with this use and should be considered
It is acceptable to use the native AI systems available from your Maryland online meeting accounts
within Microsoft Teams (CoPilot)， and Google Meet (Gemini) when logged into your Maryland.gov
account. Both Google and Microsoft have multiple tools available under the CoPilot and Gemini
names – only those within the Maryland online environment and desktop applications may be used. If
you are not sure， please reach out to your MSDE IT Partner.
Other tools for meeting notes (such as otter.ai， Fireflies.ai， Fathom， tl;dv)， and tools embedded in
programs like Notion are not permitted. MSDE data cannot be stored outside MSDE/Maryland systems.
It is not permissible to use an AI tool of any kind to replace a person’s attendance at or
participation in a required meeting.
EXAMPLES
Here are a few ideas of how one might use approved Generative AI systems. Please be aware that these
examples are not inclusive， and everything you do must align with State guidance. You are responsible
for the way you use these tools as a member of MSDE.
Permitted
• Using an approved AI tool to produce meeting notes
• These need to be reviewed by an attendee for accuracy and clarity
• Drafting reports， summaries， or non-confidential content
• Final versions need to be closely reviewed by the appropriate MSDE personnel
• Rewriting content to a different reading level or to align with “plain language” initiatives
• Changing the formatting or organization of data
• Analyzing public or aggregated data
• To analyze non-public data， additional review will be needed on the tool and it’s approved use，
including assuring the appropriate protection of the data
• Using an approved tool to speed data processing and providing resident services
• Human reviews for accuracy need to be part of unit SOPs
• No final determinations about awards， funding， eligibility， legality， compliance， disciplinary
actions， or any other policy or program decision-making may be performed by an AI.
• Create a form or survey
• Using an AI tool to assist your research on a topic
• Research will have to be verified for accuracy
• Summarizing extensive informative documents
Maryland State Department of Education | 7
Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools 2025 – 2026
Prohibited
Based on the guidance outlined in Maryland State policy and AI guidance， the following are prohibited
AI uses in MSDE. Depending on the use， any of these may be illegal or subject to disciplinary measures.
• Providing student or staff mental or emotional care services with an AI tool
• Making any determinations regarding HR， legal or compliance decisions， providing resident
services， or making partnerships. Any significant or person-affection decisions should be made by
humans.
• Using data in ways not approved or in violation of data sharing agreements or the terms of use of
any given data collection system
• Using any protected or restricted data without specific approval to use it with the particular AI
system.
• Doing “social scoring” of individuals or any other analysis which may bring bias into the analysis.
• Using AI to impersonate， defame， or harass anyone or to create misleading information or content.
• Using any unapproved tool for MSDE work.
RISK AWARENESS
Bias
AI systems may exhibit algorithmic bias that requires mitigation. Experts are concerned about how
using inherently biased training data in a statistically centered model will amplify and reinforce
systemic biases and increase levels of inaccuracy with edge cases. Text-based tools can be problematic，
but the largest concerns are aimed at image-based tools which are said to reinforce visual and racial
stereotypes.
MSDE staff and partners using AI must be aware of this and review any results produced by an AI tool
for ways to identify distorted information， reduce or eliminate inherent bias， and to train any internal
tools in a way that promotes fairness and the support of all Maryland learners.
Intellectual Property Use/Ownership
Because both text- and image/video-based Generative AI systems are often trained on large data sets
the models do not know what information is copyrighted， trademarked， or the work of an artist or
content producer. These tools will also use this data in combination with other sources to produce
“new” content without attribution， royalties， or consideration for fair use.
Using AI systems to generate code can be very effective， but this too has been controversial as the
Generative AI systems do not abide by the license terms of the code they have learned from.
MSDE must respect appropriate intellectual property use and avoid using AI systems in situations
where plagiarism may be an unintended outcome.
PROTECTED， RESTRICTED， OR PERSONALLY IDENTIFYABLE DATA
Complete a Privacy Impact Assessment before using AI with these data. Prefer aggregated or de-
identified data， include AI clauses in contracts， and never train AI with student data unless approved.
Maryland State Department of Education | 8
Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools 2025 – 2026
Please follow the MSDE and DoIT Data Classification Policies
INCIDENT RESPONSE
If AI causes an issue， such as a data breach， publication of biased or inaccurate content， or a system
failure， staff must immediately:
• Stop using the tool.
• Report the incident to the appropriate IT Partner and the MSDE CISO
• Assist with containing and investigating the issue.
• Support remediation efforts and ensure all actions are documented.
SECURITY STANDARDS ALIGNMENT
All AI systems must align with Maryland (DoIT) and MSDE Security policies.
ACCESSIBILITY
AI systems must align with federal accessibility guidelines under section 508， as well as all applicable
Maryland and MSDE laws， regulations and policies.
Maryland State Department of Education | 9

III. Creating District-level Guidance
Begin with What Already Exists
As with any emerging technology， AI is changing rapidly， and the answers won’t be available right away. Begin with
existing guidance， procedures， and policies to address immediate challenges. Consider the impact of the use of AI，
particularly in:
• Data privacy
• Assessment
• Academic integrity
Work with all invested groups to develop further guidance for the use of AI anchored in the mission， vision， and values
of the organization.
Prioritize Staff Learning
Centering people is a guiding principle for AI in education. People should be at the center of decision-making in how and
when AI is used. To do this， schools should provide differentiated professional learning opportunities for not only
teachers， but all staff.
School leaders should address risks and develop guidelines for the use of AI to support student learning. Without clear
boundaries， students may rely on AI to complete tasks they should be practicing themselves， by passing on the

between AI as a learning aid versus a replacement for thinking， ensuring students develop genuine understanding rather
than simply producing AI-assisted work. Schools must address issues of equity， academic integrity， and assessing
learning by having conversations with all members of the community before establishing clear expectations that prepare
students to use AI ethically and effectively as adults.
Encourage Innovation and Knowledge Sharing
To encourage thoughtful innovation and collaborative exploration of AI use in schools， consider the following ideas:
• Include student voice in the creation of the district/school AI guidance.
• As educators， staff， and students explore and develop new ways of using AI applications， create opportunities
for these ideas to be shared， refined， and built upon by others.
• Promote AI literacy for all learners， including how AI works and how it affects the world around us.
• Encourage open discussion about the benefits and risks of AI; outright bans can shut down opportunities for
learning and growth.
• When challenges arise， leverage their potential as learning opportunities.

General Resources

It also summarizes the Federal laws needed to ensure AI is used safely， securely， and without discrimination.

WHAT
IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE?
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer or computer-controlled
robot to mimic human tasks that require learning， problem solving， and
recognizing patterns to make predictions. Developers program AI to learn from
data and then use that information to solve problems， make predictions， and
emulate human thought-processes.
AI is powered by machine learning， which is the process that allows machines to
learn from data independently. Through machine learning， computers can pull in
large amounts of data in the form of images， video， text， and audio and learn to
recognize patterns and make predictions.
Machine learning processes often use large language models that can
understand and generate human language. These models， known as generative
AI， produce content such as text， images， and audio. Google Genesis and Open
AI ChatGPT are examples of generative AI that utilize machine learning and large
language models.
While AI may seem like the newest tool in the world of technology， it’s been
working behind the scenes for decades. Today， we are surrounded by AI in
our personal and professional lives， including Google search assistant，
virtual assistants (e.g.， Siri and Alexa)， predictive text， facial recognition，
medical procedures， and countless other applications.

ACCURACY & BIAS
AI is only as accurate as the data it processes. AI’s machine learning
models draw from large data sets， often gathered from the Internet，
which are not guaranteed to be accurate， as not all information on the
Internet is factual. Generative AI tools like Google Genesis or Open AI
ChatGPT are not specifically coded to provide accurate information. Instead， they
predict the type of information needed to best fit a prompt. Additionally， AI tools reflect the
biases in the data processed by the machine learning model and any biases that may be
programmed into the model itself. Even rules created to eliminate bias may result in their
own form of bias. Therefore， educators and students should be trained in the proper use of
AI， complete rigorous accuracy checks， and guard against the potential for biased results. { 6 }

HOW
CAN AI BE LEVERAGED IN THE CLASSROOM?
It is important to note that AI-powered tools can never replace the human element
of teaching. Educators are integral to the instructional process. They support students’
learning journeys by building relationships， developing critical thinking and creativity
skills， responding to student needs， providing timely feedback， and fostering ethical
values. AI-powered tools can enhance classroom instruction by helping educators
design personalized learning experiences and provide scaffolded support for students.
In addition to instructional uses， educators and students can use AI tools， such as
virtual assistants， to improve organization， productivity， and communication.

DIGITAL CITIZENSHIP
Digital Citizenship is a broad term that covers all aspects of
acceptable behavior when using technology tools， including:
• U sing digital tools and interacting with others safely， kindly，
and responsibly.
• Feeling comfortable using the Internet， software/apps， AI tools， and devices.
• F inding a healthy balance in time spent on various digital and
non-digital activities.
• R ecognizing the impact of media use on emotional well-being.
• B eing able to critically analyze news， information， and other media， including
determining credible sources and proper use of copyrighted materials.
It is imperative that educators receive ongoing professional development to support
their own digital citizenship skills and those of their students. Topics such as when and
how to use AI tools， citing sources， and critical analysis of information generated by
AI tools should be discussed prior to any application of AI in the classroom.
For more digital citizenship resources， visit mdek12.org/DLResources.

STRATEGIES
TO DETER CHEATING AND/OR PLAGIARISM
Before educators can introduce strategies to deter cheating， it is helpful to pause
and determine what cheating or plagiarism looks like for each assignment， student，
and context. Educators should consider what assistance AI tools can provide
and when that assistance crosses the line into cheating or plagiarism (i.e.， the
work or ideas are no longer original to the student). Once this boundary has been
established， clearly articulate the criteria to students and families. (For more
information， review Matt Miller’s blog， “AI in the classroom: What’s cheating?
What’s OK?”) Additionally， educators can employ the following strategies to deter
students from using AI tools to cheat on assignment or plagiarize material.
Reiterate rules and expectations for appropriate AI use. Before the
assignment begins， review both appropriate and inappropriate uses of AI
tools for the specific assignment. Be explicit with the websites or tools
students can use to complete the assignment and how students should
cite any information or support provided by these tools. Discuss the
consequences of cheating and plagiarism. Educators can consider making
students acknowledge these rules， expectations， and consequences in
writing as the first part of any assignment.
Know the writing style of students. Have students submit writing samples
frequently to become familiar with their writing style. This will enable
educators to quickly recognize if student work that deviates from their typical
style is submitted.
Require students to document the writing process. Have students submit
multiple unedited drafts of their work and reflections on the writing process.
These drafts can be written without technology (i.e.， paper and pencil) or
electronically. If writing at home， educators can also require that students
use a screen recording tool to document the writing processes. If writing
in class， educators can circulate the room or use monitoring software to
observe the writing process.
Consider how learning is being assessed. Educators should rethink how they
assess students’ understanding， knowledge， or skills. When possible， replace
multiple choice questions with alternative assessments such as:
» C reating real-world， hands-on projects that require students to apply their
knowledge in a practical context， thus making it difficult for AI to provide
the answers.
{ 11 }
{ 11 }
» U sing a variety of question types that require critical thinking and problem-
solving skills， including questions that are open-ended， seek students’
opinions supported by evidence， and include context-specific scenarios.
» A sking students to create their own visual responses， such as charts， graphs，
infographics， images， videos， or graphic organizers， that are difficult for AI
tools to generate.
» R equiring students to work collaboratively to co-construct knowledge， present
information， and field questions with peers.
Educators can also provide writing prompts that do not require students to
provide generic responses or basic facts. Instead， craft writing prompts specific
to a context， concept， or information discussed in the classroom， require the
student to express or identify motivations or emotions， or are based on
individual experiences.
Review version history. Google Docs and Microsoft Word both have options
to review the editing history of a document. By reviewing the version history，
educators can see the edits made to a document， including if large amounts
of text were copied and pasted instead of typed out.
Activate lock down browsers. When available， use lock down
browsers to restrict students from finding answers to questions
or writing prompts while the assignment is activated. Educators
may also consider placing time restraints on activities to keep
students focused on the current assignment.
Enter the assignment into an AI tool and evaluate
the results. Gain an understanding of the answers that can
be generated if/when students enter the prompt or question
into an AI tool. Consider sharing these responses with students
and discussing the accuracy of the responses. Have students
evaluate the responses for accuracy， tone， and writing style.
Use AI detection tools and plagiarism checkers. AI Classifiers are detection tools
that evaluate text to determine if it is AI-generated (uses predictable patterns and
uniform sentences) and return results as likely or unlikely AI-generated. Some
examples of these tools are AI Content Detector and GPTZero. Educators should
note that in most cases， these tools do not accurately detect AI-generated material，
especially material that contains only a few hundred words. Additionally， these
tools can falsely identify the writings of English Language students as generated
material simply because their writing skills are still developing. In contrast，
plagiarism checkers scan for exact or close matches of keywords， phrases， and
sentences. Plagiarism checkers such as Google’s Originality Reports and Turnitin
are useful for these reviews. Turnitin also now features AI classifier detection.

Artificial Intelligence (AI)
The world is excited about the possibilities of artificial intelligence (AI). The Jackson Public School District is no exception. We know that to prepare our students we must wisely utilize this tool for the good of our community.
AI is a way for computers to accumulate and process data to solve problems， much like we do! AI systems analyze information， identify patterns， and make predictions or decisions based on that data. In our daily lives we encounter AI through things like voice assistants on your phones or personalized recommendations when we stream videos.
Understanding the basics of AI can open exciting possibilities in the classroom. When properly used AI can be a powerful tool that enables you to personalize learning experiences for students， automate some administrative tasks， and even provide new ways of engaging with curriculum.
The following resources have been developed by leaders in the field. They will give a general understanding of Artificial Intelligence and its implications for the classroom.

Challenges
● Intellectual Property: AI can create a risk of copyright infringement.
● Plagiarism: AI may produce content too similar to existing works.
● Bias: Training data biases can result in unfair and incorrect outputs.
● Inaccuracy: AI-generated information may sound/appear accurate but be incorrect.
● Overreliance: As AI becomes more integrated into everyday tasks， people may rely on it to do
work that traditionally requires critical thinking and learning. For instance， students may use AI
to write essays， complete assignments， or answer questions without fully understanding the
underlying concepts.
● Loss of Human Interaction: The use of technology for quick， easy information creates a risk of
reduced human interaction， which can lead to a potential increase in loneliness， isolation， and
anxiety.
Benefits
● AI can provide individualized explanations or practice problems tailored to students’ needs.
● AI can assist students in brainstorming， organizing， and refining their writing.
● AI can create study materials such as practice tests， gamify academic content， and create
audible study aids such as podcasts.
● AI can help design logos or other graphics for groups.
● AI can help promote self-directed learning.
● AI can potentially serve as a personalized tutor.
● AI can provide differentiated context for students with varying needs (accessibility).
● AI can facilitate creativity in student work.
● AI can summarize complex texts or provide simplified versions for students who need additional
support.
● AI can offer immediate feedback on student responses or formative assessments.

● Accuracy and Reliability
o Concern: AI may produce inaccurate information which could mislead or confuse
students.
o Response: It is important to teach students to fact-check by using other credible
sources. Responsible use of AI means understanding that it does not always produce
accurate information due to its limitations.
● Student Dependence
o Concern: Students may over rely on AI tools， hindering critical thinking and creativity，
and possibly reducing their problem-solving skills.
o Response: Educators should model how they use AI as a starting point for writing to
show students how to analyze AI responses so that they can craft appropriate prompts.

● Academic Integrity
o Concern: Students may use AI to cheat or complete assignments without truly
understanding the material.
o Response: Educators should restructure their learning environment to address how AI
can and cannot be used in their classrooms， while also teaching students self-regulation.
The use of conferences， formative assessments， and opportunities for students to
demonstrate mastery are essential. It is important to assess and emphasize the student
honor code of the school. Establishing clear guidelines to encourage respectful and
responsible online behavior is vital to fostering ethical use of AI. Encourage the use of AI
acceptable rating scales for both students and overall school AI use.
● AI Use in Assessments
o Concern: Students may violate academic integrity standards.
o Response: AI should not be used in standardized testing without explicit state approval.
Establish AI academic integrity policies， clearly defining acceptable AI usage for
students. AI can assist in many ways such as automated grading with educator
oversight， AI-driven formative assessments to provide real-time student feedback， and
adaptive testing to personalize student learning pathways.
● Data Privacy
o Concern: Educators have concerns over how student data is collected， stored， and used
by AI systems， raising privacy and security issues.
o Response: Educators must teach students to be cautious about the information that
they include in their prompts. Prompts should never contain personal data. It is also
important that educators are aware of the age restrictions and data policies of any AI
tools that they use with students.
o Response: On the LEA level， LEAs should not allow their data or information to be used
to train the vendor’s models. This can be negotiated with the vendor. Know how your
data will be used. Guardrails can be in place to keep your data safe. Guardrails are
protocols and tools used to make sure AI systems operate within legal and technical
boundaries.
● Job Replacement
o Concern: Some educators fear AI may eventually reduce the need for human educators
or diminish the importance of the educator’s role.
o Response: While AI can synthesize information， generate examples， and assist with
conceptual understanding， it cannot determine the context that exists within the
learning environment or develop empathy for learners based on students’ body
language and expressions. AI tools do not have the empathy or creativity that humans
possess. Students still require a human presence to listen and show empathy， along with
modeling the ability to make mistakes that exemplify a growth mindset.
● Equity and Access
o Concern: Educators fear that not all students will have equal access to AI tools which
could potentially widen the digital divide.

● Direct Prompts: Asking the AI specific questions.
○ Example: What are the components of a computer?
● Open-ended Prompts: Encouraging creativity or expanding on an idea.

● Instructional Prompts: Providing step-by-step instructions on the desired output of the prompt.
○ Example: Explain how photosynthesis works in five steps.
● Role-based Prompts: Ask the AI to assume a specific role to tailor the response.
○ Example: As a history educator， explain how Brown v. Board of Education changed

● Refinement of Prompts: The ongoing process or dialogue of fine-tuning your results.
○ Example: Can you explain that in simpler terms?

A Letter from the Superintendent
Advancements in technology continually change the world where our students learn and the future world for which they are
preparing. Artificial intelligence (Al) has provided new opportunities for the community and Springfield Public Schools is committed to preparing all students for future success.
The SPS Al Handbook will provide all stakeholders with clarity of how Al is utilized to meet the mission and vision established by our Board of Education. This ranges from how we will use Al as a tool to supplement the abilities of staff and students to how we will ensure ethical and responsible use throughout instruction and operations. Strategic Plan Priorities
Governing Priority 1: Success Ready Students -
Preparing all students to be college and/or career ready， with an emphasis on each student reaching their full potential.
Governing Priority 2: Organizational Efficiency and Excellence -
Being responsible leaders and stewards of district resources.
Governing Priority 3: Collaborative Culture -
Engaging in proactive communication and collaboration with all stakeholders.
Governing Priority 4: Quality Learning Environments -
Providing safe and secure facilities that optimize learning.
SPS will strategically use AI as a tool to empower Success-Ready students， staff， and families. In our classrooms， AI will be used to supplement human inquiry and curiosity， helping students develop the critical thinking and problem-solving skills needed to thrive in an evolving global workforce. We will foster an environment in which AI serves as a tool to help each individual to reach their full potential while ensuring humans remain the primary decision-makers. As responsible stewards of our resources， we are committed to bridging the digital divide and protecting data privacy and academic integrity.
What is Artificial Intelligence?
Artificial Intelligence， or AI， is a technology where computer systems are designed to mimic human intelligence or problem-solving abilities. It allows machines to perform tasks that typically require human thought， such as recognizing patterns， understanding language， or making complex decisions. Most computer systems have followed strict pre-programmed rules， and AI represents a different way of interaction using a process called machine learning to improve their performance as they encounter new data. You likely interact with AI every day when you use predictive text on your phone， see suggested videos on social media， or use digital assistants like Siri or Alexa.
What is Generative AI?
A specific branch called Generative Al can even create entirely new content based upon patterns it has learned from vast amounts of existing information. These Large Language Models， or LLMs， are trained from a variety of data sources to allow the computer to learn patterns to generate content. The LLM is then used by an application that allows users to guide the Al tool in creating content such as text， images， videos， or music. The creation of this content is dependent upon the data contained within the LLM which means the content created can be limited or inaccurate. Human interaction or prompting of these tools requires a level of understanding and critical thinking abilities by the user to ensure content is accurate.
The purpose of the SPS AI Literacy Framework is to provide a shared model for students， staff， and parents to understand the abilities and limitations of artificial intelligence while growing the skills needed to use these tools effectively and ethically.
Pillar 1: Ethical and Responsible Use (Doing the Right Thing)
Use AI in a way that is fair， safe， honest， and respectful of others.
For Students:
Be honest. Do not cheat by passing off AI-generated work as your own. Always follow your teacher's specific rules for each assignment. Protect your privacy—never type your full name， password， address， or your friends' information into an AI tool. Properly cite when AI is used.
For Teachers & Staff:
Protect student data. Only use school-approved AI platforms that follow student privacy laws. Teach students and model how to properly credit or cite AI when it is used for brainstorming or research.
For Parents:
Talk with your child about digital safety at home. Remind them that whatever they type into a public AI tool can be stored， so they must keep personal information private.
Pillar 2: Critical Thinking Skills (Don't Believe Everything You See)
Learn to question， test， and verify AI answers instead of accepting them as fact.
For Students:
Treat AI like a helper who sometimes makes mistakes or even makes things up， which is called a ”hallucination”. You should never copy and paste what the AI tells you; instead， you must always double-check the facts using your own knowledge or trusted sources like books and library databases. It is important to be careful of bias， because AI learns from the internet and can repeat unfair ideas or stereotypes.
For Teachers & Staff:
Teach students how to verify facts. Create assignments where students practice fact-checking AI responses against trusted library databases， textbooks， and primary sources.
For Parents:
Help your child understand that AI is a prediction machine， not an all-knowing truth-teller. Encourage them to ask， ”How do we know this AI answer is actually true?” when using it for homework help.
Pillar 3: Human-In-The-Loop Methodology (Humans Are Always The Boss)
Keep a human being in charge of making decisions， editing work， and guiding the process.
For Students:
You are the author， the thinker， and the manager. The AI platform might give you a rough outline or list of ideas， but you must do the heavy lifting of writing， editing， and making the final product yours.
For Teachers & Staff:
Keep human relationships at the center of school and work. Use AI to help format lesson plans or analyze school data， but always let human judgment make the final call on student grades， behavioral choices， and emotional support.
For Parents:
Monitor your child's AI use. Ensure they are using the tool as a starting point for their ideas， but that they are still doing their own thinking， reading， and problem-solving.
Pillar 4: A Tool， Not A Replacement (An Assistant， Not A Substitute)
Use AI to assist human intelligence and creativity， never to replace our own brainpower or personal connections.
For Students:
Use AI like a calculator for ideas or a bicycle for your mind. It can help you practice vocabulary， quiz you before a test， or help you understand a confusing math step. But do not let it replace your own practicing， writing skills， or creative voice.
For Teachers & Staff:
Use AI to handle repetitive administrative tasks—like drafting emails or organizing spreadsheets—so you have more free time to connect face-to-face with your students and colleagues.
For Parents:
Treat AI as a helpful homework assistant or tutor， but ensure it doesn't replace standard study habits， real-world hobbies， reading physical books， or meaningful personal interactions.
Artificial Intelligence provides significant opportunities， and SPS is committed to using these tools to advance our mission and vision. As AI continues to evolve， SPS recognizes that our approach to AI adoption must also remain thoughtful， flexible， and responsive to new developments. To meet this commitment， we value the following principles that will guide how AI is utilized:
1. Learning and Training
The core mission of SPS is to educate. Education of staff and students on AI literacy will be a primary focus. This is to ensure each learner， adult or child， has the skills and language needed to effectively utilize AI to reach their full potential.
2. Human Centered
Our goal is to build the skills of students and staff to utilize AI with a human-in-the-loop approach. This ensures the individual is in charge of the AI interaction to create reliable， people-focused outcomes.
3. Safe and Secure Use
AI use must align with federal， state， and district regulations that protect staff and student data. This includes following district procedures for the use and adoption of AI tools along with compliance to federal laws such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA).
4. Academic Integrity
The educational experience of each student is centered around the classroom. Students and staff are expected to cite the use of AI tools appropriately. This provides transparency from all learners in leveraging technology in the creation of authentic work. AI tools are to serve as an aid to the instructional process that enhance and support learning.

One goal of this handbook is to provide clarity and guidance in the use of AI tools. These guidelines will provide common language for all stakeholders to ensure ethical and responsible use of AI. These six guidelines apply to all stakeholders and are designed to align use with our guiding principles:
You Are the Human
AI is a tool meant to supplement human work， not replace it. Humans must always lead the process and remain responsible for the final results， as AI lacks human emotion， intuition， and empathy.
Keep Private Information Private
Never enter personally identifiable information (PII) into AI tools not approved by SPS or into personal AI tools.
Always Double-Check AI Outputs
AI tools can hallucinate or provide inaccurate information due to limitations of their systems. You must always critically review content created by an AI tool against trusted sources and your own knowledge.
Check for Fairness and Bias
AI models are trained upon a variety of data sources created by humans and contain biased information. You must review content created by AI to ensure it does not discriminate against others， promote misinformation， perpetuate stereotypes， or violate the law.
Use Only District-Approved Tools
District-approved tools have been vetted to ensure data privacy requirements are met. This ensures your information is not used to train AI models and that data is not shared publicly.
Be Transparent About AI Use
Cite and disclose the use of AI in completion of school work or staff-created materials. AI is a tool and transparency in its use creates trust and ensures academic integrity throughout the educational experience.

The use of all AI tools are treated in the same way as all other software applications. All staff and students are required to use technology in support of the education experience which includes using AI in a safe manner that protects all stakeholders.
This looks like never sharing personal details of students， staff， or other confidential information with AI tools. This includes， but is not limited to: full names， addresses， phone numbers， ID numbers， educational records， personnel records， health information， or financial information. When using approved AI tools， it is still preferred to anonymize information to avoid the potential sharing of PII.
Only using approved AI tools is one of the many ways you can safeguard this information. Using publicly available AI tools or personal accounts with AI tools can release this information and make it accessible to those that should not have access.
Take these steps in your use of AI tools to ensure you are being safe and responsible.
Only use approved AI tools.
Never provide confidential， sensitive， or personally identifiable information when using AI tools.
Never use copyrighted materials (such as District curriculum) with AI tools without express permission by the owner to do so.
Be transparent in your use of AI tools by citing or referencing its use in your work.

The District's guaranteed and viable curriculum remains the primary instructional resource， while Al is leveraged as a support tool to strengthen teaching and learning. Educators are responsible for guiding the use of Al in their courses. These guidelines provide a shared set of expectations with the goal of empowering educators to ensure Al is used to enhance their classroom environments. Al generated content does not replace district-vetted， high-quality instructional materials.
Set Clear Guidance in Your Courses
Specify if AI is allowed to be used for an assignment.
Provide guidelines for how AI should be used such as: a brainstorming partner， generating specific content like images， etc.
Set the method of how AI use will be cited or referenced when used.

Be transparent in your own use of AI by following the same guidelines you set for students.
Model human-in-the-loop use of AI by reviewing AI generated content and how you evaluate for bias and accuracy of information.
Discuss how to apply critical thinking while using AI tools to fact-check results against trusted sources of information.
Protect Data and Privacy
Teach students how to protect their privacy when using AI tools.
Ensure students understand never to share personally identifiable information (PII) with AI and what PII might mean for them.
Grading Practices
Teachers make the final decision in all grading decisions.
Use of AI in grading must be verified to ensure fairness and accuracy.
Follow all academic integrity guidance in grading， including transparency of when AI has been used in grading.
Grow Your AI Literacy

Practice prompting techniques to explore how the use of AI does and does not enhance your practice.
Participate in the discussion with students and fellow educators of how AI functions.

Differentiating Reading Levels
Context:
A middle school social studies teacher wants to use a high-quality article about the Missouri Compromise， but several students in the class read three grade levels below their peers and struggle with the complex vocabulary.
Steps:
The teacher inputs the text of the article into an SPS-approved generative AI tool， such as Google Gemini， and prompts it to ”Rewrite this text for a 5th-grade reading level while keeping all historical facts and key names identical”. The teacher then reviews the output to ensure no ”hallucinations” occurred and that the core lesson objectives are still met.
Explanation:
This type of differentiation is appropriate when the standard does not require students to read a grade level passage. These steps allow for personalization of instruction， ensuring all students can access the curriculum at their level while the teacher remains the ”human-in-the-loop” responsible for accuracy.
Creating a Classroom Newsletter
Context:
A principal needs to send a monthly newsletter to a diverse community and wants to ensure the tone is welcoming and the message is accessible to families who speak multiple languages.
Steps:
The principal drafts the main updates and uses an approved AI tool to ”Reframe this newsletter to be more inviting for families and provide a Spanish translation of the key dates”. The principal then reviews the translation for accuracy before distribution.
Explanation:
This streamlines a routine administrative task， freeing the principal to focus on direct community connection and empathy-driven leadership.
Students are responsible for actively participating in their educational experience. This includes following guidance from their teacher and understanding expectations of academic integrity. These guidelines set students up for success by providing clarity of how to use Al in their academic journey.
Understand When To Use AI
Check your assignment for directions on how or when to use AI.
Always check with your teacher if you have questions about if it is appropriate to use AI for an assignment or not.
Uphold Academic Integrity
Always clearly state and appropriately cite when you have used AI in your course work.
Use AI to help brainstorm ideas， provide feedback on your work， or research a topic to support your work. Never use AI to write an entire essay or complete homework for you.
Verify Content
Always double-check facts provided by AI using trusted sources from your class or library.
Check for bias or misinformation in AI generated content. You are responsible for any content you turn in.
Be a Good Digital Citizen

Do not share personal information with AI tools such as your name， address， phone number， or ID number.

Consequences For Student Misuse
To ensure that technology is used fairly and safely， Springfield Public Schools (SPS) follows the following steps in addressing the misuse of AI tools. This matrix aligns with the SPS Student Handbook and the Discipline Code of Conduct to provide clear steps for handling the misuse of AI tools.
Discipline is viewed as a learning opportunity with the goal of improving behavior and school climate while maintaining high academic expectations.
SPS AI Misconduct Levels (
See Student Handbook
)
Using someone else's work and claiming it as your own， even if it is unintentional， is considered being academically dishonest. Examples of academic dishonesty include， but are not limited to， using Artificial Intelligence programs or apps on assignments， online translators for world language courses， and plagiarism. It is important that students cite sources and use quotation marks appropriately to avoid violating the Academic Honesty policy.
Levels of AI misconduct by definition of action and typical response
Misconduct Level
Definition of Action
Typical Response
Level I (Minor)
Using a non-approved AI tool during school hours or violating basic electronic device rules.
1:1 conversation with the student， warning， and review of safer alternatives.
Level II (Serious)
Academic Dishonesty:
Submitting AI-generated work as your own without proper citation.
Follows the three-offense sequence for academic honesty (see below).
Level III (Severe)
Using AI to create harmful， bullying， or sexual content， or attempting to hack/bypass district filters.
Discipline referral， parent notification， loss of technology privileges， and possible suspension.
Academic Integrity Sequence
When a student is suspected of using AI to be academically dishonest (claiming someone else's work as their own)， SPS follows these mandatory steps:
1st offense
: Following the teacher conference， student will be allowed to redo assignment for full credit and a formal warning will be issued.
2nd offense
: Following the teacher conference， student will be allowed to redo assignment for a maximum grade of 50% and a second formal warning will be issued.
3rd offense (and subsequent)
: Following teacher， parent/guardian， student， and administrator conference， student will receive a zero for assignment.

Student Misuse Guidelines for Staff and Administrators
When assigning a consequence， administrators must consider the student's age， intent， and willingness to repair the harm.
AI-Writing Detectors
: SPS does not support using AI-writing detectors as they are often unreliable and can be biased. Instead， teachers should engage in a conversation with the student to discuss their writing process.
Right to be Informed of the Charges
: Every student has the right to notice of the charges and an opportunity to respond before any disciplinary action is taken.
Parental Involvement
: Student behavior management is a team effort between families， educators， and administrators. Parents will be notified promptly if any serious AI-related misconduct occurs.
Privacy Violations
: Any student or staff member who enters Personally Identifiable Information (PII) into an unapproved AI tool will be subject to an administrative investigation and may face disciplinary action for violating data privacy laws.
Scenario: Brainstorming for a Science Project
Context
: A 10th-grade student is struggling to come up with a unique topic for a project on renewable energy and feels stuck.
Steps
: With the teacher's permission， the student uses an approved generative AI tool to ask， ”Give me 10 unique examples of how solar energy is being used in urban farming”. The student reviews the list， selects one idea， and then performs independent research using library databases to verify the facts.
Explanation
: The student uses AI as a ”thought partner” to overcome writer's block while ensuring the final work is fundamentally their own and properly cited.
Staff members at SPS are able to leverage Al tools in a variety of ways to enhance their practice and streamline work. These guidelines exist to clarify expectations of how Al should be used in support of our shared mission.

Utilize AI tools to streamline repetitive tasks while verifying that output is accurate.
Integrate AI into workflows while documenting the purpose and method of use to ensure repeatable and high quality use.
Grow Your AI Literacy
Participate in district provided AI training opportunities and request additional training through Information Technology.
Understand how to effectively prompt AI tools that result in quality content being generated.
Engage your colleagues and supervisors in conversation about how you are using AI.

Violating Data Privacy
Enter personally identifiable information (PII) such as a student's name and educational record into a public AI tool that is not approved by the district.
Share security related information with an unapproved AI tool such as a school's emergency management plan.

Consequences for Staff Misuse
To ensure technology is used in a professional and ethical manner， Springfield Public Schools (SPS) expects all staff members to take personal responsibility for their use of Al and any harm it may cause. Failure to follow the rules outlined in this handbook or other district policies will result in disciplinary action.
Staff Disciplinary Responses
Staff members who violate AI use prohibitions or data privacy standards are subject to discipline according to Board Policy GBCB (Staff Conduct) and Policy EHBC (Data Governance and Security) or other board policies as applicable. Consequences are determined based on the severity of the misuse and may include:
Formal Warnings and Negative Evaluations
: For minor or first-time errors， such as failing to cite AI use in a non-consequential document， a supervisor may issue a warning or include the incident in a performance evaluation.
Administrative Leave or Suspension
: In cases where an investigation is needed—such as a suspected data breach or harassment—a staff member may be placed on administrative leave (with Human Resources approval) while the district reviews the situation.
Termination of Employment
: Serious violations， such as entering Personally Identifiable Information (PII) into unvetted tools， creating altered media to harass others， or using AI for significant academic/professional dishonesty， are grounds for dismissal.
Key Compliance Standards
The ”Nexus” Rule
: Staff may be disciplined for AI misuse even if it occurs off-campus， provided the action creates a ”nexus” (a harmful connection) to the district's educational or work environment.
Privacy Violations
: Any employee who improperly handles student or staff data will be subject to an administrative investigation and may face disciplinary action for violating state and federal data privacy laws.
Contractual Alignment
: All disciplinary actions will be handled in alignment with the Employee Handbook and applicable Collective Bargaining Agreements (CBAs) to ensure due process and legal compliance.
Mandatory Reporting
: If AI misuse involves illegal acts， such as the creation of harmful images or the theft of district data， the district will contact law enforcement or other legal authorities to report the activity.

Scenario: Writing a Letter of Recommendation
Context
: A high school counselor needs to write several college recommendation letters and wants to use AI to help organize their notes into a professional draft.
Steps
: The counselor first drafts the letter manually， including specific student achievements and character traits. To polish the tone， they use an approved district tool but refer to the student only as ”the student” or ”Candidate A，” ensuring they never enter Personally Identifiable Information (PII) like the student's full name or ID number into the prompt.
Explanation
: This ensures the final product is of high quality while strictly adhering to Board Policy EHBC and FERPA regarding data governance and student privacy.
Springfield Public Schools (SPS) believes that families and community members are essential partners in our mission to prepare Success-Ready Students. As technology changes how we learn and work， we want our community to feel supported and informed about how Al is used in our schools.
These guidelines mirror the expectations for our students and staff， focusing on a Collaborative Culture where we work together to use technology safely and honestly.
Partner in Academic Integrity
We encourage families to explore AI with their children， but the work students turn in must always be fundamentally their own.
Support， Don't Replace
: Use AI to help your child brainstorm ideas or get extra practice， but never use it to write an entire essay or complete their homework for them.
Encourage Disclosure
: If your child uses AI to help with a project， remind them to disclose and cite exactly how the tool assisted them， as required by their teacher.
Focus on the Journey
: Talk to your child about the ”learning journey” rather than just the final grade. Ask them questions like， ”How did this tool help you think deeper about the topic?”
Protect Student Privacy and Safety
Protecting the well-being of each student is our top priority， and that includes keeping their private data safe.
Keep PII Private
: Never enter a student's Personally Identifiable Information (PII)—such as full names， ID numbers， home addresses， or grades—into public AI tools like ChatGPT.
Use District-Approved Tools
: Encourage your child to use only the AI applications that have been officially vetted and approved by the district to ensure they meet strict safety laws like FERPA.
Monitor Age Rules
: Be aware that many AI tools have strict age limits (often 13 or 18). Always follow the district's rules regarding parental consent for these technologies.
Build AI Literacy Together
We want our community to understand how AI works and how it is used in our classrooms.
Discuss Ethics
: Talk with your children about the ethical awareness of AI， including the risks of ”hallucinations” (made-up facts) and human biases that can appear in AI results.
Stay Informed
: Read our district newsletters and attend learning opportunities about how AI tools are being used in the classroom.
Verify and Critical Thinking
AI is a powerful tool， but it is not perfect and often makes mistakes.
Check for Accuracy
: Always remind your child to double-check facts provided by AI using trusted sources like the school library or teacher-provided materials.
Identify Bias
: AI learns from data created by humans and can reflect human prejudices. Help your child think critically about whether an AI response is fair or if it might be treating some groups differently.
Open Communication
We believe in an open dialogue between the school and the home.
Talk to Teachers
: If you are ever unsure about how AI should be used for a specific assignment， please reach out to your child's teacher for clarification.
Report Concerns
: If you or your child encounter concerning or inappropriate content generated by an AI tool， stop using it immediately and notify a school administrator.
Respect Options
: We respect family preferences. If you prefer that your child does not use independent AI tools， SPS will provide alternative assignments that meet the same learning goals.

This FAQ is designed to help the Springfield Public Schools (SPS) community understand how artificial intelligence is being used to support our mission of providing high-quality academic opportunities.
What exactly is Artificial Intelligence (AI)?
AI refers to computer systems and software that mimic human intelligence or problem-solving abilities to perform tasks like recognizing patterns or understanding language. You likely use AI every day through features like predictive text on your phone， navigation apps， or movie recommendations.
Will AI replace human teachers or staff?
No， AI is a powerful tool meant to supplement human thought and decision-making rather than replace it. While AI is good at processing data， human teachers are unmatched in providing the empathy， intuition， and personal connection that students need.
Is using AI considered cheating?
Using AI to do an assignment for you is a form of academic dishonesty. However， using AI to brainstorm ideas， organize your thoughts， or get extra practice is encouraged as long as you cite the tool and describe how it helped you.
How should students cite AI if they use it?
Students must clearly disclose which tool they used and the nature of the assistance it provided， such as ”brainstormed ideas using Google Gemini.” Teachers may require full citations in MLA or APA format for formal papers to ensure transparency.
Is my personal information safe when using AI?
Protecting your privacy is a top priority， and we only use tools that comply with strict laws like FERPA. Users should never enter ”Personally Identifiable Information，” like full names or student ID numbers， into public AI tools.
What are ”hallucinations” in AI?
A hallucination is when an AI tool provides a confident-sounding answer that is actually incorrect or completely made up. Because of this， it is very important to always double-check AI-generated facts using trusted， credible sources.
Can AI be biased or unfair?
Yes， because AI is trained on data created by humans， it can sometimes reflect human biases or stereotypes. Educators and students must critically review AI content to ensure it is fair and does not treat anyone differently because of who they are.
Which AI tools are allowed at SPS?
To ensure safety， stakeholders should only use AI applications that have been officially vetted and approved by the district. We maintain a ”Vetted Tools List” to help students and staff know which tools meet our high standards for data privacy.
What if I don't want my student to use AI?
We respect family preferences and will provide alternative learning activities for students who do not have permission to use AI. These assignments will focus on the same learning goals so that no student is placed at a disadvantage.
Will SPS use AI-writing detectors to grade work?
No， the district does not support using AI-writing detectors for grading or discipline because they are often unreliable and can be biased against certain groups. Instead， teachers will evaluate student work through conversations about the writing process.
Are AI-enabled wearables， like smart glasses， allowed in class?
Currently， AI-enabled wearables such as smart glasses or pins are not permitted on campus. We are continuing to monitor this technology as it becomes more common in everyday devices to determine how it can be handled safely and fairly.
Why is it important to learn about AI now?
By 2030， a huge number of jobs will change because of AI technology. Learning how to use these tools responsibly and ethically now ensures that SPS graduates are Success-Ready for their future careers.
Algorithm:
A set of step-by-step instructions that a computer follows to complete a task. You can think of it like a recipe for a computer to follow.
Artificial Intelligence (AI):
A branch of computer science that creates machines or software capable of mimicking human intelligence， such as learning， reasoning， and solving problems.
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI):
A future version of AI that could perform any intellectual task as well as a human， including the ability to reason， plan， and understand emotions.
Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI):
AI that is designed to do one specific task very well， such as translating a language， suggesting a movie， or playing chess.
Chatbot:
An AI program designed to simulate human-like conversations through text or voice， such as ChatGPT， Copilot， or Gemini.
Generative AI (GenAI):
A specific type of AI that can create brand-new content—like text， images， music， or computer code—by learning patterns from massive amounts of existing data.
Large Language Model (LLM):
The ”underlying plumbing” of many AI tools. These models are trained on huge amounts of text to identify patterns in language so they can generate human-like responses to questions.
Machine Learning:
A part of AI where computers learn from new data to improve their performance over time without being specifically programmed for every new situation.
Output:
The final information， text， or image that an AI tool produces after you give it a command.
Prompting:
Prompting in relation to AI is the process of giving clear instructions， questions， or context to an AI tool so it can generate a useful and relevant response.
Academic Integrity:
The commitment to doing your own honest work. In the world of AI， this means using technology to help you learn without letting it do the work for you or pretending AI-generated content is your own.
AI Ethics:
Guidelines that ensure AI is developed and used in a way that is fair， safe， and respectful to all people.
AI Literacy:
The skills and knowledge needed to understand how AI works， use it effectively， and think critically about its impact on society.
Bias (Algorithmic Bias):
When an AI system produces unfair results or favors certain groups over others because the data it was trained on contained human prejudices.
Data Privacy:
The practice of protecting personal information from being collected or used by AI companies without permission.
Digital Citizenship:
Being a responsible， ethical， and safe user of all technology， including AI.
Hallucination:
When an AI tool provides an answer that sounds very confident but is actually incorrect or completely made up.
Human-in-the-Loop:
An approach where humans remain in charge by reviewing， guiding， and making the final decisions on anything produced by an AI tool.
Personally Identifiable Information (PII):
Private details that can identify a specific person， such as full names， student ID numbers， home addresses， or grades.
Prompt:
The specific instructions， questions， or examples you type into an AI tool to get a response.
Prompt Engineering:
The process of carefully designing and refining your prompts to get the most accurate and helpful results from an AI.
Transparency:
Being open and honest about when and how AI is being used in school or for district work.
To ensure that Springfield Public Schools maintains high standards for academic integrity， students and staff must clearly cite any use of AI in their work. Below are specific examples of how to cite AI using MLA and APA formats， as well as a sample for general disclosure.
MLA Format Example
To cite AI in MLA format， you should include the prompt used， the name of the tool， the version， the company， the date it was generated， and the web address.
Format:
Prompt， name of tool， version of tool， company， date of generation， general URL of tool.
Example:
Microsoft Copilot. ”Describe Hamlet's philosophical struggle with action and inaction and how it impacts the outcome of the play.” Copilot， 17 Apr. 2024，
https://copilot.microsoft.com
.
APA Format Example
To cite AI in APA format， you should include the name of the company， the year and date， a description of the media in brackets， the name of the model， and the web address.
Format:
Company， year of version， name of model including date， [media descriptor]， general URL of tool.
Example:
Microsoft Copilot. (2024， April 17). [Chat message]. Copilot.
https://copilot.microsoft.com
.
Sample Disclosure of AI Use
Sometimes a full citation isn't needed for every small task， but you still need to be transparent about how you used the tool. You can place a disclosure like this at the beginning or end of your document:
”AI was used in the following ways to support the research and development of my project:
Brainstormed ideas and narrowed down my topic using Microsoft Copilot.
Conducted initial research using Perplexity.
Edited and proofread my final draft using Grammarly.”
Important Reminders for Citations
Always Ask Your Teacher:
Different assignments may require different levels of detail. Always check with your teacher to see if they want a full citation or a simple disclosure.
Cite Images Too:
If you use an AI tool to create an image for a presentation， include a note with the tool's name， the year， and the prompt you used (for example: ”Image generated with Adobe Firefly using the prompt 'field of bluebonnets，' 2024”).
Be Prepared to Share History:
To stay accountable， you should be ready to show your AI chat history to your teacher if they ask to see how you developed your ideas.

AI (Artificial Intelligence)
The Washoe County School District is committed to the responsible， ethical， and effective use of AI to strengthen teaching， learning， and operations. Our goal is to use AI as a supportive tool that empowers educators and staff， prepares students for their future， and builds trust with our community.
Our Vision for AI in Education
WCSD has established a framework that ensures AI is used responsibly， ethically， and effectively. This framework aligns with the Nevada Department of Education’s STELLAR initiative and anticipates statewide guidance under Senate Bill 199. AI is positioned as a support tool -- not a replacement for educators -- and our governance emphasizes academic integrity， equity， efficiency， and data protection.
Key Principles and Guardrails
Our Three Core Guardrails
To guide safe and effective AI use， WCSD follows three core guardrails that apply to all staff and students:
Always Protect Student and Staff Confidentiality:
Staff are prohibited from entering personally identifiable information into public AI tools to safeguard privacy and remain compliant with FERPA.
Use AI Purposefully and Transparently:
AI use should be aligned with the district's mission and professional standards. Staff and students must acknowledge when AI contributes to their work.
Always Keep a Human-in-the-Loop:
All AI-generated content must be reviewed， verified， and approved by a human expert. Human judgment and professional standards must always be maintained.
AI for Teachers and Staff
AI for Students and Families
Resources
WCSD Approved AI Tools
AI provides powerful tools to streamline time-consuming processes and empower staff to work proactively. By automating tasks such as differentiation， data analysis， and image generation， AI can enable educators to devote more time to personalized instruction， fostering student creativity， and building authentic relationships. WCSD is committed to providing professional learning opportunities for employees to ensure they understand how to use AI ethically and effectively. The district has also formed an advisory committee of leaders， operational employees， administrators， and teachers to guide its position on AI.
Students are the next generation of creators and ethical stewards of AI. WCSD encourages students to engage with AI as a collaborative partner to amplify their voice and creativity， not suppress it. The district is also focused on preparing students to thrive in an AI-transformed world by cultivating sound judgment and ethical decision-making， not just technical skills.
To help students and staff understand the appropriate balance between human effort and AI assistance， the district has developed the
Human Agency Scale for AI Use
. This framework outlines four levels of agency:
Fully Human (High Agency):
The task is completed entirely through human effort， without AI assistance.
Human-Led with AI Support (Balanced Agency):
The individual leads the task but uses AI for specific support like brainstorming， drafting， or organizing， while maintaining full control and accountability.
AI-Led， Human-Reviewed (Low Agency):
AI manages most of the task， but a human evaluates， adjusts， or interprets the output. This should be used with caution and the human must reflect and revise the output.
Fully AI (No Agency):
AI completes the task with minimal human input or review. This is not allowed as it violates integrity policies.

Administrative Regulation 7212
Artificial Intelligence and Digital Learning
Responsible Office: Office of Academics and Office of Information Technology
PURPOSE
This Administrative Regulation establishes guidelines regarding the use of Artificial
Intelligence (AI) technologies in academics and operations within the Washoe County
School District (District).
DEFINITIONS
1. “21st Century Competencies” refers to transferable skills， knowledge， expertise，
and literacies needed to succeed in work and life in a globally interconnected
world， including the ability to process， communicate and exchange multiple
forms of information across multiple contexts， such as home， school， the
workplace， and social networks.
2. “Artificial Intelligence” (AI) refers to the theory and development of computer
systems able to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence， such as
visual perception， speech recognition， decision-making， and translation between
languages.
3. “Assistive Technology refers to any item， piece of equipment， software， or
product system—whether acquired commercially off the shelf， modified， or
customized—that is used to increase， maintain， or improve the functional
capabilities of a student with a disability. This includes both high-tech tools (e.g.，
speech-generating devices， screen readers， adaptive keyboards) and low-tech
tools (e.g.， pencil grips， visual schedules， communication boards).
4. “Chatbot” refers to a computer program designed to simulate a conversation
with a human user over the internet.
5. “Cheating” refers to the improper appropriation of information from and/or giving
information to another student， individual， or other source. Obtaining， seeking to
obtain， or aiding another student to obtain credit for work by a deceptive or
dishonest means.
6. “Digital Learning Tools” are computer software， mobile apps or applications， or
web-based tools provided by a third-party to a school or district that students
and/or their parents access via the internet and use as part of school activity.
Administrative Regulation 7212
Artificial Intelligence and Digital Learning
Page 2
7. “Generative Artificial Intelligence” (Generative AI or GenAI) refers to AI
technology that can produce content， including text， imagery， audio， or synthetic
data. These tools can paraphrase， reword inputted text， solve problems or
equations， author computer code， answer questions， create art， and generate
written content.
8. “Plagiarism” refers to instances where a student uses another writer’s work
without providing credit for the source. Plagiarism typically occurs when a
student uses an author’s words or ideas without giving proper credit to the
original author.
REGULATION
1. Academics
a. 21st Century Competencies.
i. Generative AI tools are widely popular， increasingly simple to use，
and represent challenges regarding traditional academic integrity
standards. While Generative AI tools may be used in productive，
creative， and educational manners， they can also be misused to
cheat， plagiarize， or attempt to disguise plagiarism.
ii. Students will encounter AI in their future work and lives.
Increasingly， AI tools are being integrated into existing
technologies and to maintain a culture of academic integrity and
respect， these Generative AI tools should not be used in the
automated completion of coursework， assignments， or
assessments.
b. Curriculum Philosophy.
i. Generative AI tools offer many advantages， and may be used by
students with teacher approval， oversight， and guidance.
ii. Students and teachers must maintain responsibility for the learning
process， rather than relying on AI. While technology can assist
students in creating content， it should not be used solely to
produce content on their behalf.
iii. AI may enable educators to address variability in student learning
because of its inherent adaptability. AI may empower educators to
support individualized student needs for coaching， feedback， and
support.
Administrative Regulation 7212
Artificial Intelligence and Digital Learning
Page 3
iv. Educators may:
1. Determine if or how Generative AI could be integrated into
instruction as a factor in lesson planning;
2. Establish clear expectations for use of AI with students;
3. Utilize a documentation process， where teachers ask
students to produce documents to prove that words /
content were not copied or to ensure that information was
properly cited， or require students submit rough drafts，
notes， and copies of materials as proof of research;
4. Consider writing prompts that rely on personal experiences
such as “connect to your work environment” or “describe
what you remember”;
5. Design assignments as a process to explore ideas， reason，
and expand critical thinking rather than a fixed output;
6. Consider testing existing “tried and true” prompts by running
them through a Generative AI Tool and evaluating the
output;
7. Utilize AI tools to support instructional planning，
differentiation， communication， and accessibility for students
with disabilities， provided the tool is approved through the
District Digital Learning Tools process and so long as
personally identifiable information (PII) or sensitive student
data is not input into AI application， unless approved for
such use; and
8. Utilize automated plagiarism checking tools to check whether
writing was potentially authored by Generative AI. Plagiarism
detection software offers mechanisms that check for
conventional plagiarism， in addition to determining an overall
percentage of the document that AI writing tools may have
generated.
