when interacting with AI tools. The District reserves the right to monitor， log， and review activity on District
technology resources to ensure compliance with this policy and applicable law.
A.5 Monitoring and Enforcement
The District may block or restrict AI tools that are unsafe， misused， inappropriate， or not approved for District
use. Violations of this addendum may result in:

• Disciplinary action under the Student Code of Conduct or employee handbook
• Notification to parents， guardians， or supervisors as appropriate
• Legal action in cases involving violations of law

Students may use AI tools only when the teacher or assignment directions specifically permit it. If AI use is not
specifically allowed， students should assume it is not permitted for that assignment. Students who use AI
without authorization may face academic and disciplinary consequences.
A.7 Staff-Specific Expectations
Staff must use only District-approved AI tools for instructional and operational work involving student data.
Staff may not independently contract for， purchase， or require students to use AI tools that have not been
approved through the District's review process. AI outputs in official District communications and documents
must be reviewed by an appropriate employee before use.
A.8 Policy Reference

academic integrity， and consequences， see the District's Artificial Intelligence Use Policy (Board Policy - AI)

EMPLOYEE AND STUDENT ACCEPTABLE USE POLICY
FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
OVERVIEW
The Ouachita Parish School Board recognizes the rapid growth of artificial intelligence
(AI) technologies and their potential to enhance educational experiences. This
addendum to the School Board’s Acceptable Use Policies outlines the expectations for
using AI within our schools. The objective of these guidelines is to ensure that all tools
used to support teaching， learning and school operations align with our mission and
values.
DEFINITIONS
• Artificial Intelligence (Al): Computer systems or software that perform tasks
requiring human intelligence， including but not limited to learning， decision-making，
and language processing.
• Machine Learning: A subset of Al that involves computers learning from data without
being explicitly programmed for specific tasks.
• Natural Language Processing (NLP): Al's ability to understand and generate human
language. To the best of its ability， the School Board will work to ensure Al tools are
accessible to all students， including those with disabilities and English Language
Learners， in compliance with ADA and Section 504 requirements.
• Generative Al: Al technologies that can generate new content， including text，
images， audio， and video， based on their training data. These tools can be used
for creative and educational purposes， but must be used with consideration for
accuracy， appropriateness， and originality. (i.e. Google Gemini， ChatGPT)
• Deepfake: An image or recording that has been convincingly altered and manipulated
to misrepresent an individual as doing or saying something that was not actually done
or said.
• Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (NCII): Sexual content， including photographs or
videos， that is distributed without the consent of the person depicted. This includes
manipulated imagery to misrepresent an individual， imagery captured without the
victim’s knowledge and the nonconsensual sharing of consensual imagery.
ACCESS AND PERMISSIONS
• Access to approved Al tools is granted to students， faculty， and staff for educational
and administrative purposes only. Ouachita Parish Schools maintains up-to-date PII
agreements which can be found through THIS LINK.

Cf: GBRA， IFBGA
• A list of district-approved Al tools will be maintained by the Information Technology
Department and reviewed biannually. Staff may request evaluation of additional tools
by submitting a formal proposal to the Information Technology Director.
ETHICAL USE
• Users must not employ Al tools to conduct or support cheating， plagiarism or any
academic dishonesty. The use of AI in the classroom should not undermine
academic integrity and individual skill development. AI should always be used to
support student learning. Products submitted using AI as a tool should reflect the
student’s own understanding and effort of the concept.
• Generative Al content that is inappropriate， offensive or harmful is prohibited.
Examples of inappropriate use of AI: submitting AI-generated responses as
one’s own work with minimal or no personal revision.
• Using AI to impersonate another student， teacher， administrator， or faculty
member or create a false source.
• Uploading a PDF of assignments or task rubrics without teacher approval.
• Respect and courtesy must be maintained when interacting with Al systems，
recognizing their impact on the learning environment.
• Users should be aware of the potential for Al bias in tools and consider this when
interpreting Al-generated information or content. The School Board encourages
critical thinking and scrutiny of Al outputs and training data sets for large language
models and other generative Al tools. Teachers are encouraged to guide age-
appropriate discussions on Al bias as part of digital literacy instruction.
• When used responsibly and with permission， AI tools should enhance
understanding. It is expected that when using AI tools， users will engage honestly
with proper instruction and permission and promote critical thinking.
PRIVACY， SECURITY， AND DATA PROTECTION
• Users must be aware of data privacy concerns with Al tools， especially regarding the
handling of personal and sensitive information.
• Personally identifiable information， confidential information and/or sensitive
information should never be shared with an Al tool unless such sharing is explicitly
approved by the School Board.
Ouachita Parish School Board 2 of 6
FILE: EFAB
Cf: BE， EFA
Cf: GBRA， IFBGA
• All Al tools must comply with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)，
the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and other relevant privacy laws.
• Students in fifth grade or below may only use Al tools compliant with COPPA and
explicitly approved by the School Board.
• The Information Technology Department ensures that Al tools employed have robust
security measures to protect user data from unauthorized access.
• Users are expected to be aware of and comply with the terms and conditions of all Al
tools， specifically with respect to age requirements.
• The Information Technology Department conducts regular security assessments of Al
technologies to safeguard against vulnerabilities.
DEEPFAKE AND NON-CONSENSUAL INTIMATE IMAGERY
• The use of AI technology to create Deepfake or Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery
(NCII) are subject to Policy JCDAF on bullying and Policy GAEAA on sexual
harassment or other forms of harassment.
ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
Al tools should supplement the educational process without undermining the integrity
of academic work. The use of AI tools should be honest and transparent about how
the tool is used. Examples of appropriate use include generating ideas for
brainstorming sessions， providing tutoring in specific subjects， outlining， clarification
of concepts， and grammar and spelling check.
Direct submission of Al-generated work as one's own without proper attribution or reliance
on Al for completing assignments without understanding the content is prohibited.
When Al-generated content is used in academic work， users must include an attribution
statement.
Example of Attribution:
• Portions of this content were generated with the assistance of [Al tool name].
• In written assignments， this attribution must appear in a footnote or at the end of
the document.
• Users must respect copyright laws and intellectual property rights when using Al
tools. This includes not using Al to replicate or modify copyrighted materials without

Cf: GBRA， IFBGA
authorization and properly citing all sources of content， including Al-generated
content， to avoid plagiarism.
ACOUNTABILITY AND VERIFICATION CLAUSE
Teachers may ask students to explain their work or decision-making process verbally
and/or request students submit the prompt and/or AI tool(s) used while completing an
assignment. Students may be required to alternatively demonstrate understanding to
justify a suspected AI assignment submission.
ACCURACY， VERIFICATION AND ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
When a teacher or administrator has reason to believe that submitted work may not
reflect a student’s own understanding or effort， the teacher may initiate a verification
process. This process is intended to confirm learning and ensure academic integrity， not
to presume misconduct. A part of verification， a student may be asked to:
• Explain their reasoning verbally or in writing
• Rework a portion of the assignment independently
• Describe how AI tools were used， including prompts and revisions
If a student is unable to demonstrate reasonable understanding after verification
opportunities， the teacher may require the assignment to be revised or redone andmay
document the concern.
A determine of academic dishonesty will be made only when there is clear evidence that
the work was submitted without genuine understanding or appropriate attribution， and
after the student has been given an opportunity to clarify their process. Disciplinary
action， if warranted， will follow school guidelines and be proportional to the violation.
STAFF USE IN INSTRUCTION
Educators are encouraged to use AI to support instructional design and
differentiation， but should maintain final judgment over instructional decisions and
avoid fully automating feedback or grading without human oversight.
PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT
The School Board will provide ongoing professional development on ethical and
effective AI use for educators and staff to ensure confidence and competence in
using these technologies.
Ouachita Parish School Board 4 of 6
FILE: EFAB
Cf: BE， EFA
Cf: GBRA， IFBGA
STUDENT AND PARENT EDUCATION
The School Board will provide students and parents with resources to understand Al
tools， their appropriate use and related risks.
MONITORING AND ENFORCEMENT
• The School Board reserves the right to monitor the use of Al tools to ensure
compliance with this policy.
• This may include real-time monitoring of network activity and/or maintaining a log
of Internet activity for later review.
• Users should have no expectation of privacy when using School Board technology
or networks. All activity may be monitored to ensure compliance with this policy.
• Violations of this policy may result in disciplinary action， including but not limited to
suspension of access to technology resources， disciplinary measures as per the
student and employee handbooks and notification of supervisors， parents or
guardians.
EXAMPLES OF ACCEPTABLE USE FOR STUDENTS
*Only when allowed by teacher or administration
• Brainstorming ideas
Writing assistance (not used as substitution) (e.g. initial research， proof reading，
organization of content， study preparation)
• Language translation support
• AI-powered tools used as Assistive Technology (AT)， as documented in a student’s
Individualized Education Program (IEP) or Section 504 Plan to provide equitable
access to curriculum. (e.g.， predictive text， speech-to-text， text-to-speech， text
simplification， AI-driven reading assistants， or organizational ‘executive function’
coaches)
EXAMPLES OF ACCEPTABLE USE FOR STAFF
• Assisting with grading， lesson planning， and differentiated activities
• Educators may use approved AI tools to assist in the drafting of IEP goals，
progress monitoring summaries， and the adaptation of general education materials
Ouachita Parish School Board 5 of 6
FILE: EFAB
Cf: BE， EFA
Cf: GBRA， IFBGA
(e.g.， modifying reading levels or creating visual supports). However， AI-generated
content must be reviewed and verified by the teacher to ensure it reflects the
specific， individualized needs of the student.
EXAMPLES OF UNACCEPTABLE USE
• Submitting Al-written essays (plagiarism) or AI solved math problems as original
work
• Using Al to bypass assigned reading
• Fully automating student grades
• Use AI tools to gain answers on assessments as original work
• Using AI to create damaging artwork， videos， or any media to cause harm to anyone
• Data Privacy and Sensitive Special Education Information: Users are prohibited from
inputting Personally Identifiable Information (PII) or sensitive diagnostic data from an
IEP， 504 Plan， or evaluation report into any AI tool not explicitly cleared by the district
for ‘High-Sensitivity’ data. This includes student names， date of birth， specific
disability diagnosis， or medical histories.
• Automated Evaluation in Special Education: AI shall not be used as the primary or
sole determinant for special education eligibility， placement decisions， or the formal
evaluation or student progress toward IEP goals. Professional judgment by qualified
personnel must remain the governing factor in all high-stakes special education
decisions.

but should maintain final judgment over instructional decisions and avoid fully
automating feedback or grading without human oversight.
NEW POLICY FILE: IFBGB
PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT
Ascension Public Schools will provide ongoing professional development on ethical AI
use for educators and staff to ensure confidence and competence in using these
technologies.
STUDENT AND PARENT EDUCATION
The School Board will provide students and parents with resources to understand Al
tools， their appropriate use， and related risks.
MONITORING AND ENFORCEMENT
● The School Board reserves the right to monitor the use of AI tools to ensure
compliance with this policy.
● This may include real-time monitoring of network activity and/or maintaining a log of
Internet activity for later review.
● Users should have no expectation of privacy when using School Board technology or
networks. All activity may be monitored to ensure compliance with this policy.
● Violations of this policy may result in disciplinary action， including but not limited to
suspension of access to technology resources， disciplinary measures as per the
student and employee handbooks， and notification of supervisors， parents， or
guardians.

title: Technology Guidance incl. AI Toolkit (Maine Department of Education)

Technology Guidance for Maine SAUs
The Maine Department of Education approaches new technologies using an asset-based lens. We know that technology， once adopted by the masses， becomes a part of education. Technology prohibitions prevent students from learning critical skills to function in today’s technology-enriched society and do not prepare them for the reality they will face as they move beyond their primary education. Recognizing this， Maine DOE focuses its efforts on exploring the impact of technology on individuals and groups to assess how to best support the healthy and safe use of it. From providing guidance on digital well-being to exploring what skills students need to be prepared for upcoming advancements in technology， there are overarching skills that are both necessary and relevant to all technology use; by focusing on these foundational principles， the Department works to ensure that all students and educators are equipped and prepared to effectively engage with technology as it changes and develops.
Bell to Bell Policy
The implementation of bell-to-bell restrictions on student use of personal electronic devices during the school day represents a significant shift in school environments across Maine. While this policy is designed to reduce distractions and support student engagement， it also creates an important opportunity to more clearly define the role of technology in learning， strengthen equitable access to digital tools， and reinforce instructional practices that leverage technology in meaningful and developmentally appropriate ways.
Implementation Guidance Bell-to-Bell Policy
Cell Phone Ban Toolkit
Bell-to-Bell Policy Funding Amounts
Acceptable Use Policies
Acceptable Use Policies for technology lay the foundation for responsible technology use in Maine schools. They should evolve alongside the tools we use and the challenges we face.
Consider the following best practices for AUPs
Include guidance on devices (including personal devices)， internet access， social media， AI， digital citizenship， cybersecurity， and data privacy.
Engage students， staff， and families in AUP development and review.
Emphasize the importance of digital citizenship， accountability， and clear expectations.
Reframe AUPs as a teaching tool and a working toolkit， not just rules and regulations.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) In Education
AI is reshaping how we learn and teach. Maine supports thoughtful， ethical integration of AI in education， while helping students understand how these tools work and how to use them responsibly.
Consider the following best practices for AI in Education
Use AI to support—not replace—human connection and critical thinking.
Teach students to evaluate and question AI-generated content.
Ensure transparency and clear boundaries in the classroom use of generative AI tools.
Promote equity， privacy， and digital literacy in all AI-related instruction.
Maine DOE AI Guidance Toolkit is designed to empower the confident integration of AI tools and foundational knowledge in Maine classrooms， preparing our students to thrive in an AI-influenced world. This toolkit is designed to help empower schools to make informed decisions about AI in education technology and contains critical information for anyone engaging with AI that sets foundational understandings for the effective integration of AI in education and beyond.
Explore AI Toolkit
Cell Phones & Personal Devices in Schools
Creating healthy boundaries around personal devices supports focus， wellness， and positive school culture. The Maine Department of Education encourages districts to adopt clear and developmentally appropriate expectations for mobile phone and personal device use.
Consider the following best practices for Cell Phones and Personal Devices in Schools
Establish policies that reflect local values while supporting learning environments.
Involve students and families in creating shared agreements around personal device use.
Address the impact of device use on attention， relationships， and mental health.
Use personal devices intentionally and with purpose through integrated instruction.
Emphasize the importance of digital wellness and digital citizenship
Additional information about cell phone policies from SAUs across Maine (curated by The Maine Principal's Association)
Cell Phone Policies
Computer Science Education
Computer science education provides a critical baseline of skills for all students to be successful in believes computer science is for all students. CS empowers learners to think critically， solve problems creatively， and understand the digital systems that shape our world.
Consider the following best practices for AUPs
Integrate CS across all grade levels and subject areas.
Focus on equity， inclusion， and access—especially for underrepresented groups.
Emphasize computational thinking， data science， coding， and cybersecurity.
Provide educators with tools and training to confidently teach CS concepts.
Explore CS Education
Cybersecurity in Schools
In today’s connected world， cybersecurity is essential. Maine schools are responsible for protecting student data and maintaining secure digital environments.
Consider the following best practices for Cybersecurity in Schools
Conduct regular security assessments and keep software and devices updated.
Implement multi-factor authentication， strong passwords， and secure backups.
Educate staff and students about phishing， scams， and social engineering threats.
Encourage a culture of shared responsibility; cybersecurity is everyone’s job.
Cybersecurity Planning Tools
Digital Citizenship & Wellness
Maine educators play a vital role in helping students navigate the digital world with integrity， balance， and purpose. Digital citizenship and wellness are essential components of a healthy learning environment; both online and offline.
Consider the following best practices for Digital Citizenship and Digital Wellness
Teach students to act responsibly and ethically in digital spaces， including how to communicate， share， and participate in online communities.
Promote awareness around managing screen time， reducing digital distractions， and protecting mental and emotional well-being.
Embed conversations about media literacy， digital footprints， and online reputation into everyday instruction.
Model respectful， reflective， and intentional technology use as educators and school communities.
Digital Citizenship Toolkit

Maine’s Learning Through Technology Team is here to support schools with implementation， planning， and professional learning. We believe in collaboration and continuous improvement to ensure technology works for all learners.

title: Montana Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education Guidelines (Office of Public Instruction)
full_text:
Montana Artificial Intelligence
in K–12 Education Guidelines
Prepared primarily for Montana district and school leaders， with guidance for educators， families， school
boards， and policymakers
Version 2.0 | August 2026 | Reviewed Twice Annually | Feedback invited via frontierlearninglab.io/feedback
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 1
Welcome and Acknowledgments
Thank you for reviewing this second version of the Montana Artificial Intelligence in K–12 Education Guidelines，
referred to throughout this document as the Montana AI Guidelines. The guidelines support district leaders as they
develop and refine local guidance， policy， professional learning， and implementation practices. Grounded in
Montana’s educational vision， they provide a foundation for responsible AI use， stronger AI literacy， and local
systems that can adapt as technology changes.
The Montana Office of Public Instruction (OPI)， in collaboration with the Frontier Learning Lab at the Montana Digital
Academy (MTDA) and key education partners， leads the development and twice-annual revision of this guidance.
We extend our gratitude to everyone who contributed to the drafting process. The Montana School Boards
Association provides complementary model-policy resources for local boards and districts， and we thank them for
their leadership.
This work reflects Montana’s rural， urban， and tribal communities. Its purpose is to support safe， ethical， and locally
responsive AI use that expands access and educational opportunity for Montana students.
Thank you for your partnership，
Susie Hedalen Jason Neiffer
Superintendent of Public Instruction Executive Director， Montana Digital Academy
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 2
How to Use These Guidelines
The Montana AI Guidelines are designed primarily for district and school leaders developing local guidance， policy，
and implementation plans. They also provide context for educators， families， school boards， and policymakers.
These guidelines address the selection， governance， and instructional use of artificial intelligence tools only. They do
not address the amount of time students spend using technology， one-to-one device programs， personal-device
policy， or screen-based instruction generally. Those decisions rest with local boards and districts， and nothing in this
document is intended as guidance on them.
These guidelines are advisory. They support local decision-making and do not replace local board policy， district
procedures， professional judgment， or advice from qualified legal and accessibility experts. Montana districts vary
widely in size， staffing， connectivity， resources， and community priorities; each district should adapt the
recommendations to its local circumstances while meeting applicable requirements.
Readers new to this work can begin with Core Principles for AI Integration and Getting Started: Three
Immediate Actions. The Implementation Roadmap supports longer-term planning and improvement. Universal
Access and Learner-Centered Design address barriers affecting learners and local implementation. Safety，
Privacy， and Responsible Procurement provide practical safeguards for tool review and synthetic-media response.
Throughout the document， recommendations describe strong practices for local consideration. Mandatory language
applies to obligations arising from applicable law or locally adopted policy， not from the Montana AI Guidelines
themselves.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 3
Benefits and Risks of AI in Education
Artificial intelligence may support K–12 education in useful ways， but its value and risks depend on the tool， purpose，
learner， and implementation. Districts should consider potential benefits alongside foreseeable harms， local capacity，
and available safeguards.
Benefits
● Differentiated instructional materials: AI may help educators draft or adapt materials for different reading
levels， background knowledge， languages， or learning needs. Educators remain responsible for reviewing the
accuracy， suitability， and accessibility of those materials.
● Educator capacity: AI may reduce time spent on some routine drafting， formatting， and planning tasks.
When those uses produce reliable results， educators may have more time for direct student support，
instructional decisions， and relationship-building.
● Accessibility support: Features such as text prediction， translation， speech-to-text， and text-to-speech may
improve access for some students with disabilities or language needs when selected and implemented
appropriately.
● Simulation and exploration: AI may support simulations， guided practice， and exploration of real-world
scenarios that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce in a classroom.
Risks
● Bias， inaccuracy， and misinformation: AI systems may produce false， incomplete， or biased outputs that
appear credible. Unreviewed output can mislead students， educators， and families.
● Overreliance: When AI performs important parts of a learning task， students may have fewer opportunities to
practice critical thinking， problem-solving， and productive struggle.
● Substituting AI for human instruction: AI use that replaces discussion， collaboration， or educator feedback
may reduce interactions that matter for learning. Districts should consider what an AI tool is being asked to do
in place of a person.
● Barriers to access: Tools that require reliable broadband， current devices， paid subscriptions， or specialized
staff may be difficult for some districts and students to use.
● Data collection and monitoring: Tools that collect extensive student information， including some
assessment and monitoring systems， may create privacy and security risks and may generate detailed
records of student activity beyond what the original purpose requires.
● Developmental and ethical concerns: Student age， maturity， learning goals， and the sensitivity of the
activity should inform whether and how an AI tool is used.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 4
AI and Teaching and Learning
Section 1: Core Principles for AI Integration
AI use in Montana classrooms should be driven by instructional needs， not technological novelty. District policies and
practices should reflect the following principles:
1. Evidence-Driven Adoption: Districts should evaluate AI tools using credible research， local instructional
priorities， and observed results rather than relying on vendor claims alone. Evidence is emerging and varies by tool，
learner， subject， and use case. Improvements in immediate task performance do not necessarily demonstrate
independent mastery， long-term retention， or transfer to new contexts. Districts may conduct limited， well-designed
pilots with clear learning goals， a human in the loop， and a plan for evaluating results before expanding use.
2. Preserving Productive Struggle: Learning requires cognitive effort. AI tools can reduce friction and provide
immediate answers， but easier does not always mean better. Educators should use AI to support learning rather than
bypass the critical thinking， problem-solving， practice， and productive struggle that learning requires.
3. The Human in the Loop: AI output does not replace professional judgment， empathy， or pedagogical expertise.
Educators remain responsible for reviewing and verifying AI-generated content used in the classroom and for the
instructional decisions surrounding its use.
4. Protect Student Data: Districts should establish clear processes for reviewing and approving AI tools， minimizing
the collection and sharing of student information， and communicating permitted uses. Educators should use locally
approved tools and avoid entering protected or sensitive information unless specifically authorized. Local review
processes should account for applicable federal and Montana privacy requirements， vendor data practices， security，
and potential bias.
Section 2: Guidance for Educator Use
Reducing administrative burden is a promising and comparatively lower-risk use of AI in education. For some
specific， repetitive tasks， AI may save educators time that can be redirected toward student interaction and
instruction. Districts should evaluate whether a tool produces reliable results， protects sensitive information， and
creates meaningful time savings in local practice.
Potential Uses for Educators:
● Routine drafting and formatting: Preparing draft newsletters， general communications， forms， and other
materials without entering protected information into an unapproved tool.
● Instructional preparation: Drafting differentiated reading passages， practice questions， examples， and
possible lesson openings.
● Rubrics and explanations: Creating a starting point for a rubric or generating alternative explanations and
analogies for educator review.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 5
Professional Responsibility for Verification: Generative AI can produce factual errors， fabricated information， and
biased output. Educators should independently review AI-generated materials for accuracy， age appropriateness，
accessibility， and respect for Montana's people before using them with students.
Section 3: Guidance for Student Learning
Student-facing AI is changing rapidly. District guidance should distinguish acceptable assistance from academic
dishonesty and give students clear boundaries for each learning activity.
Understanding the Evidence Gap: Research on student-facing AI is developing rapidly， and findings vary across
tools， subjects， age groups， and instructional designs. Stronger performance on a task completed with AI assistance
does not by itself demonstrate independent mastery， retention， or transfer. Districts and educators may choose to
test promising uses on a limited basis， with clear learning goals， appropriate safeguards， and a plan to evaluate
whether students can demonstrate learning without the tool.
Establishing Boundaries for Student Use: Districts should establish a simple continuum that communicates three
conditions: AI use is not permitted， AI use is permitted within stated boundaries， or AI use is expected as part of the
learning activity. Districts and educators determine when each condition applies based on local policy， student age，
subject， learning purpose， assignment design， and accessibility needs.
● When AI Use Is Not Permitted: Educators may restrict AI when students need to develop or demonstrate
foundational knowledge and skills independently.
● When AI Use Is Permitted Within Boundaries: Educators may allow defined uses of AI， such as
brainstorming， receiving feedback， exploring a historical perspective， or asking for another explanation of a
complex concept. The permitted uses should be stated clearly for the activity.
● When AI Use Is Expected: Educators may require AI use when it is itself part of the learning goal， such as
evaluating AI output， practicing responsible use， or demonstrating AI literacy.
● Disclosure Expectations: Districts and educators should clearly communicate when and how students are
expected to disclose AI assistance. Expectations should reflect student age， subject， assignment purpose，
accessibility needs， and local academic-integrity policy. Minor assistance， accessibility supports， and
substantial AI-generated contributions may warrant different forms of disclosure.
● Demonstrating Learning: When independent mastery or authorship matters， educators should use
appropriate ways for students to demonstrate their learning. Depending on the task， this may include
discussing their decisions， showing selected stages of their process， revising in response to questions， or
completing part of the work independently.
Clear boundaries can help students use AI responsibly while continuing to develop independent knowledge， skills，
and judgment.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 6
Universal Access and Learner-Centered Design
Montana's rural， urban， and tribal communities differ in geography， local capacity， connectivity， language， and student
needs. Districts should consider those differences when selecting and implementing AI so that the technology does
not create new barriers to learning.
Accessibility should be considered from the beginning， not added after a tool has been selected. Universal Design
for Learning (UDL)， the framework developed by the Center for Applied Special Technology (CAST)， helps educators
anticipate learner variability and remove barriers during design. Applying UDL principles during selection and
implementation can reduce the need for costly or incomplete changes later， which is particularly important for small
and rural districts with limited resources.
Two related ideas should guide local decisions. First， UDL and assistive technology work together but serve different
purposes: UDL builds flexibility into instruction， while assistive technology responds to an individual student's
documented needs. Second， consistent with CAST's Center on Inclusive Technology in Education Systems (CITES)
model， districts should coordinate assistive technology， educational technology， and information technology decisions
so that accessibility is considered whenever a tool enters a classroom.
Guiding Principles
● Remove Barriers to Learning: AI use should expand educational opportunity and not narrow it. Districts
should identify and address barriers related to disability， geography， connectivity， language， cost， and local
capacity， and should consider both the barriers an AI tool may create and the barriers it may remove.
● Design for Access from the Start: Districts should select and implement AI tools using UDL principles，
including multiple means of engagement， representation， and expression. Where possible， evaluations
should include input or evidence from the learners the tools are intended to serve， including students with
disabilities and multilingual learners.
● Meet Accessibility and Disability Requirements: AI tools must support compliance with the Individuals
with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA)， Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act， and Section 508， and should
conform to recognized standards such as WCAG 2.1 AA. Note that the updated ADA Title II rule extends
WCAG conformance requirements to the web content and mobile applications of public schools on a phased
timeline. Districts should confirm current compliance dates with legal counsel.
● Cultural Relevance and Respect: AI may support instruction， but meeting Indian Education for All requires
educator expertise to ensure that content and teaching strategies remain culturally relevant and respectful. AI
does not replace this judgment. Districts and educators should honor tribes’ existing guidance and
established approaches to delivering tribal content when considering the use of AI tools in education.
Recommended Practices
● Require accessibility evidence during vetting. Vendors should document how their tools support students
with disabilities and multilingual learners. Independent verification， such as CAST's UDL Product Certification，
may provide additional evidence for purchasing decisions. This practice connects directly to the Vendor
Vetting Checklist in Safety， Privacy， and Responsible Procurement.
● Build educator capacity for accessible use. AI capabilities are increasingly incorporated into assistive
technologies such as text-to-speech and speech recognition， but educators need support to use them
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 7
appropriately. The Frontier Learning Lab can help districts connect AI tools， UDL practice， and accessible
educational materials at no cost.
● Recognize the limits. AI-enabled assistive tools may support student autonomy， engagement， and access to
content， but accuracy， infrastructure， and educator readiness can limit their usefulness. A human should
remain in the loop.
● Consider where barriers are greatest. When allocating funding or implementation assistance， districts and
supporting organizations should consider barriers related to geography， connectivity， staffing， cost， and
student needs.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 8
Getting Started: Three Immediate Actions
Moving from principles to daily practice requires local processes that support educators， protect students， and honor
Montana's tradition of local control.
These three immediate actions give district leaders a practical starting point. They are not a complete
implementation process; the Implementation Roadmap later in this document provides a longer-term path for
developing， monitoring， and improving local practice.
Step 1: Assemble a Local AI Guidance Team
AI decisions should not fall solely to an IT department or a single administrator. Because AI affects instruction， data
privacy， procurement， accessibility， student conduct， and community expectations， districts should establish a
cross-functional team or comparable local process to guide implementation.
Possible Participants:
● District administrators: Provide oversight， coordinate local processes， and identify needed resources.
● Technology staff: Review vendor data practices， security， system compatibility， and technical controls.
● Instructional leaders: Connect AI decisions to academic standards， curriculum， assessment， and learning
goals.
● Educators: Contribute classroom experience and evaluate how tools affect teaching and learning.
● School board and community representatives: Support transparency and bring local values and concerns
into the process.
● Students: Offer insights into daily classroom use， student needs， and peer perspectives on academic
integrity and responsible AI use.
The Team's Work: Depending on local governance and assigned authority， the team may review state guidance，
recommend local policy， identify AI features already present in district software， support tool review， and help
maintain an approved-tool list. Local boards retain authority for policies requiring board adoption. The team should
also consider model-policy resources from the Montana School Boards Association (MTSBA).
Smaller districts may combine roles， use an existing committee， or work with regional schools， curriculum consortia，
the Frontier Learning Lab， or the Montana Educational Technologist Association.
Step 2: Provide Evidence-Informed Professional Learning
Before introducing AI tools to students， districts should prepare the employees responsible for selecting， supervising，
or supporting those uses. Professional learning should extend beyond tool demonstrations to address AI literacy，
instructional purpose， data privacy， accessibility， verification， and appropriate uses for routine work.
Support from the Frontier Learning Lab: Districts may use no-cost support from the Frontier Learning Lab at
MTDA as they develop local professional learning.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 9
● AI Help Desk: Educators and administrators can contact the Frontier Learning Lab AI Help Desk at
ai.help@mtda.org for person-to-person support with tool review， prompting， local guidance， and related
questions.
● Role-specific learning: Professional learning should prepare educators to remain the human in the loop by
reviewing AI-generated content for accuracy， appropriateness， and accessibility before using it with students，
families， or the community.
Step 3: Engage the Community and Communicate Clearly
AI creates new questions about how student work is produced， supported， and evaluated. Districts should clearly
communicate local expectations to students， families， employees， and the broader community.
Suggested steps include:
● Review existing policies: Consider whether acceptable-use policies， academic-integrity policies， student
handbooks， employee guidance， or related local documents need to address AI.
● Communicate approved uses: Tell students， families， and employees which tools and uses are locally
approved and where they can ask questions.
● Create opportunities for discussion: Explain why the district is considering AI， what safeguards apply， how
student information is protected， and how the district will respond to misuse， including malicious synthetic
media and violations of academic integrity expectations.
These steps provide a practical starting point. Districts can adapt the participants， sequence， and scope to their
governance structure， resources， and community priorities.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 10
Policy and Governance
AI policy and governance in Montana should reflect the state's legal framework， cultural commitments， local-control
tradition， and rural context. District policies and practices must comply with applicable law and should respond to
local needs and community priorities.
Constitutional Players
Montana's education governance distributes authority among several constitutional players: the Legislature， the
Governor， the Board of Public Education， the Board of Regents of Higher Education， the Superintendent of Public
Instruction， and local school boards.
The Legislature establishes statutory frameworks and funding parameters that shape technology adoption. The
Governor may coordinate cross-agency initiatives and workforce priorities. The Board of Public Education
establishes administrative rules， educator-preparation standards， and accreditation requirements. The Board of
Regents oversees higher education policy. The Superintendent of Public Instruction provides guidance and technical
assistance to districts. Within this broader framework， local school boards make decisions about locally adopted
policy， tool approval， staff preparation， and student-use expectations.
MTSBA provides complementary guidance for local policy development and district implementation. Current
resources are available at mtda.link/mtsbaaipolicy.
Tribal Sovereignty and Consultation
Tribal nations possess inherent sovereignty that predates the United States. In education， the Montana Constitution
states that ”The state recognizes the distinct and unique cultural heritage of the American Indians and is committed
in its educational goals to the preservation of their cultural integrity.”
Montana's constitutional commitment is reflected in Indian Education for All， which requires instruction about the
distinct and unique cultural heritage of American Indians. This responsibility requires accurate， culturally respectful
teaching about Montana's tribal nations and communities.
In the context of AI， tribes maintain jurisdiction over their data and digital materials， possess authority to regulate
technology that affects their communities， and determine whether and how AI systems interact with their cultural
knowledge. Those developing AI policy must recognize tribal authority and engage in meaningful consultation when
state initiatives could affect tribal communities， cultural materials， or data-sovereignty rights.
Local Control and Rural Realities
Montana's commitment to local control places many AI implementation decisions with local boards and districts.
Small and rural districts may have limited technology staffing， broadband access， budgets， or procurement capacity.
They may choose to work with regional cooperatives， state-supported resources， or shared-service arrangements
when evaluating and implementing tools. Districts should consider connectivity， remote administration， staff
workload， community values， and demonstrated educational value before adopting a tool.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 11
Higher Education and Workforce Connections
Districts should consider connections among K–12 education， educator preparation， higher education， and workforce
development. The Montana University System can support educator preparation and research that informs local AI
decisions.
Legal Considerations and Liability
AI use can create legal and operational responsibilities involving privacy， accessibility， procurement， student conduct，
intellectual property， records， and other areas. District leaders should use established review processes and seek
qualified advice when a proposed use presents legal or liability questions.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 12
Safety， Privacy， and Responsible Procurement
Districts need a consistent review process to protect students， meet applicable requirements， and manage local risk.
The following guidance applies to every AI tool under consideration， including pilots and free versions.
Part A: Vendor Vetting Checklist
Districts should not deploy an AI tool unless the local review process verifies each of the following criteria:
● Privacy and data protection: The tool and its proposed use must comply with the Family Educational Rights
and Privacy Act (FERPA) and other applicable federal and Montana student-privacy requirements. Review
what information the tool collects， how it is used， whether it is shared， how long it is retained， and how it can
be deleted.
● Security: The vendor should provide evidence of appropriate security practices， incident-response
procedures， and notification terms. Districts should understand which responsibilities belong to the vendor
and which remain local.
● Algorithmic bias: Districts should require vendors to provide available documentation about how the system
has been evaluated for bias.
● Age， notice， and consent: The proposed use must comply with the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act
(COPPA)， vendor age restrictions， and applicable federal， Montana， and local requirements for family notice，
consent， and school authorization. Districts should communicate approved tools and their data practices to
families， consistent with Getting Started: Three Immediate Actions.
● Design and engagement practices: Districts should review whether a tool uses features intended to
maximize time spent in the product rather than support learning， such as streaks， variable rewards， autoplay，
persistent notifications， or personas that encourage prolonged interaction. Vendors should disclose these
features， and districts should confirm which of them can be disabled.
● Accessibility: The vendor should provide evidence that the tool supports applicable accessibility
requirements and the needs of students with disabilities and multilingual learners.
● Contract and data-privacy terms: The vendor must sign the Montana Student Data Privacy Agreement or
an equivalent agreement approved through the district's established review process.
The Frontier Learning Lab periodically reviews tools for use in Montana schools. Tools that complete this process
and meet MTDA and University of Montana procurement standards are available through the MTDA Catalog.
Part B: Deepfake and Synthetic Media Protocol
Malicious synthetic media can seriously harm students， employees， school climate， and community trust. Districts
should address nonconsensual and malicious deepfakes directly in local policy and incident-response procedures.
● Zero tolerance for malicious creation or distribution: Local policy must classify the creation or distribution
of nonconsensual deepfakes depicting students or employees as a severe offense comparable to severe
bullying or harassment.
● Immediate law-enforcement collaboration: Explicit synthetic media involving minors may constitute child
sexual abuse material (CSAM) or otherwise implicate sexual-exploitation laws. Administrators must
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 13
immediately involve local law enforcement and the Montana Department of Justice when explicit deepfakes
are discovered.
● Support for the targeted person: The district's first response must center the safety， privacy， and support
needs of the targeted student or employee. Districts must provide clear reporting pathways designed to
reduce retaliation， unnecessary redistribution， and further public exposure.
Part C: Companion and Conversational AI
Students may encounter general-purpose chatbots and companion-style AI that are designed to sustain conversation
and can present as confidants. Even when these tools are not district-provided， staff will encounter their effects， and
districts should be prepared to respond.
● Understand the distinct risks: Conversational systems may provide inaccurate or harmful guidance， respond
inappropriately to disclosures about self-harm or abuse， encourage prolonged emotional reliance， or collect
sensitive personal information a student would not otherwise share.
● Do not treat AI as a support service: AI tools are not counseling， assessment， or crisis services， and should
not be presented to students as a substitute for school counselors， qualified staff， or family support.
● Apply existing safety procedures: A student disclosure of harm， threat， or crisis warrants the district's
established response regardless of whether the disclosure occurred in conversation with an AI system. Staff
should understand that these procedures apply.
● Review companion-style tools separately: Tools designed to sustain an ongoing relationship with a student
warrant review beyond the standard checklist， including whether the design encourages emotional
dependence and whether age-appropriate safeguards exist.
● Communicate with families: Districts should include conversational AI in family communication about
approved tools， local expectations， and how to raise a concern.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 14
Implementation Roadmap
After completing the three immediate actions outlined earlier， districts can use this longer-term roadmap to develop
and refine local implementation. The sequence is flexible; districts may adapt it to their governance structure，
resources， priorities， and experience.
Capacity-Building Support
● MTDA and the Frontier Learning Lab: These organizations can provide professional learning and technical
support for local planning， tool review， and implementation.
● Regional cooperatives: These organizations may provide professional learning， collaborative networks， or
shared technical expertise for districts that cannot sustain those functions independently.
● State education organizations: MTSBA， School Administrators of Montana， the Montana Rural Education
Association， the Montana Small School Alliance， and other education organizations may provide guidance
and professional learning.
● Higher education partners: Universities， community colleges， and tribal colleges may support joint
professional learning， research， and educator preparation.
![Implementation roadmap showing five connected areas: foundation and vision， responsible policy， capacity building，
access， and continuous improvement.][image6]
I. Establish a Foundation and Local Vision
Build on the three immediate actions by documenting local purpose， decision-making responsibilities， and priorities.
● Define purpose and goals: Explain which local needs or opportunities AI may address and how proposed
uses connect to district priorities and learning goals.
● Confirm participation and responsibility: Review whether the local team or process includes the
knowledge and perspectives needed for the decisions under consideration. Districts determine participation
based on local governance and community context.
● Build shared understanding: Provide appropriate orientation for district leaders， board members，
educators， and others involved in local decisions so they understand AI's potential uses， limits， and risks.
II. Develop Policies and Practices for Responsible Use
This stage connects local AI use to existing policy， safeguards， and community expectations.
● Review existing policies: Determine whether academic-integrity， acceptable-use， privacy， grading， records，
accessibility， employee-use， and digital-citizenship policies adequately address AI.
● Use consistent principles: Connect local policy to privacy， transparency， accountability， universal access，
the human in the loop， and academic integrity.
● Communicate clearly: Explain locally approved uses， foreseeable risks， safeguards， and ways for the
community to ask questions or provide feedback.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 15
● Apply the vendor-vetting checklist: Use the review process in Safety， Privacy， and Responsible
Procurement for every tool under consideration. Do not enter personally identifiable information into an
unapproved tool.
● Keep a human in the loop: Educators remain responsible for reviewing AI-generated materials and for the
instructional decisions surrounding their use.
III. Build Capacity Through Professional Learning
Professional learning should reflect employee roles and locally approved uses.
● Provide role-specific learning: Address AI literacy， instructional purpose， privacy， accessibility， verification，
and practical strategies relevant to each role.
● Support structured practice: Give educators appropriate opportunities to test approved tools， evaluate
output， reflect on benefits and risks， and learn with colleagues.
● Develop appropriate AI literacy: Determine what employees and students need to understand about AI， its
limitations， and responsible use based on their roles and learning needs.
IV. Support Universal Access and Local Implementation
Districts should consider whether proposed uses create or remove barriers related to disability， geography，
connectivity， language， cost， staffing， or local capacity.
● Consider access requirements: Review the devices， connectivity， tools， support， and local capacity
required for a proposed use.
● Pilot before expanding: When appropriate， begin with a limited use， evaluate local experience， and address
problems before expanding.
● Adapt to local capacity: Small and rural districts may use cooperative or shared arrangements when those
options fit local needs.
● Consider partnerships: Districts may work with universities， tribal colleges， workforce programs， or other
partners when those relationships support local goals.
● Use learner-centered design: Prioritize tools that meet applicable accessibility requirements and support
students with disabilities and multilingual learners.
V. Monitor， Reflect， and Improve
Because tools， evidence， law， and local experience change， districts should review their practices regularly.
Montana AI in K-12 Education Gudelines， Version 2 Page 16
● Review twice annually: Examine local policies and practices as part of the Montana AI Guidelines review
cycle and revise them when local needs or material changes warrant action.
● Invite feedback: Provide appropriate ways for students， employees， families， and community members to
share local experience and concerns.
● Reflect on Local Experience: Periodically review educator and student experience， observed instructional
value， implementation problems， privacy or safety incidents， and whether continued use remains worthwhile.
Districts should avoid collecting new student-level data solely to monitor AI implementation unless a clear
local need and appropriate safeguards justify it.
● Share useful lessons: When appropriate， share local experience with other Montana districts and support
organizations.
The Frontier Learning Lab provides statewide support for local planning and implementation. Contact the AI Help
Desk at ai.help@mtda.org.

Glossary
This glossary defines terms used materially in the Montana AI Guidelines.
Artificial intelligence (AI): Computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing speech， analyzing
data， making predictions， or generating content.
Generative AI: AI that produces content such as text， images， audio， video， or code in response to a user's
instructions.
Algorithm: A set of rules or instructions a computer follows to perform a task， analyze information， or produce an
output.
Bias in AI: Patterns in a system's data， design， or operation that can produce systematically unfair， inaccurate， or
unrepresentative results.
Data privacy: The rights， rules， and practices governing how personal information is collected， used， stored，
retained， shared， and deleted.
AI literacy: The knowledge and skills needed to understand， evaluate， and use AI appropriately， including
recognizing its capabilities， limitations， risks， and effects.
Academic integrity: Honesty and responsibility in learning and academic work， including following stated
expectations for assistance， attribution， and independent work.
Human in the loop: A person who actively reviews AI output， applies professional or contextual judgment， and
remains responsible for the resulting decision or action.

How These Guidelines Are Reviewed
These guidelines are reviewed twice annually through a six-month participation and revision process. The process is
designed to keep the guidance responsive to changes in artificial intelligence， education practice， policy， research，
and Montana’s local context while preserving time for focused discussion and careful review.
Months 1–3: Nominations and Participation
● Invite nominations for contributors to the next revision cycle.
● Clarify the perspectives， roles， and communities that should be represented.
● Collect candidate information and confirm participation.
● Gather initial observations and proposed topics for revision.
Months 4–6: Discussion and Revision
● Close the nomination phase so the revision group can focus on the submitted priorities.
● Conduct focused discussions about proposed revisions.
● Review evidence， policy developments， implementation experience， and stakeholder feedback.
● Draft， reconcile， edit， verify， and approve the next version.
Each review does not necessarily require a new published version. Revisions are released when the review identifies
changes that materially improve the guidance's accuracy， usefulness， or relevance.

How AI Supported the Development of This Document
The Montana AI Guidelines were developed through a collaborative process led by OPI， the Frontier Learning Lab at
MTDA， and partner educators. AI tools assisted with research， drafting， synthesis， and document design. Human
authors remained responsible for reviewing AI-generated material and making editorial and policy decisions.
Specific uses of AI include:
● Comparative research: AI assisted with reviewing and summarizing guidance from peer states and national
and international frameworks.
● Updated research: AI assisted with searches for recent state guidance and research concerning AI in K–12
education.
● Draft support: AI suggested language for principles， implementation pathways， and glossary definitions.
Human authors reviewed and revised that material.
● Document design: AI tools assisted with illustrative graphics， including draft cover artwork.
Keeping a Human in the Loop
AI was not assigned final responsibility for policy determinations or high-stakes judgments. Human authors reviewed，
edited， or replaced AI-generated material and retained responsibility for the document's content.

D. Understanding Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Understanding Generative Artificial Intelligence and Related Concepts
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a type of AI that creates new content， such as
text， audio， video， images， or code， using machine learning models. Unlike
traditional AI， which focuses on recognizing patterns or classifying data， generative
AI produces outputs that mimic human-created content.
What Is Artificial Intelligence (AI)?
Artificial intelligence is a branch of computer science focused on building machines
and software capable of performing tasks that usually require human intelligence.
These tasks include learning， reasoning， solving problems， understanding language，
and interpreting sensory inputs. AI systems use algorithms and models to analyze
data， identify patterns， and make decisions or predictions with minimal human
input.
What Are Large Language Models (LLMs)?
A large language model (LLM) is a specific type of AI designed to understand and
generate human-like text. These models are trained on massive amounts of text data
and use neural networks with billions or even trillions of parameters. This training
allows them to recognize complex linguistic patterns and produce coherent
responses. LLMs can answer questions， translate languages， write creatively， and
perform other language-based tasks.
Human Intelligence vs. AI
Human intelligence refers to the natural ability to think， learn， solve problems， and
adapt to new situations. It involves cognitive functions such as memory， attention，
language comprehension， and abstract thinking. Human intelligence also includes
creativity， emotional understanding， and social interaction， which make it distinct
from AI. While AI can analyze large amounts of data and perform specific tasks
efficiently， it lacks the emotional and social dimensions of human intelligence.
Enhancing Understanding of Generative AI
Generative AI has immense potential but also comes with challenges:
• Applications: It can be used in education to create personalized learning
materials， automate administrative tasks， and provide real-time feedback to
learners.
• Ethical Concerns: Responsible use is essential to address issues like bias，
misinformation， and copyright infringement.
• Accessibility: Generative AI can make content more accessible， such as
generating captions or translations for videos.
• Collaboration with Humans: AI should be seen as a tool to enhance human
capabilities， not replace them.
By understanding these concepts， educators， policymakers， and the general public
can better navigate the opportunities and challenges of generative AI， ensuring its
responsible and effective integration into society.
E. The Importance of Family Engagement in AI use in Schools
The Importance of Family Engagement in AI Use in Schools
As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes an increasingly integrated part of teaching and
learning， schools have a critical responsibility to engage families in conversations
about how these tools are being used. Transparent， inclusive communication
ensures that AI supports—not replaces—the relationships at the heart of student
learning.
Why Family Engagement Matters
1. Builds Trust and Transparency
Clear communication about AI tools， their educational purpose， and data
privacy protections helps build trust between schools and families. When
families understand how AI is being used—and what it is not used for—they
are more likely to support its thoughtful implementation.
2. Supports Shared Responsibility
Families are essential partners in reinforcing ethical use， academic integrity，
and digital citizenship. When students understand that their families are
informed and involved， they are more likely to reflect on their own technology
use and learning behaviors.
3. Promotes Access and Inclusion
Engaging families ensures that all voices—including those from marginalized
or underrepresented communities—are part of the conversation. This helps
prevent unintentional bias in AI use and ensures that practices are responsive
to diverse needs and values.
4. Addresses Concerns Proactively
AI is a rapidly evolving field， and it’s natural for families to have questions or
concerns. Schools that communicate openly and proactively can help
families navigate the complexities of new technologies and make informed
decisions about their child’s learning.
Best Practices for School Communication
• Notify families before introducing new AI tools， including their purpose and
how student data will (or will not) be used.
• Provide opt-out options when possible and reasonable， particularly for non-
instructional tools.
• Use plain language to explain AI concepts and avoid jargon.
• Offer learning sessions for parents and caregivers on how AI supports
instruction.
• Share student reflections on AI use as a way to involve families in learning
conversations at home.
F. The Role of Generative AI in Education
Generative AI in Education: Enhancing Learning and Empowering Educators and
Learners
Generative AI is a transformative tool that can complement traditional teaching
methods by fostering creativity， critical thinking， and problem-solving skills. Rather
than replacing human intelligence， it extends the abilities of educators and learners，
creating richer， more personalized educational experiences. A key to maximizing its
potential is crafting clear prompts， enabling users to achieve meaningful and
efficient outcomes. As AI continues to shape the future of education， mastering the
art of effective prompt writing becomes essential for productive interactions
between humans and machines.

How Generative AI Can Enhance Education
1. Personalized Learning Experiences
Generative AI tailors lessons to meet the unique needs of individual learners.
For example， adaptive learning platforms can analyze a learner’s strengths
and weaknesses， then generate customized practice questions， explanations，
or content reviews at their pace and skill level. This personalized approach
supports competency-based education by helping learners achieve mastery，
while educators guide and contextualize the learning process.
2. AI as a Brainstorming Partner
Generative AI serves as an idea generator， sparking creativity for projects，
essays， and research topics. By responding to prompts and open-ended
questions， AI can offer multiple perspectives， outlines， or suggestions. This
partnership encourages learners to critically evaluate and refine their ideas，
while educators use AI-generated content as discussion starters to deepen
understanding.
3. Enhancing Problem-Solving Skills
Generative AI can simulate real-world scenarios or complex systems，
particularly in STEM education. These interactive exercises challenge learners
to analyze data， hypothesize solutions， and predict outcomes. By fostering
hands-on learning， AI helps learners develop critical thinking skills， with
educators guiding discussions about strategies and reasoning.
4. Support for Language and Writing Skills
Generative AI tools provide real-time feedback on grammar， style， and
coherence， helping learners improve writing skills and learn languages more
effectively. For essays or creative projects， AI can assist in drafting and
exploring different styles or tones. However， educators remain essential in
assessing originality， depth， and clarity， ensuring that AI is a support， not a
substitute， for human evaluation.
5. Independent Study and Tutoring Support
Generative AI offers instant， round-the-clock support， answering questions
and explaining challenging concepts. AI-powered tutoring platforms can
provide examples， simulate quizzes， and guide self-assessment. This
empowers learners to learn independently， with educators addressing more
complex or nuanced topics in the classroom.
6. Immersive and Interactive Learning Experiences
AI-powered tools create immersive learning opportunities， such as virtual
labs， simulations， and interactive models. In subjects like history or science，
AI can help learners visualize concepts， explore historical events， or
experiment in virtual environments. Educators guide these experiences，
helping learners connect them to broader learning goals and real-world
applications.
7. Time Management and Productivity Support
Generative AI can act as a personal assistant， helping learners manage their
schedules and stay organized. AI tools can create to-do lists， break large
projects into smaller tasks， and set reminders. These features are especially
useful for learners juggling multiple responsibilities， helping them develop
strong time-management skills.
8. Accessibility for Diverse Learning Needs
Generative AI makes learning more inclusive by creating resources tailored to
diverse needs. For example， AI can generate simplified text， visual aids， audio
descriptions， or captions for videos. It can also convert written content into
sign language or assist learners with disabilities in accessing educational
materials， ensuring equal opportunities for all learners.
Generative AI as an Educational Ally
Generative AI is a powerful ally in education， enhancing rather than replacing human
intelligence. It fosters critical thinking， creativity， and personalized learning by
tailoring lessons， supporting writing and language development， and sparking ideas.
Interactive scenarios help learners build problem-solving skills， while educators
guide deeper understanding. Additionally， AI improves organization， accessibility，
and independent study， making education more inclusive and manageable.
By supplementing educator-led instruction， generative AI empowers learners to
explore actively， learn effectively， and develop essential skills for the future. With
thoughtful integration， it has the potential to transform education into a more
engaging， accessible， and learner-centered experience.
G. Developmentally Appropriate Use of AI in Early Learning
(Pre-K-Grade 2)
As artificial intelligence (AI) enters classrooms， its integration must be thoughtfully
designed—especially for our youngest learners. Children in preschool through
second grade are in a foundational stage of growth.
Their development hinges on direct interactions，

sensory-rich environments， and exploratory play. AI

explore， play， and interact with
