requires users to be at least 13 years old and requires parental or legal guardian consent for students between
the ages of 13 and 18. The website warns that “ChatGPT may produce output that is not appropriate for all
audiences or all ages and educators should be mindful of that while using it with students or in classroom
contexts.”

aspects of education. We embrace these technologies cautiously to prepare students for a future where these
technologies are everywhere. Please reach out with any questions or input on these principles as we navigate
this rapidly changing terrain together. We thank you for your support.

OUR VISION:
The Barrington School District believes education is about learning how to think， not just what to know. Learning begins with a connection， and we strive to empower every child through the collaboration of our staff， students， and community.
Our district recognizes Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a tool to supplement and support learning， but never as a substitute for teaching and critical thinking. It is our responsibility to equip our community of learners to navigate these technologies and ignite curiosity while ensuring universal accessibility and student privacy.
We are committed to center every decision on student achievement and growth while navigating this evolving landscape with integrity. As the district prepares students for the future， we remain rooted in what matters most: the belief that every student’s voice， mind， and individuality are irreplaceable.

-
What is Artificial Intelligence
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a type of technology that lets computers learn to do things that usually require a human brain—like solving problems， recognizing pictures， or answering questions.
Think of AI like a highly advanced ”Search” tool. While a regular search engine points you to a website， AI can look at millions of pieces of information and use them to help you brainstorm ideas， summarize a long article， or even help you write a line of code.  It is important to remember that AI doesn't actually ”know” things the way we do. It is a powerful assistant that is great at finding patterns， but it still needs a human to:  Check the facts: AI can sometimes make mistakes.
Add creativity: AI can help start a project， but it can’t replace your unique voice.  Use it safely: We teach our students to use AI honestly and responsibly.
+
-
How are students using it?
Students may use generative AI to:
Help brainstorm ideas for writing
Ask questions about academic content
Receive feedback on work
Practice math problems
Explore coding
Create images or designs for projects
While these tools can be helpful， responsible use and adult guidance are essential.
+
-
How does Barrington ensure students are using AI responsibly?
We are:
Incorporating age-appropriate AI literacy lessons throughout the subject areas.
Training staff on how to guide students in ethical AI use.
Communicating clearly with students and families about what is and isn’t allowed.
+

What can I do as a parent to learn more about AI?
Common Sense Media offers a wealth of information， and is a great place to start your AI journey:

title: Regulation 6325 - Artificial Intelligence (Richland School District One)
full_text:
(Regulation 6325)
(Adopted – October 15， 2025)
The District recognizes the potential benefits of using artificial intelligence (AI) in the classroom and for the operation of schools. For the purpose of this policy， AI is any technology that can produce content including， but not limited to， text， images， audio， or simulated data. It can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence， such as understanding language， recognizing patterns， solving problems， and making decisions. In the educational context， it can support personalized learning， accelerate learning， automate administrative tasks and provide interactive and engaging learning experiences. Teachers can use Al for a broad range of educational reasons. Teachers and staff should integrate technology tools that benefit the educational process. The district will provide education on Al’s role in enhancing instruction and productivity. However， it is also recognized that there are potential risks associated with using AI， including cheating or the impact its unguided use may have. Staff and students should never rely solely on AI content without review.
The Superintendent or designee is authorized to develop regulations to implement this policy. The regulation shall incorporate additional information regarding staff and student privacy， promote academic integrity and provide students with developmentally appropriate instruction on the ethical use of AI. Misuse or malicious use of Al technologies will lead to disciplinary action. Personally identifiable information (PIT) and confidential information about students and employees should never be input into any Al system without prior authorization. PPI includes， but is not limited to， a person’s name， address， email address， telephone number， Social Security number， or other personally identifiable information. Confidential information includes， but is not limited to， information in a student’s education record， such as their grades and information about an Individualized Education Plan (IEP).
The safety of student data is of the utmost importance. The school district shall adhere to federal and state regulations， which include:
FERPA (The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act): FERPA is a federal law that protects the privacy of student educational records. It requires schools to obtain written permission from the parent or eligible student before disclosing personally identifiable information from the student’s educational records， except in certain circumstances.
COPPA (The Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act): COPPA is a federal law that imposes specific requirements on operators of websites or on1ine services directed to children under 13 years of age and on operators of other websites or online services that have actual knowledge that they are collecting personal information online from a child under 13 years of age.
The district will implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect student data collected by AI systems from unauthorized access， destruction， use， modification or disclosure in accordance with FERPA and COPPA. When contracting with third party vendors providing AI systems or services， the district shall ensure that the vendor complies with all applicable FERPA and COPPA regulations and maintains appropriate safeguards to protect student data privacy and security.
For all of the benefits of AI， it is also recognized that there are potential risks associated with the use of Al， including cheating or the impact its unguided use may have. Inappropriate uses of AI can include:
Using AI to collect， store or analyze student data without explicit consent and clear educational purpose. Student privacy rights (e.g.， FERPA， COPPA) must be maintained;
Implementing AI systems that perpetuate bias or discrimination;
Al should not replace essential human elements of teaching and mentoring. While AI can augment teaching， it must not substitute for the personalized and empathetic interaction between teachers and students;
Allowing unsupervised use of Al tools by students; and
Allowing AI to learn passwords， confidential or proprietary or sensitive district data.

Generative AI
Charleston County School District is building a thoughtful， responsible approach to AI by preparing students and educators for a rapidly changing world while protecting academic integrity and student well-being.
Artificial intelligence is reshaping how people learn， work， and solve problems. CCSD recognizes that students entering today's classrooms will graduate into a world where AI fluency is a foundational skill and that educators need the training and tools to guide that learning responsibly.
Rather than reacting to AI as a challenge to academic integrity alone， the district is taking a proactive stance: developing clear policies， building educator capacity， and creating conditions for AI to serve as a genuine learning tool for every student.

Fall 2025
Stakeholder engagement & research
The district partnered with

， a national consulting group， to begin developing its AI strategy. CCSD held in-person collaborative sessions with parents， students， teachers， and staff to surface ideas and concerns. The Committee of the Whole received an hour-long workshop in November 2025 on the state of generative AI in K–12 education.
December 2025
Policy drafting
A cross-stakeholder working group finalized a draft AI policy covering literacy， tool use， and ethics. Deputy Superintendent Dr. Luke Clamp presented the framework at a district leadership press conference， describing it as the foundation for professional development and structured AI integration.
January 2026
Board approval
The Board of Trustees formally adopted CCSD's AI policy. The approved guidelines provide recommended guidance for teachers' use of generative AI in academic work and establish guardrails protecting students in high-stakes decisions.
Spring 2026
Implementation planning
The district began work on procedures， strategy， and licensing. CFO Daniel Prentice gathered input from students across multiple schools， including elementary， middle， and high school students， as well as parents， teachers， administrators， and representatives from Google. Funding for software and AI infrastructure was included in the FY2027 budget.
2026–27 School Year
Training & full implementation (Phase 2)
The district plans to roll out educator training and begin full classroom implementation during the upcoming school year， building on the policies and infrastructure established in Phase 1.
What families should know
Will students be required to use AI tools?
No. Teachers have discretion over whether and how AI tools are used in their classrooms. The district's framework provides guidance， not mandates， for classroom use.
How will CCSD protect student data?
Any AI tool adopted by the district must meet data privacy and security standards consistent with FERPA and district policy. Student information will not be used to train commercial AI models without appropriate authorization.
What about academic integrity and cheating?
Academic integrity is a core component of the district's AI framework. Teachers will establish clear expectations for each assignment， and the district is developing guidance to help educators assess authentic student work in an AI-enabled environment.
Can AI be used to make decisions about my child?
No. District policy explicitly prohibits AI from serving as the sole basis for high-stakes decisions， including discipline， special education placement， or academic advancement. Human judgment and oversight are required in all such decisions.

Section: I - Instructional Program
Philosophy
Purpose
The instructional program philosophy defines the coherent system of concepts and values that underlies instructional policies in Greenville County Schools.
P
hilosophy
I.
Introduction
Schools should use Instructional Policies as the basis for meeting the GCS Education Plan goals， the South Carolina Standards for Learning， and the Advanc-ED Standards for Accreditation.
Meeting high expectations outlined by the goals and standards will prepare students for lives as productive citizens， both personally and professionally.
As the Education Plan states， “We collaborate with the home and community to provide educational experiences which prepare students for life-long learning and for ethical， productive participation in a democratic society and the global community.”
The Instruction Policies define the comprehensive， rigorous curriculum to be taught in Greenville County Schools.
They contain benchmarks outlined in the South Carolina Standards
for Learning
， as well as additional objectives that offer students opportunities to extend their learning based upon their aptitudes， interests， and goals for the future.
The Board of Trustees is dedicated to educating the whole child by offering and assessing instructional programs designed to promote creativity， collaboration， communication， and critical thinking in addition to specific content knowledge， and to promote emotional and physical wellness. Student-centered teaching and learning are fundamental to the GCS commitment to students and their families.
II.
Artificial Intelligence
Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers potentially valuable educational opportunities for students and educators in the District.
The Board recognizes that the use of AI can， when used appropriately， enhance student learning by providing effective and creative ways to support learning， independent research， critical thinking， and problem-solving.
The following parameters are designed to support the responsible and effective use of AI in schools:
a.
Educational Use
:
Approved AI will be used to enhance teaching and learning， promote critical thinking， and support personalized learning in furtherance of the curriculum.
b.
Student Privacy and Security
:
AI used in schools will comply with all applicable laws， including the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act.
All AI will be evaluated to maximize safe practices for students while protecting from unlawful disclosure of student information and other risks to students and staff.
c.
Ethical Use
:
Schools will use AI in an ethical manner avoiding bias and discrimination and promoting responsible use of AI in schools.
d.
Accessibility
:
The use of AI will promote accessibility to students， including in furtherance of the Americans with Disability Act and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act， through the use of assistive technology.
e.
Professional Development:
Staff development will include training to support the effective use of AI in instruction.
f.
Transparency
:
The use of AI will be transparent so that parents/guardians can understand and become knowledgeable of the specific technology used in schools.
g.
Monitoring and Evaluation
:
The Administration will regularly monitor and evaluate the use of AI in instruction to ensure that the technology is achieving the intended instructional goals and to identify areas of improvement.
The use of AI will not replace necessary teaching but instead will be used as a supplemental tool by teachers and instructional staff.
Teachers will assist and monitor student use of AI in the classroom and during instruction， ensuring that it aligns with board policy and applicable law.
The Administration will develop and implement consistent procedures among schools pertaining to the student use of AI， including
the amount of use permitted in specific classes and assignments.
Inappropriate use of AI， including plagiarism， will result in discipline in accordance with board policy， including Board Policy JCDA (Behavior Code).
III.
District Educational Technology
Schools shall effectively integrate District devices and technology into instruction to enhance student learning and advance District goals.
While technology can improve student learning， schools must be cognizant of limiting the use of and dependence on technology to ensure that technology does not negatively impact student growth， including student interpersonal skills， collaboration， creativity， and critical thinking.
Schools will monitor screen time for students to promote independent work， and prevent use of technology that is not academically beneficial or excessive in duration.
The Superintendent will develop additional parameters in an accompanying administrative rule pertaining to the effective integration of technology into instruction and the appropriate use of artificial intelligence.
Review/Reporting
This policy shall be reviewed in accordance with the Board policy review process.

YSD1 and Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to transform the education sector by providing personalized learning experiences， automating administrative tasks， and offering insights into the learning process that allow teachers to focus more on instruction. Recognizing its value as an innovative educational tool， the Board is committed to its responsible and ethical integration in accordance with district policies and state and federal laws， including FERPA， CIPA， COPPA， and IDEA. However， because AI tools are trained on large datasets and can generate inaccurate， inappropriate， or biased outputs， their use will be limited to approved educational purposes requiring human judgment and agency to maintain academic integrity. To foster a safe and supportive learning environment， the district will maintain transparency by informing staff， students， and parents of all related procedures. Ultimately， AI is best understood through the metaphor of an ”electric bike”; a partnership that multiplies the user’s effort while ensuring that the core role of human agency remains in control of the journey
Human Agency and AI Education
To harness the potential of artificial intelligence while preserving the human core of education， we must shift from product-oriented tasks to authentic， learner-driven experiences where AI serves as a collaborative partner， not a replacement for thinking. In connection with the South Carolina Profile of a Graduate， students embodying appropriate utilization of AI apply
World Class Knowledge
to evaluate information， use
World Class Skills
like critical thinking and collaboration to direct tools effectively， and embody
Life and Career Characteristics
by making intentional， ethical decisions with integrity. This balance is reinforced by the 80/20 rule of AI use: while AI can support up to 80 percent of routine tasks like information processing and content generation， the remaining 20 percent must be reserved for the high-value human contributions that require decision-making， personalization， and critical reasoning. Clear， direct， and well-structured use of AI strengthens its effectiveness， but it is this essential human 20 percent that transforms AI from a shortcut into a tool for deeper learning， ensuring individuals take ownership of their work and remain accountable in an AI-rich world.
AI Utilization by Students
In YSD1， AI is viewed as an educational tool that can support learning when used appropriately， ethically， and in alignment with district and teacher expectations. While AI can be a helpful learning partner， it is not always accurate and should not replace a student's own thinking， creativity， or responsibility for learning. AI should be used by students to deepen understanding and explore ideas， while continuing to think critically， verify information， and take responsibility for demonstrating their own learning. When using AI as part of a learning task， students should reflect on how it supported their work and what responsibilities they retain as a learner， considering issues of transparency， fairness， and authorship.
Student Role for Human Agency
For students， human agency is about moving from passive completion to active sense-making， using AI as a ”thinking partner” rather than a replacement for their own intelligence.
Stay in control of your learning: Use AI as a support tool， but rely on your own thinking， judgment， and decisions.
Build World Class Skills: Strengthen critical thinking， creativity， collaboration， and communication when using AI tools.
Follow the 80/20 rule: Let AI help with basic or routine tasks， but complete the most important thinking， problem-solving， and personalization yourself.
Use AI with purpose: Ask clear， thoughtful questions to improve results and deepen your understanding.
Show your thinking: Be prepared to explain， defend， and reflect on your work—even when AI is used.
Take ownership: You are responsible for the final product and the decisions made along the way.

Teachers are responsible for providing age-appropriate training and support to students on the safe and ethical use of AI technologies. This includes educating students on the potential risks and benefits of AI， promoting responsible usage (prompting techniques and various applications of AI)， and guiding them in understanding the ethical implications of AI applications.
Modeling Appropriate AI Use for Students
Educators must serve as role models for ethical and responsible AI use， exemplifying a developmental progression that keeps the
core role of human agency
at the center of all learning. All students can and should learn ABOUT AI in age-appropriate ways before they are ready to learn WITH AI. This modeling follows a clear grade-band trajectory:
Grades K-2:
Learning About AI. Teachers model foundational curiosity and computational thinking by helping students learn about AI indirectly through ”unplugged” and literacy-rich activities. Educators demonstrate how AI exists in the world around us while keeping young learners away from direct chatbot interaction.
Grades 3-5:
Practice Using AI. In teacher-guided， contained environments， educators model how to practice using AI with clear intent. Teachers demonstrate how precise language and ”Clarity in Communication” improve AI responses， guiding students to use these tools as brainstorming partners for structured tasks.
Grades 6-8:
Applying AI Knowledge. Educators transition to coaching students in applying their knowledge， modeling how to critically evaluate， verify， and critique AI outputs for bias and accuracy. Teachers model the shift from simple execution to the ”World Class Skill” of evidence-based justification.
Grades 9-12:
Leading with Highly Effective AI Use. At this level， educators model how to lead through strategic tool selection and transparent， accountable collaboration. Teachers require students to provide a ”Human-AI” disclosure for all work， modeling the Life and Career Characteristic of personal integrity by ensuring students remain fully responsible for the final product’s impact and accuracy.

IJNDC - Artificial Intelligence Responsible Use
Code IJNDC
The board recognizes that artificial intelligence can be a valuable educational tool that can enrich
the district’s instructional program by providing students with innovative and effective learning
experiences when incorporated and used in a responsible and ethical manner.
The use of AI in the instructional program will be limited to approved educational purposes and
will comply with the applicable state and federal laws， including， but not limited to， the Family
Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)， the Children’s Internet Protection Act (CIPA)， the
Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA)， and the Individuals with Disabilities
Education Act (IDEA).
The Board recognizes the potential of AI tools to enhance and transform a student’s educational
and co-curricular experience in the district. However， AI tools are not inherently knowledgeable
and are trained from large amounts of data collected from various sources. Outputs generated by
an AI tool may be inaccurate， inappropriate， or incomplete. Therefore， to ensure the responsible
use of AI and to maintain academic integrity， students shall be required to comply with the
district’s Acceptable Use of Technology Resources. AI platforms and programs will be used in a
manner consistent with district policy， IJNDB， Acceptable Use of Technology Resources.
The district will inform staff members， students， and parents/legal guardians of the district’s policy
and procedures regarding the enforcement of this policy by posting them on the district website
and making them available for review at the district office.
Definitions
For the purposes of this policy， the term “AI programs” encompasses generative artificial
intelligence， open-source artificial intelligence， and any other artificial intelligence computer
systems or programs.
Artificial Intelligence， or “AI，” refers to a computer system that performs tasks that ordinarily
require human intelligence， such as recognizing patterns， learning from experience， drawing
conclusions， and making predictions.
Generative Artificial Intelligence refers to a type of artificial intelligence capable of creating
various types of content (e.g.， visual/audio， text， conversational， and data augmentation)， solving
problems， understanding language， and recognizing patterns by mimicking human intelligence.
For purposes of this policy， Generative AI includes， but is not limited to， applications such as
ChatGPT， Bing AI， Google Gemini， Meta AI， or chatbots.
Open-source Artificial Intelligence refers to AI programs and resources designed for use on
publicly available platforms.
Personally identifiable information includes， but is not limited to， a person’s name， email address，
phone number， social security number， medical information， education records， and information
regarding a student’s individualized education program (IEP) or Section 504 plan.
Acceptable Use
Students may， with permission from the classroom teacher， use AI in the classroom to assist with
completing classroom assignments. Assignments completed using AI may not be submitted as the
student’s original work and should include proper citations. Students should fact-check their work
as AI may not always provide accurate or up-to-date information. The classroom teacher will
oversee the use of AI in the classroom to ensure academic integrity and maintain a balance between
technology and traditional learning methods.
The superintendent or his/her designee will develop procedures to promote student safety and to
ensure that AI programs and resources are not used for any purposes prohibited by law or board
policy. AI programs used in the district schools and educational programs will be evaluated on an
ongoing basis for age-appropriateness， privacy protections， bias， accessibility standards， and data
security by Director of Technology.
Before using any AI programs， staff members must educate themselves. Teachers must only use
AI programs and resources that have been approved for use by the district’s Information and
Technology Department.
Prohibited Uses
Academic Dishonesty
Students are prohibited from obtaining improper assistance from AI programs to complete
assignments， engage in cheating， plagiarism， or any other form of academic dishonesty. Students
are expected to complete assignments independently and without the assistance of generative AI
programs.
The improper use of generative AI programs to complete assignments will be considered a
violation of the student conduct policy.
Privacy Violations
Students will not share personally identifiable or confidential information about themselves， other
students， staff members， or other individuals with AI programs.
Discrimination， Bullying， and Harassment
The district prohibits the use of AI programs for the purpose of harassing， intimidating， or bullying
students or staff members. Students found to be in violation of this policy will be subject to
discipline， up to and including expulsion， consistent with policy JICA， Code of Conduct.
The district prohibits the use of AI programs to discriminate against any individual on the basis of
race， religion， sex (including pregnancy， childbirth， or any related medical conditions)， color，
disability， age， genetic information， national origin， or any other applicable status protected by
local， state， or federal law.
Discipline and Reporting
If any user violates this policy or any related procedures， the student’s access to the district’s
internet system and computers or other technology devices will be suspended， revoked， or denied，
and he or she may be subject to additional disciplinary action. Actions that violate local， state， or
federal law may be referred to local law enforcement.
Warranties/Indemnification
The district makes no warranties of any kind， express or implied， in connection with its provision
of access to and use of its computer networks， the internet， and AI programs provided under this
policy. This policy does not imply endorsement by the district of any AI programs or resources.
The district is not responsible for any information that may be lost， damaged， or stolen when using
AI programs or resources.
The district is not responsible for the dissemination， replication， or alteration of any information
or data input into any AI tool or resource by any student or staff. The district is not responsible for
any unauthorized charges or fees resulting from access or use of AI programs or resources.

The Superintendent or designee， in consultation with district staff， including the district
instructional and technology team， shall develop the district’s comprehensive AI Plan as an
Administrative Rule.
The district’s comprehensive AI Plan will include details addressing the following:
• An approved list of AI programs or tools that may be used by a staff member and students
to enhance learning opportunities， experiences， and task products or outcomes.
• Student Guidelines and Best Practices for AI Use: Clear expectations and best practices
for student use of AI tools during learning experiences， including appropriate purposes，
ethical use， academic integrity， transparency， and limitations of AI when completing
learning tasks.
• Staff Guidelines for Leveraging AI in Instruction: Guidance for staff on how to
effectively and responsibly integrate AI into classroom instruction， including when， how，
and to what extent a staff member may permit or restrict student use of AI tools to support
learning objectives and complete learning tasks.
• A procedure for the district instruction and technology department to approve and review
the use of AI tools and a process to ensure strategies will be implemented in the district to
address inappropriate student use of AI. This may include， but not limited to， areas such
as academic integrity， bias， inaccuracy/misinformation， copyright/licensing unknowns，
privacy violations， and equity of access
• A procedure to inform parents and receive parental consent in the beginning of each
school year for the student to be permitted to use AI during learning experiences and to
complete learning tasks in accordance with this policy and Acceptable Use of
Technology Resources policy (IJNDB)
• A list of prohibited uses of AI that violate this Policy or the district’s Code of Student
Conduct， which may include any use of AI which does not align with the conditions set
during the learning experience or when a learning task is assigned was provided to the
student; using AI to complete an assignment in a way that falsely represents the
assignment as the student’s own; using AI to purposefully create misinformation or to
misrepresent others with the intent of harming， bullying， or intimidating an individual(s);
using AI with confidential student or staff personal information; and other prohibited
behaviors and/or conduct listed in the district’s Acceptable Use of Technology Resources
policy (IJNDB)
• A list of consequences if a student violates any provision of this Policy or AI Plan， which
will be included in the District’s Student Behavior Code， and a procedure to be used by
staff members to address student violations， such as suspected plagiarism or academic
dishonesty while using AI in a student’s assignment;
• A procedure where the district， supervisors， administrative staff members， and other staff
members review the procedures used in determining the activities where AI may be
permitted to be used by students to ensure staff members are implementing AI procedures
in accordance with this Policy and the district’s AI Plan;
The district’s AI Plan will be reviewed and/or revised as needed. In the event the Superintendent
determines a provision(s) of this Policy or the district’s AI Plan becomes inapplicable，
inappropriate， undesirable， and/or irrelevant for any reason in the school setting， the
Superintendent may revise or suspend a provision(s) of this Policy or the district’s AI Plan. In
such case， the Superintendent will report to the Board the reason for the revision or suspension
and recommend the Board ratify the Superintendent’s actions.

AI Acceptable Use Scale
Spartanburg School District Four is committed to fostering an environment of
academic integrity while embracing the evolving landscape of technology. To
ensure clarity and fairness， the following guidelines govern the use of Artificial
Intelligence (AI) within our classrooms. Assignments must be completed without
the use of AI tools unless the teacher provides explicit， written permission for a
specific task. Teachers hold the responsibility for clarifying which uses of AI are
appropriate or prohibited for any given project. Depending on the learning
objectives， a teacher may permit the use of generative AI for some or all parts of
an assignment. To determine the permitted level of involvement， students and
faculty should refer to the Generative AI Acceptable Use Scale. If a student is
uncertain about whether an AI tool is allowed， the student must confirm with their
teacher before proceeding with the work.
Spartanburg School District Four has implemented the Generative AI Acceptable
Use Scale to:
Promote Equity and Responsibility: Ensure that all stakeholders have equitable
access to technology while understanding the ethical implications of
responsible AI use.
Establish Clear Expectations: Build a common language and shared
understanding among students， parents， and staff regarding the role of AI in
the educational process.
Ensure Academic Integrity: Provide a framework for the fair and equitable
treatment of issues related to suspected plagiarism or cheating involving AI in
the educational setting.
10
Spartanburg Four
11
Spartanburg Four
AI Responsible & Prohibited
Use Examples
Level 1: AI Free (Red)
Responsible (YES):
Rashad uses a standard spellcheck tool to correct his rough draft for English class.
Sally copies her teacher’s provided vocabulary list into Quizlet to generate flashcards.
Automated correction and manual scans are considered “standard” spell check tools.
Intelligence Level Spell Check (tools such as Grammarly) are strictly prohibited.
Prohibitive (NO):
Stewart writes an essay and then plugs it into an AI tool to rewrite it for him. This prevents
the teacher from assessing Stewart's actual growth as a writer and violates Spartanburg
School District Four’s Acceptable Use Guide. Level One RED is defined as NO AI assistance
in whole or part.
Level 2: AI Assisted (Yellow)
Responsible (YES):
Zakya uses AI to suggest subpoints for her science research topic. She selects three and
writes the content herself without copy-pasting AI text.
Colby asks AI for an example of a haiku about baseball to understand the format， then
writes his own original poem.
*AI citation required
Prohibitive (NO):
Bob asks AI to rewrite a specific sentence for his history essay because he likes the AI’s
phrasing better， then copies it directly into his paper and violates Spartanburg School
District Four’s Acceptable Use Guide.
Level 3: AI Partnered (Green)
Responsible (YES):
Lisa is working on a science research project and uses AI to generate an original
illustration for one of her slides， including a formal citation for the AI tool.
Prohibitive (NO):
Elena is working on a group presentation on the Revolutionary War and uses AI to create a
speaking character using the voice and image of her teacher without obtaining
permission first and violates Spartanburg School District Four’s Acceptable Use Guide.

Spartanburg Four
Guidelines for Citing and
Disclosing AI Use
Disclosure Statements
Because today’s generative AI tools can not actually create content without
some level of human participation and guidance， it is generally considered
best practice to acknowledge the use or partnership with the AI tool when a
formal citation is not required.
Spartanburg School District Four requires students to acknowledge any
partnership with MagicSchool AI. If traditional citations are not required for
a specific assignment， a disclosure statement must be included in an ”AI
Credits” section.
Educators should clearly outline the expectations for students in their
assignments and provide examples of how to properly cite Al-generated
content.
A link to AI chats can be shared on most major LLM platforms. This is a great
way for teachers to see a student’s learning process and how the student
partnered with the AI to complete work.
Example Disclosure Statements
”Created with editing assistance from MagicSchool AI.”
”I used MagicSchool AI to help me organize my thoughts into a finished
product.”
”Image created in partnership with MagicSchool AI. Prompt: [Insert
Prompt Used].”
13
Spartanburg Four
Informal Citations
If an informal citation is expected， include MagicSchool AI and a link to the
generation.
Example Informal Citation:
MagicSchool. https://app.magicschool.ai/tools/[Tool-Name]?share=[Unique-
Alpha-Numeric-Code]
Formal Citations
If an formal citation is expected， both MLA and APA provide guidance on
their websites for creating citations. Currently most online citation tools do
not include AI in the options. You can ask your LLM to create citations， but as
with anything else， the user will need to verify that the details and format
are correct.
MLA Formal Citation Guidelines
https://bit.ly/ai-mla
APA Formal Citation Guidelines
https://bit.ly/ai-apa-1
14
Spartanburg Four
Grading and Providing
Feedback with AI
Generative AI tools offer the potential to significantly reduce the
administrative burden of grading， a task that traditionally consumes a
substantial portion of an educator's time. By streamlining the evaluation of
student essays， these tools provide efficiency and logistical advantages.
However， it is essential that Spartanburg School District Four educators
maintain diligent oversight to ensure a ”human-in-the-loop” approach. This
human element is vital to guarantee that every student receives a fair，
consistent， and personalized assessment of their work.
Educators must adhere to the following directives regarding AI-assisted
evaluation:
Formative Assessment Only: AI must only be used to provide feedback
on formative tasks. It is strictly forbidden to use AI to assign summative
letter or number grades.
Humans Must Always Be in the Loop: Teachers are required to review all
AI-generated comments for accuracy and tone before they are shared
with students. Human AI Human
Verify Accuracy: AI tools frequently ”hallucinate” errors (e.g.， claiming a
correct sentence is grammatically incorrect). Teachers must verify AI
evaluations against the original student work.
15
Spartanburg Four
Suspected Plagiarism and AI
Detectors
Image credit: Holly Clark of The Infused Classroom
The Problem with Detectors
AI detectors are currently deemed unreliable by the district for the following reasons:
False Positives: Human-written text is frequently flagged as AI-generated， which can
lead to false accusations and damage the student-teacher relationship.
False Negatives: AI-generated text often passes through detectors unnoticed，
providing a false sense of security.
Inability to Validate Origin: These tools can only estimate probability; they cannot
definitively prove the origin of a text.
Alternative Response Strategies
Teachers must use ”Human-First” approaches when AI-plagiarism is suspected:
Non-Accusatory Conversation: Ask the student， ”Can you walk me through your writing
process and how you developed these specific ideas?”
Growth Indicators: Compare the suspicious work against writing samples collected in-
class throughout the year.
Evidence of Learning: If integrity is in question， provide the student an opportunity to
redo the assignment in a supervised， AI-free environment.
*Students found in violation of Spartanburg School District Four’s Acceptable Use Guide
may face disciplinary action in accordance with school-level procedures.
16
Spartanburg Four
Protecting Data Privacy
Personally Identifiable Information (PII) must never be entered into any AI
platform.
Prohibited Information (What NOT to Share):
Identity: Names， addresses， phone numbers， SSNs， or birth dates.
Educational Records: Grades， transcripts， IEPs， or disciplinary records.
Health Information: Medical records， therapy notes， or allergy information.
Financial Info: Family income or bank details.
Photos or Videos: Images or recordings of students.
Communication: Personal logs， emails， or student-teacher messages.
Best Practices for Anonymizing Data*
1.Remove PII: Exclude all identifiers from prompts entirely.
2.Generalize Information: Describe educational needs (e.g.， ”a student struggling
with phonics”) rather than specific student details.
3.Use Hypothetical Scenarios: Create ”mirror” scenarios that reflect a student's
educational context without revealing their identity.
Privacy Protocol: Minimal Disclosure
Even with strict safeguards， data fragments can sometimes be reassembled to
identify an individual. To mitigate this risk， adhere to the principle of data
minimization. Share only the essential information required for context and
support; protecting privacy is most effective when you limit the details provided.
Employees are required to complete annual training regarding FERPA (Family
Educational Rights and Privacy Act).
Questions regarding PII or FERPA should be directed to school adminstration.
*Examples from Eric Curts of Control Alt Achieve
https://www.controlaltachieve.com/2024/03/ai-tools-and-student-data-
privacy.html
17
Spartanburg Four
MagicSchool Guidelines
Spartanburg School District Four’s adopted AI platform for students is
MagicSchool ONLY. Other platforms utilized by students are in direct
violation of Spartanburg School District Four’s Acceptable Use Guide.
Age Restrictions: MagicSchool， an AI platform built for K-12， allows users
of any age. Student users are added to the platform and supervised by
their teacher.
COPPA Compliance: MagicSchool AI and other tools must be used in
accordance with the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act. Use for
students under 13 requires strictly district-approved， ”built-for-
education” models.
Content Appropriateness: MagicSchool utilizes built-in AI moderation
and custom safety features which are continously refined.
AI Literacy: Before any student is permitted to use MagicSchool AI，
students will receive annual instruction on AI literacy (including but not
limited to fact-checking， formal/informal citations， and data privacy
protections) to understand the technology's limitations， ethical
implications， and Spartanburg School District Four’s policies.

AI Guidance for Education Ver. 1.0 Page 4 of 50
(Issued: January 23， 2026)
Part 1: Foundations
A Note on Terminology
This guide uses the term ”AI” (artificial intelligence) throughout. Artificial intelligence is a
broad classification. This guide most often refers to generative AI and the agentic
systems built on top of this technology. See the Glossary for complete definitions.
Introduction & Vision
The tight relationships between school staff and students， and close communities that
exist in Vermont Schools give us a unique advantage in the age of Artificial Intelligence:
we can implement these powerful tools while maintaining the personal connections that
define Vermont education. As AI impacts society， Vermont can model a human-
centered approach， one that uses AI to enhance rather than replace the relationships
between educators， students， and communities. A human-centered approach is
necessary not just to enhance learning， but to protect the cognitive and social
development of students from the risks of over-reliance and automated thinking.
Navigating this transition requires an intentional balance， one that honors the real risks
inherent in adopting these tools by proactively addressing the potential for AI to disrupt
student well-being or academic integrity. This balance is maintained through the
deliberate guardrails of human agency， where experienced educators ensure
technology is used as a tool to support the instructional core. By prioritizing student
learning outcomes and the cultivation of content knowledge expertise， schools ensure
that technological advancement never supersedes the development of human intellect.
Vermont schools have long championed personalized learning through personalized
learning plans (PLP)， proficiency-based learning and project-based learning. AI has the
potential to amplify these strengths in three powerful ways.
Personalizing Learning at Scale - AI technology can adapt to the unique interests and
needs of each learner. Tight integrations of AI with curricular materials can provide
tutoring support， freeing teachers to work individually with students. AI also assists in
providing accommodations for students with special needs by taking notes， providing
support for students with visual or auditory impairments， and assisting students with
speech impairments. Additionally， while adaptive learning systems can adjust the pace
of instruction， AI empowers students in upper grade levels to leverage these tools within
project-based learning to navigate their own individualized learning pathways.
Empowering Educators - AI potentially gives teachers a capable assistant tool that
can simultaneously tutor multiple students， differentiate instruction， and handle routine
tasks. Teachers gain the power to strategically choose what to delegate to AI and what
to handle personally - much like a flipped classroom model but with far more flexibility.
While AI handles skill practice and supports content delivery， teachers can focus on the
AI Guidance for Education Ver. 1.0 Page 5 of 50
(Issued: January 23， 2026)
high-impact moments: guiding discussions， providing emotional support， sparking
creativity， and helping students make meaningful connections. AI technology has the
potential to adapt to each teacher's approach; however， it's up to us as educators to
harness it effectively.
Transforming Student Engagement - AI enables new learning experiences such as
immersive simulations， intelligent project partners， real-time language translation for
multilingual families， and dynamic activities that respond to students’ interests. Students
can collaborate with AI to create， explore， and solve problems in ways that prepare
them for their future.
Why This Guidance Matters for Vermont
This guidance reflects Vermont's commitment to giving all students roots and wings by
grounding students in essential knowledge while preparing them to thrive in a rapidly
changing world. In a world where AI can generate text， solve equations， and retrieve
information instantly， some have asked whether students still need to learn content
deeply. The answer is an emphatic yes.
Students cannot think critically about information they don't understand. They cannot
evaluate AI-generated outputs without the background knowledge to recognize errors，
biases， or gaps. They cannot ask good questions of AI tools without foundational
understanding of the subject matter. Far from making content knowledge obsolete， AI
makes it more essential: the students best positioned to use these tools effectively are
those with strong foundations in reading， writing， mathematics， and disciplinary
knowledge.
The transferable skills defined in the Education Quality Standards and integrated
throughout Vermont’s Portrait of a Graduate relate directly to the skills students need to
be successful in a world transformed by AI. The World Economic Forum's 2025 Future
of Jobs Report shows that employers increasingly value creative thinking， analytical
reasoning， resilience， and curiosity alongside technological literacy. These are not
replacements for traditional academic skills， rather they are built upon them. AI replaces
routine tasks， not the human capacity for judgment， problem-solving， and meaning-
making that strong education develops.
We must confront two false narratives: that AI will solve all of education's challenges，
and that AI will pose only risks to avoid. The greater risk lies in doing nothing， leaving
students without the skills to navigate an AI-integrated world， and leaving educators
without clear guidance on responsible use.
Students need strong content knowledge now more than ever. To be discerning
consumers and ethical users of AI， they must have the background knowledge to
evaluate AI outputs， the critical thinking skills to question what they see， and the
creativity to apply AI as a tool rather than a crutch. AI literacy is not a replacement for
foundational learning; it depends on it.
AI Guidance for Education Ver. 1.0 Page 6 of 50
(Issued: January 23， 2026)
A Note on Using This Guidance
Vermont's approach to AI should be intentional and problem focused. This guidance
explores multiple possibilities. Each school should identify its unique challenges， then
determine which AI tools， if any， best address those needs. Technology should serve
our educational mission， not define it.
Key Concerns for AI in Education
These opportunities don’t come without concerns. While the concerns are highlighted
here， they are explored in detail later in this document， along with strategies to mitigate
each of these concerns.
• Academic integrity considerations
Students may use AI to complete assignments without permission， potentially
bypassing the learning objectives and violating academic honesty policies. Learn
how to address this concern.
• Cognitive offloading
Over-reliance on AI for tasks can prevent students from developing essential
skills through productive struggle and practice. Learn how to find the right
balance.
• Data privacy and security
Student data and intellectual property must be protected when using AI systems
to comply with FERPA， COPPA， and potentially HIPAA requirements. Learn how
to protect student data.
• Bias and fairness
AI systems can perpetuate stereotypes and biases through their training data，
potentially leading to unfair or inaccurate outputs. Learn how to mitigate bias.
• Student well-being and safety
AI can be misused to create harmful content. Deepfakes and non-consensual
images threaten student safety. Learn how to protect students.
• Mental health considerations
Students may develop unhealthy relationships with AI companions， with 72% of
teens having used AI companions at least once. (Common Sense Media， 2025)
Learn how to support healthy AI use.
• Equitable access
Not all students have equal access to AI tools and technology， which potentially
widens achievement gaps. Learn how to support equitable access.
• Ethical considerations
AI raises concerns about intellectual property， environmental impact， and job
displacement that students need to address. Learn how to navigate these issues
with your students.

Developmental Appropriateness of AI
Schools and teachers should feel empowered to determine when student AI usage is
inappropriate; for example， AI chatbots are not developmentally appropriate for all
students. Developmental appropriateness depends on student maturity as well as AI
literacy. The example of a literacy timeline presented here is a modified and condensed
version based on North Carolina’s AI literacy timeline (North Carolina Department of
Public Instruction， 2024).
We can view students’ developmental process through three stages:
1. AI Awareness: The ability to recognize when AI is present in daily life and
understand its basic role as technology trained on data to solve problems.
2. AI Literacy: The technical knowledge， durable skills， and future-ready attitudes
required to engage with， create with， manage， and design AI systems while
critically evaluating their benefits， risks， and ethical implications.
3. AI Fluency: The practical ability to effectively leverage AI as a collaborative tool
through hands-on experience， combining technical understanding with skilled
application in real-world contexts.
School districts and individual schools should feel empowered to modify the timeline
below to meet the needs of their students. These are new technologies and each
school’s readiness for this technology will be different. It is recommended to pilot AI
technologies with students before engaging in larger rollouts.

these guidelines based on their specific context， student populations， and local

Students in grades PreK – 2 should not use AI chatbots.
Teachers may use tools that incorporate AI， such as literacy screening tools or tools for
developing instructional materials.

The Four Principles Framework
This guide is organized around four principles that categorize how AI can be utilized in
education. This is based on work by SREB’s guidance for the use of AI in educational
settings (Southern Regional Education Board， 2025).
1. Using AI to streamline the administrative and planning work of education
2. Using AI to support personalized learning
3. Developing students’ AI Literacy
4. Using AI-infused tools to develop more cognitively demanding tasks that increase
student engagement with creative problem-solving and innovative thinking.
Principle #1: Use AI to streamline administrative and planning work
The first of these principles is using AI to streamline administrative and planning work.
This is not the first because it is the most important or powerful; rather， it is first because
it is the best place for teachers and staff to first gain experience using AI.
Many of these tasks avoid using student data， and they provide ample time for the
educators to review anything generated by AI， making these the ideal use cases for
utilizing AI for the first time. Efficient use of time on administrative tasks can enable
educators to spend more time working directly with students and collaborating with
colleagues.
Opportunities Without Student Data
AI as a Planning Partner
Generative AI tools allow teachers to have a planning partner with vast background
knowledge， excellent writing skills， and the ability to read and analyze lengthy materials.
Some of these use cases include:
• Assistance with aligning class activities to curricular standards
• Editorial review of draft writing
• Brainstorming activities and assignments
Improve and Enhance Current Assignments
Educators can use AI tools to personalize assignments and ask for ideas to increase
cognitive demand， differentiate them for specific learning needs， or provide more
interactive activities. With the click of a few buttons， teachers may also use these tools
to develop slides and graphic organizers or to develop questions based on a reading，
image， or video. AI tools can also create samples of student work based on the
assignment that students can utilize for practicing fact-checking， grammar and tone
editing， and giving feedback.

Support with Other Aspects of Teaching
While lesson and unit planning are essential aspects of a teacher’s job， teachers also
have a myriad of other tasks they need to accomplish each day. AI can act as an editor，
assisting with the tone of emails， editing parent newsletters， and proofreading reports. It
can also support multilingual English learner students by translating assignments and
other learning materials.
Differentiate Course Materials
Educators can develop worksheets and readings at different levels or focus on the
different interests of their students. AI is a tool that can help educators better
differentiate instruction to meet each individual student’s personal learning needs.
Opportunities With Student Data
Caution: Never put student data into an AI system unless the district’s IT department
has vetted that system and has authorized its use in this way.
While most systems today don’t interact directly with district data systems， this will
change in the next few years， with SIS (Student Information System)， LMS (Learning
Management System) and MTSS (Multi-Tiered System of Supports) platforms building
AI integrations directly into their systems enabling new tools for teachers and
administrators that leverage rich and up to date information about students.
Administrative Tasks Related to Student Support
By mining student data， AI can make many processes more efficient. For instance， a
teacher who is preparing personalized updates for parents and guardians can have AI
draft individualized updates， making use of the available data. Administrators who want
to understand their data can use natural language to have a conversation about the
meaning of their data.
Care must be taken when utilizing AI to analyze data. AI systems can make mistakes;
the analysis provided by the AI system should always be verified against the educator's
own understanding of the data.
Providing Feedback on Student Work
AI can instantly provide students with detailed feedback on early drafts of a writing
assignment. Teachers can set up the AI system by providing assignment instructions，
rubrics， examples of student work， and appropriate feedback to provide the AI system
with the context necessary to accomplish the task. The AI can provide feedback on
writing style/quality， supply students with reflective questions to consider for future
drafts and encourage deeper analysis and inquiry.
The main advantage of using an AI is the speed at which students can receive feedback
to improve the writing process. This can be incorporated into the writing process and
combined with writing conferences to support students over multiple drafts.

Generative AI systems are inherently biased， based on their training data. The output

Federal and state laws mandate that districts and schools protect students’ data and

Student Intellectual Property
AI systems， not vetted by school districts， may be training their AI model using data

Cognitive Offloading
When utilizing AI for administrative tasks， educators should ensure that automation

Fact-Checking and Reviewing AI Output
Educators must carefully review all AI-generated output. AI systems demonstrate strong
writing capabilities， which may obscure subtle errors in logic. Generative AI models do
remember precise information， which can result in the model making up facts， including
sources. All facts and references generated by AI require verification. Providing

Principle #3: Develop students’ AI Literacy
AI Literacy refers to the ability to understand， evaluate， and use AI. Several frameworks
exist for teaching AI literacy， including Digital Promise's AI Literacy Framework8， the
AILit Framework9， and CSTA/AI4K12's AI Learning Priorities10. This guidance draws on
Digital Promise's framework for its accessibility and alignment with Vermont's existing
ISTE Standards adoption. Districts interested in deeper computer science integration
may find value in exploring AI4K12's approach.
What is presented here should be viewed as an example approach and is not meant to
be prescriptive.
Understanding AI
Understanding AI means knowing how it works， not through metaphors like ”thinking” or
”learning”; rather， it should be understood mechanistically. Generative AI systems use
data， apply statistical models to identify patterns， and generate outputs by predicting
what comes next. Students benefit from understanding where training data comes from，
how models are built， and why outputs can sound confident despite being incorrect.
Elementary School Example
Using Google's Teachable Machine， students train a simple image classifier to
recognize different hand gestures. Students quickly discover that training requires far
more examples than they expected: a few photos aren't enough. The model needs
dozens of images from different angles， distances， and lighting conditions to work
reliably. When it fails， students can diagnose the problem and improve the training data
themselves. This hands-on experience builds intuition for how AI learns from patterns in
data rather than from understanding， and why robust training requires more data than
most people assume.
Secondary School Example
In a social studies unit， students examine how algorithmic curation shapes public
discourse. The class studies documented examples showing how trending algorithms
can surface different stories to different communities. Students analyze primary
sources: excerpts from Congressional testimony by tech executives， summaries of
academic research on filter bubbles， or journalist investigations of algorithmic
amplification. Students discuss the civic implications that arise when citizens in the
same community encounter different information landscapes.

Evaluating AI
Evaluating AI means critically assessing outputs for accuracy， bias， and
appropriateness. This includes asking: Is this information correct? Whose perspectives
are represented or missing? Is AI the right tool for this task?
Students' skills evaluating AI develop most naturally through disciplinary practice. Nick
Potkalitsky describes this as the ”knowledge asymmetry problem”11: students can only
catch AI errors in domains where they have genuine expertise. When students compare
an AI-generated historical summary with primary sources， they strengthen both
historical thinking and AI evaluation skills simultaneously. When they check an AI
explanation of a scientific concept against their experimental observations， they deepen
both their science understanding and their critical stance toward AI.
Elementary School Example
A third-grade science class observing plants might record what they notice (leaf shape，
stem characteristics， flower placement)， then compare their observations with an AI-
generated plant description. What did AI get right? What did it miss? What can only be
known through direct observation? This teaches students that AI predicts based on
patterns while scientists verify with evidence. This is a foundational AI literacy concept
embedded naturally within existing science standards.
Secondary School Example
In a social studies class studying the American West， the teacher might ask AI to
describe life in frontier towns or generate images of the American West， then have
students examine the response against primary sources like diaries， photographs， and
census records. Students learn that AI reflects patterns in its training data， developing
biases and stereotypes， which can overrepresent popular narratives and
underrepresent marginalized perspectives.
Using AI
Using AI means making informed decisions about when and how to employ AI tools.
Digital Promise identifies three types of use: interacting with AI， creating with AI， and
problem-solving with AI.
The skills of using AI line up with the ISTE Student Standards， which have been
updated to cover AI usage for learning. Many Vermont schools will be able to integrate
the skills of using AI into their existing digital literacy curriculum.
Secondary School Example

Principle #4: Use AI-infused tools for cognitively demanding tasks
These use cases are generally not recommended for elementary students， and in many
cases， middle school students. See developmental appropriateness of AI for details.
Overview
AI opens opportunities for students to engage in sophisticated intellectual work that
would be difficult or impossible to accomplish independently. This principle goes beyond
using AI as a tool; it positions AI as a thinking partner that enables students to tackle
complex problems， engage in deeper analysis， and explore ideas at a level of
sophistication previously reserved for advanced study.
When implemented effectively， AI becomes a cognitive amplifier. Students can engage
in Socratic dialogues where AI challenges their reasoning， participate in complex
simulations and debates with an adaptive opponent， teach concepts to an AI that asks
probing questions， and reflect on their learning with a partner that helps identify patterns
and blind spots. These interactions require students to think more deeply， defend their
reasoning more rigorously， and examine their assumptions in ways that traditionally
required one-on-one mentorship from a teacher or subject expert.
This approach fundamentally shifts what we can expect from student work. When
students have access to an AI thinking partner， the bar for acceptable work rises
significantly. A research paper should demonstrate more sophisticated analysis. A
problem-solving exercise should tackle greater complexity. A creative project should
show a deeper exploration of possibilities.
However， this principle requires careful implementation. Students need strong
foundational knowledge and well-developed AI literacy skills before they can effectively
collaborate with AI on complex tasks. The goal is to develop students who can leverage

AI to extend their intellectual reach while maintaining ownership of their learning and
demonstrating genuine understanding. This is most appropriate for grades 9-12， where
students have developed the metacognitive skills necessary to engage AI as a true
intellectual partner rather than a crutch.
In addition， teachers should incorporate formative assessment structures for assessing
student learning. In class conferencing， student presentations， class discussion and
student reflections should be used to focus on what the student learned from the
activity.
Opportunities
Interactive Learning Partnerships
AI can engage students as a Socratic partner， challenging their thinking through
targeted questioning and counterarguments. Students defend complex positions，
identify flaws in reasoning， and navigate philosophical or ethical dilemmas with AI
pushing their logic. This goes beyond simple Q&A—students must articulate nuanced
arguments and respond to sophisticated challenges that adapt to their reasoning.
Teaching Through Role Reversal
Students solidify their understanding by teaching concepts to an AI that plays the role of
an intelligent but naive learner. The AI asks probing ”why” and ”what if” questions that
reveal gaps in student understanding， forcing students to examine assumptions and
edge cases. For example， a student explaining a physics concept must respond to AI
questions about real-world applications and theoretical limits， deepening their own
comprehension through the act of teaching. It is helpful to use a well-crafted AI prompt
like the one Ethan Mollick has shared12.
Complex Simulations and Debates
AI can serve as an adaptive opponent or partner in sophisticated scenarios. Students
might argue historical positions against an AI representing opposing viewpoints with
historically accurate counterarguments， negotiate complex business deals where AI
adapts its strategy based on student moves， or navigate evolving ethical dilemmas
where AI introduces complications that challenge initial moral stances. These
interactions develop critical thinking and argumentation skills at levels difficult to achieve
through traditional assignments.
Collaborative Problem-Solving and Creation
Students work with AI to tackle problems beyond their independent capabilities. In
scientific inquiry， AI helps generate hypotheses and analyze data while students design
experiments and interpret results. For complex writing projects， students produce initial

Part 3: Responsible AI Usage
Risk Mitigation Strategies
Risk of Doing Nothing
Schools that avoid addressing AI usage expose themselves to a different set of risks.
Students are more likely to use AI systems outside of school without any guidance or AI
literacy training. Staff may utilize public AI systems in ways that risk data privacy.
Students will graduate unprepared for a world that is being radically transformed by AI.
Doing nothing also introduces equity and access issues， as some students have access
to strong AI models and develop the skills to use them， while others do not.
The risks of using AI described below are real; however， this is not a reason for inaction.
There are steps that can be taken to minimize each of the concerns below.
Academic Honesty
Academic honesty concerns are the single most cited concern related to AI amongst
school leaders. Students， who may have previously reached out to friends or siblings，
can now turn to AI for help. Despite this， an ongoing research study by Stanford
researchers suggested that cheating amongst U.S. High Schoolers did not increase with
the release of ChatGPT (Spector， 2023).
Schools need to have a consistent strategy for promoting academic honesty; it is much
more difficult for each teacher to address these issues independently. Developing these
strategies are important discussions for school leaders to facilitate amongst their faculty.
AI can be utilized on assignments in multiple ways. It is not as clear-cut as simply
saying， “AI usage is not allowed.” AI is being baked into the word-processing
applications that students utilize every day. Does using a grammar check count as AI
usage? What about Grammarly， a product that goes beyond the classic grammar
check? What about a student who uses AI to help conduct research or to explain a
concept to them?
To respond to these concerns:
• Be clear that there are times when the use of AI by students is inappropriate.
Teachers should feel empowered to tell their students that the use of AI is
inappropriate in these situations.
• Review academic honesty policies with respect to AI. AI for education has a
helpful short guide for drafting an AI academic policy at your school14.

• Discuss how students should cite AI usage. Both MLA and APA now have
formats for citing AI use. Educators should inform students whether they should
save and submit their AI chat logs.
• Foster transparency by having educators lead by example， modeling
transparency and academic honesty about their own use of generative AI tools.
• Encourage teachers to focus on ”process” over ”product.” Students often seek
help in getting the product completed， but this is the mere artifact of the learning
process. Teachers can focus on the process by asking students to reflect on their
learning， providing in-class one-on-one feedback on early drafts or stages of
work， and asking students to show and explain their work. Teachers should
include this ”process” as part of their assessment and grading， which refocuses
students on the learning process and not simply completing the ”work.”
• Determine how teachers currently handle AI usage and discuss a common
language that can be utilized. Instead of accusing a student of cheating， these
situations are best handled with curiosity， asking more about the student’s
process and how they developed their product.
• Encourage teachers to move more assessments into class time and not use
homework as the sole means of grading. Beyond tests and quizzes， this can
include formative assessments like writing conferences， class presentations，
structured class discussions， reflective writing prompts， etc. Activities like this
support active learning and are good teaching practices.
• Consider AI-resistant assignments. Assignments involving reflection or
discussion of class experiences cannot easily be completed by AI without effort
from the student.
• Treating the academic honesty issue as a cry for help from students can be very
effective. Most often， students in these situations are confused by the material
and overwhelmed by the pressure to stay on top of their coursework. They need
to be provided with a means to catch up with the class and support to better
understand the course content.
• Do not rely on AI auto-detection tools. These tools are not reliable enough to be
used in academic honesty disputes， sometimes show false positives， and they
are easily bypassed by students.
• Developing consistent messaging to explain how AI usage can occur on an
assignment is important. Many schools have discovered that a more nuanced
scale of AI usage is preferable to a simple traffic light system. One of the better-
known examples is the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS). Lamoille South Supervisory
Union developed their own Student Generative AI Acceptable Usage Menu for
their teachers， which is presented here as a positive example that provides clear
guidance for teachers. Schools are encouraged to develop their own scales，
using either the AI Assessment Scale or LSSU's menu as a starting point.

Cognitive Offloading
AI gives us the ability to ”cognitively offload” tasks， essentially outsourcing our thinking
to a tool. For professionals， this is a powerful way to increase efficiency and yield a
superior final product. For students， however， offloading the wrong tasks can interfere
with learning and skill development.
The central challenge for educators is to determine when AI serves as a valuable
learning tool and when it becomes a crutch that hinders skill development. As author
and researcher Ethan Mollick discusses in his post， “Against Brain Damage，”15 improper
use of AI can inadvertently prevent students from engaging in the productive struggle
necessary for learning. Just as we wouldn’t want a student to use a calculator when
they are first learning multiplication and division， there are situations where AI usage，
particularly open unstructured AI usage， is harmful to the learning process. Teachers
should feel empowered to say when AI usage is inappropriate.

The decision to use AI should be driven by the lesson's learning objectives. Before

1. What are the primary skills I want students to develop with this activity?
2. Will AI's role in this task help them practice that skill， or will it perform the skill for
them?

• Education-specific AI platforms tailored to your activity or AI， with an initial
prompt created by the teacher， can provide a structure to ensure that AI is
supporting the learning process
• When students use general-purpose AI， teachers need to be able to structure
and teach students how to use these AI systems. This requires a greater level of
AI literacy for both the teacher and the students.
• We need to teach students to lean into the hard work of learning. We know from
research that learners are not always the best judges of how well they are
learning a topic. Vox created a great video that explores this topic through a
series of interviews with students and teachers16.
Data Privacy
Schools need to protect student data， conforming to both FERPA and COPPA. In
addition， generative AI uses data to train AI systems， and schools should be concerned
about the intellectual property of students being utilized to train these systems.
Providing teachers and students with approved， secure AI systems is one of the best
ways to protect student data. A separate section of this guide covers tool vetting in
depth. When schools do not provide official tools and clear instructions for these tools，
teachers and students will be tempted to utilize public AI systems instead.
It is not enough to remove student-identifiable information before submitting student
work to an AI system. This still exposes the student’s intellectual property to the system.
SU/SDs should have a privacy agreement with vendors that include promises not to
train AI models based on chat conversations. This is the case for education-specific AI
systems as well as generic systems with AI versions (Gemini for Education).
Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) data (medical data) is a
particular concern， as it has requirements that are not a part of FERPA or COPPA. Most
educational AI systems have not been designed to comply with HIPAA. In many cases，
it is simpler for schools to avoid the use of AI for HIPAA protected data. In the future， it

Mental Health Risks
There are real concerns that people can form unhealthy relationships with AI systems.
Kids， who may be seeking companionship， can find these systems very appealing. As
these systems integrate voice communication and avatars， this may be a part of a
growing problem. Common Sense Media17 reports that 72% of U.S. teens have used AI
companions at least once (Common Sense Media， 2025) and they recommend that
teens avoid using AI companions18.
The same report outlines concerns for these companion style apps， with one third of
teens using AI for social interaction and relationships. For example， 12% report that
they can say things to AI that they can’t talk about with friends and family. The report
asks that educators take the lead on digital literacy to help kids safely navigate an AI-
powered world. The APA (American Psychological Association) issued a health
advisory19 on similar notes， which outlines these concerns.
AI is not a substitute for professional mental healthcare20. While nearly half of students
with mental health challenges report using AI for counseling21， these systems lack the
nuanced empathy， cultural competence， and crisis-response capabilities of trained
professionals. School staff should emphasize that 'simulated empathy' cannot replace
the genuine human connection and clinical expertise found in school-based services. To
ensure student safety， staff must proactively direct students to school counselors， social
workers， or psychologists for confidential， evidence-based support.
School leaders may need to navigate students having unhealthy interactions with AI
outside of school time and need to support families navigating these issues. One
example is the increasingly popular toys for young kids with AI embedded in the
product. Kids can form intense relationships with these toys when they do not yet have

Student Well-Being and Safety
AI can be used for misinformation， and these uses can threaten students’ well-being
and safety. Deepfakes and non-consensual intimate images (NCII) can be generated to
malign and cyberbully students.
The Center for Democracy and Technology issued a report， “In Deep Trouble: Surfacing
Tech-Powered Sexual Harassment in K-12 Schools”25. The report identified non-
consensual intimate images as a significant problem in K12. Female and Lesbian， Gay，
Bisexual， Transgender， and Queer/Questioning (LGTBQ+) students were the most
concerned about non-consensual images and had lower confidence in their school’s
ability to prevent and respond to deepfakes. (Report – In Deep Trouble: Surfacing Tech-
Powered Sexual Harassment in K-12 Schools， 2024)
School leaders should assess what policies in their student handbook and district
policies cover this behavior， and how they can potentially respond. The Center for
Democracy and Technology released a model policy and resources26 that can serve as
a resource.

Bias and Fairness
Generative AI models are trained on huge corpuses of data; in the case of large
language models， this includes all quality text on the internet as well as other text the AI
company can access. Baked into this text are a lot of pre-existing biases and
stereotypes. The text is also detached from real world experience. AI companies further
train their AI on sample conversations， and while these are meant to mitigate bias， they
can often introduce unforeseen outcomes. These factors lead to models that
incorporate biases and stereotypes. In addition， generative AI is probabilistic in nature，
always generating different output even given the same input.
Educators and students need to use these models， keeping these potential biases in
mind. AI systems are excellent writers， which means that they sound convincing even
when they are incorrect.
Some mitigation techniques include:
• Provide a way for teachers and students to provide feedback on the AI system.
Survey teachers and students to determine if they encounter bias when using an
AI system.
• Provide AI literacy training for staff & students， including digital literacy training
covering how to verify data.
• Ensure that a human is responsible for reviewing the output (a separate section
addresses human oversight)
To explore bias， stereotyping， and logical blind spots in AI systems， consider the
following prompts:
